collections.label: The Legal Test and the Craft It Produced

entries.name: The Four Axes
entries.description: Erotica does not have one taxonomy. It has four, and they are orthogonal.
entries.principle: A work in this form occupies one position on each of four independent axes — literary mode (what kind of made thing this is), relational contract (what it promises about the ending), content domain (what is depicted), and market formation (who published it and for whom). Almost every confusion in the popular guidance about the form is a collision between two of them.
entries.example: "BDSM erotica" names a content domain; "the Black Lace list" names a market formation; "the erotic memoir" names a mode; "no happy ending" names a contract. A single book sits somewhere on all four at once, and a taxonomy that mixes them produces categories that cannot be reasoned about.
entries.application: Before placing your book, answer the four questions separately. If a subgenre label you are given cannot be resolved onto one axis, it is a marketing term rather than a category, and it will not tell you anything about how to write the next chapter.

entries.name: The Literary Erotic Novel
entries.description: Book-length erotic fiction published and reviewed inside literary rather than genre infrastructure.
entries.principle: The mode whose practitioners most often deny being in the genre at all. Its distinguishing feature is not explicitness or quality but *reception apparatus*: it is reviewed in literary pages, shelved outside the category, and judged by criteria that treat the erotic content as a subject the book is about rather than a service the book performs.
entries.example: The mode's characteristic problem is visible in the Bad Sex in Fiction Award, which ran from 1993 to 2019 and deliberately excluded pornography and erotica in order to target serious literary novelists — an anti-incentive aimed at exactly this mode and at no other.
entries.application: Decide which apparatus you are writing into, because it determines what your explicit passages will be read as. The same scene is a craft achievement in one and an embarrassment in the other, and the difference is not in the prose.

entries.name: The Libertine Dialogue and the Philosophical Demonstration
entries.description: Erotic writing as argument — the dialogue, the demonstration, the systematic transgression with a thesis.
entries.principle: The oldest continuous mode in the Western tradition, in which sexual material is the vehicle for a philosophical position rather than the object of the writing. Its structural marker is the *demonstration*: a proposition is stated, enacted, and then discussed by the participants, and the discussion is not an interruption but the point.
entries.example: The mode is still funded and still named: the Prix Sade, founded in 2001 by Lionel Aracil and Frédéric Beigbeder, awards contemporary literature and what it calls contemporary libertinism, and its laureates include essayists and documentary writers as readily as novelists.
entries.application: If you write in this mode, the argument must be falsifiable inside the book — a demonstration that no character can contest is a lecture. And know that the mode's readers arrive expecting the discussion, so cutting it to accelerate the scenes removes the thing they came for.

entries.name: Erotic Memoir and the Confessional
entries.description: Non-fiction first person, in which the writer rather than a character bears the exposure.
entries.principle: The mode carries a truth-contract the fictional modes do not, and with it two problems fiction never has: third-party consent, since the other people in the account did not agree to appear, and the impossibility of revision, since the events cannot be improved for structure. What it buys in return is the only claim to authority the form has.
entries.example: The subculture's own award structure treats non-fiction as a first-class form rather than an adjunct, running separate honours for the book-length work and the article — a field organised around the made object recognising that this mode is a made object too.
entries.application: Decide your obligation to the other people in the account before you draft, not at the copy-edit. And treat the impossibility of revision as a structural constraint rather than a limitation: the shape the events actually had is the only shape you may use, and finding what it was is most of the work.

entries.name: The Short Story and the Anthology
entries.description: The form's economic backbone for thirty years, and the place a new writer actually enters it.
entries.principle: Erotica is more short-form than any adjacent genre, and the anthology is a made thing with an author — the editor — rather than a container. The mode's craft demand follows from its length: a story with no room for a courtship must generate its own stakes in a page, which is why the form leans so heavily on situation, institution and prior relationship.
entries.example: The field's only form-based award scheme honours the short fiction and the anthology *separately*, which is the tradition telling you the two are different achievements.
entries.application: Write to the anthology's brief rather than around it — the editor's frame is the collaboration, not a constraint on it. And in a short work, establish the constraint before the encounter: the reader must know what is at stake by the time anything happens, because there is no room to explain afterwards.

entries.name: Erotic Poetry
entries.description: Ancient, continuous, and sustained almost entirely by literary rather than commercial institutions.
entries.principle: The mode with the longest unbroken line and the smallest market. Its craft advantage over prose is compression — a poem can hold an erotic charge without narrating an event, which is the effect prose has to work hardest for — and its structural constraint is that it cannot escalate, so it must find its whole shape in a single movement.
entries.example: The classical erotic-verse line runs through Sappho, Catullus and Ovid and has never fully lapsed; the modern mode is carried by literary presses and prize schemes rather than by any genre market, and no general erotica award has ever had a poetry category.
entries.application: Use compression as the mode's actual tool rather than treating it as brevity. And do not expect the commercial apparatus of the prose form to apply — this mode is published, reviewed and rewarded by a different set of institutions entirely.

entries.name: Serial and Episodic Erotica
entries.description: The chaptered, cliffhangered form — from the Victorian part-issue to the contemporary platform serial.
entries.principle: A mode defined by the interval between instalments rather than by content. The serial cannot rely on a reader holding the whole shape in mind, so it repeats its premise, ends each unit on an unresolved escalation, and accumulates rather than develops — which makes it unusually vulnerable to the form's characteristic failure of repetition without change.
entries.example: The Victorian clandestine trade ran on part-issue publication, and the structural habits it produced — the recap, the instalment-ending threshold, the indefinitely extensible cast — reappear intact in the platform serial a century and a half later.
entries.application: Give each instalment one state change that survives into the next, and write the recap as characterisation rather than summary. The mode's readers tolerate repetition of situation; they do not tolerate repetition of state.

entries.name: Fan-Fiction Erotica and the Archive
entries.description: Non-commercial, community-moderated, enormous, and the pipeline into everything else.
entries.principle: The largest body of erotic writing currently being produced sits outside the commercial market entirely, on archives that are free to read and free to publish into. Its economics invert the commercial form's: there is no gatekeeper, no advance and no scarcity, so the constraints that shape it are social and infrastructural rather than editorial — the tag, the kudos, the comment, and the platform's own terms of service.
entries.example: The tagging and content-warning apparatus these communities invented is materially more granular than any retailer's classification scheme, and it is author-applied rather than imposed — a working solution to the signalling problem the commercial market has never solved.
entries.application: Read the tag vocabulary as craft information rather than as metadata: it is the most detailed public record that exists of what readers of this form actually seek and avoid. And note that the platform's terms of service are the operative constraint here, which makes them this mode's censorship regime.

entries.category: The Ending Contract and Its Seams
entries.name: The Ending Contract
entries.description: The pack's spine. What this form promises about the ending is nothing, and everything follows from that.
entries.principle: Erotica makes no guarantee about where the arc lands. That single absence is what separates it from its nearest neighbour and what creates its hardest craft problem, because the form has no native mechanism for ending: the sexual sequence is repeatable and therefore cannot conclude itself, so every ending must be imported from outside it.
entries.example: The absence is legible in the market as well as on the page. The categories that guarantee an ending have a formal apparatus — retailer codes, category lines, reader expectations enforced by review — and the categories that do not have almost none, because there is no promise for an institution to police.
entries.application: Choose your ending deliberately and early, because it is not implied by anything in the sexual material. Then check that nothing in the first chapter accidentally promises a different one — a reader who infers a guarantee you never made will report the book as broken.

entries.category: The Ending Contract and Its Seams
entries.name: Seam One: Erotica and Erotic Romance
entries.description: The boundary the field itself draws, and does not hold steady.
entries.principle: The distinction turns on the ending alone: erotic romance requires a happy-ever-after or happy-for-now, and erotica carries no such requirement. Passionate Ink, the erotic-fiction authors' body that separated from the Romance Writers of America in 2005, states the requirement plainly and also records that the older publisher definition has changed as mainstream heat has risen — so the line is contested and drifting rather than settled, and this card takes no side on where it currently sits.
entries.example: The same body's own working test — whether the sexual content could be removed without damaging the plot — settles erotic romance against merely steamy romance, and does not settle erotic romance against erotica, because both would fail it.
entries.application: State your ending contract where a reader sees it before purchase. The most reliably reported complaint at this seam is not explicitness in either direction; it is a reader who expected a guarantee and did not get one. The guaranteed-ending side of this seam is the romance pack's; the hand-off card for it is `subgenre-20`.

entries.category: The Ending Contract and Its Seams
entries.name: Seam Two: Erotica and Pornography
entries.description: A value distinction rather than a formal one, and the field knows it.
entries.principle: No stable formal property separates the two. The distinction in general use is evaluative — one framing holds that erotica differs from pornography as love does from rape, another that erotic literature simply offers a more plausible depiction of human sexuality — and both are widely held, both are contested, and neither can be applied to an unseen text to sort it.
entries.example: The instability is visible in the vocabulary: the same books are called erotica by their publishers, pornography by their critics and smut by their readers, with the last currently carrying no pejorative weight at all among the people using it.
entries.application: Notice which of the two framings a given piece of guidance assumes, because it determines what that guidance will tell you to cut. This card records the dispute and does not adjudicate it; a writer needs to know the argument exists more than they need a ruling on it.

entries.category: The Ending Contract and Its Seams
entries.name: Seam Three: Erotica and Literary Fiction That Contains Sex
entries.description: Where the awards actually draw the line, and where the misattribution risk is highest.
entries.principle: The operative distinction here is institutional rather than textual: a book is treated as literary fiction containing sex when it is published, reviewed and judged by literary apparatus, and as erotica when it is not. Because the distinction is carried by institutions rather than by the page, it is the seam at which credits, prizes and shelf categories are most often misattributed in both directions.
entries.example: The clearest evidence is an award that policed the boundary from the literary side for twenty-six years by mocking sexual writing in serious novels while explicitly excluding erotica from consideration — a prize whose whole design assumed the two were separate populations.
entries.application: Establish which apparatus a comparison title actually sits in before you use it as a model, because its craft choices were made for that apparatus. And never accept a prize credit at this seam without naming the category and the year.

entries.name: BDSM and Power Exchange as a Written Tradition
entries.description: Explicit depiction of negotiated dominance and submission, carried by a literary institution of its own.
entries.principle: A written tradition with its own presses, its own canon and its own award structure, distinct from the mass-market version that reached general readers after 2011. Its craft signature is that the negotiation is dramatised rather than assumed: the terms are stated, contested and revised on the page, and the scene's tension comes from the terms rather than from their absence.
entries.example: The subculture's award scheme is the strongest evidence that this is a parallel literary institution rather than a subgenre of romance — it is organised by form rather than by content and names its honours after its own authors and organisations, which is canon-formation by nomenclature.
entries.application: Write the negotiation as the charged scene rather than as paperwork before the charged scene. And distinguish which tradition you are writing into, because the two have different conventions about what may be left unsaid, and a reader arriving from one will misread the other's silences.

entries.name: Queer Erotica: The Gay Men's Line
entries.description: A publishing history that ran parallel to the mainstream rather than inside it.
entries.principle: The line developed its own presses, its own distribution and its own canon under legal conditions materially different from those governing the general market, so its conventions are not a variation on the mainstream form — they are answers to a different set of constraints. Its craft inheritance is heavier on the explicit and on the community-facing than the general literary line, because for long periods those were the only venues available.
entries.example: The tradition names its own figures in its institutions, including an award for short fiction named for an author who was both a novelist and an editor of the field — the same canon-by-nomenclature pattern the wider erotic field uses.
entries.application: Read the tradition's own presses and periodicals rather than its mainstream reception, which is thin and late. And treat its legal history as craft history: the conventions were shaped by what could be posted, stocked and imported.

entries.name: Queer Erotica: The Lesbian and Sapphic Line
entries.description: A separate market, separate institutions, and a separate legal threshold.
entries.principle: The sapphic line is not the gay men's line with the participants changed. It has its own presses, its own award apparatus and — critically — a different legal history, because the works that were prosecuted in this line were often prosecuted for what they depicted socially rather than for anything explicit on the page.
entries.example: The Well of Loneliness was prosecuted despite containing nothing explicit, which establishes that this line's legal threshold has at times been about the relationship rather than the description — a different test from the one applied to the rest of the form.
entries.application: Do not import the general form's assumptions about what makes a passage risky. And note that the community's own award structures run inside sapphic literary societies rather than inside erotica institutions, which is where this line's canon is actually recorded.

entries.name: Queer Erotica: Trans, Bi and Non-Binary Lines
entries.description: The most recently institutionalised lines, and the ones whose category vocabulary is still moving.
entries.principle: These lines are carded together not because they are one thing but because their institutional recognition arrived together and late, and because the category vocabulary that names them is still in active revision by the people it describes. The craft consequence is that a writer cannot rely on a stable label to signal the book, and must signal in the text and the front matter instead.
entries.example: The major identity-based award scheme consolidated its separately-gendered erotica honours into a single category over time, which is a taxonomy fact as much as an administrative one — the scheme's own view of how the lines relate changed.
entries.application: Signal specifically rather than by category name, because the category names are contested and are read differently by different parts of the readership. And check the currency of any vocabulary you take from a reference work, including this one.

entries.name: Erotic Horror
entries.description: Works in which the erotic is the organising subject and horror is the register — not the reverse.
entries.principle: The boundary runs on which element is doing the organising. Where fear is the subject and the erotic is one of its instruments, the work belongs to horror; this pack holds the works where desire is the engine and dread is the atmosphere it runs in. The distinction matters because the two produce opposite structural demands: horror needs the threat to escalate, and this form needs the wanting to.
entries.example: The interaction the mode depends on — that arousal decays more slowly than the emotion producing it, so a frightening scene intensifies whatever follows — is established in the media-response literature and belongs to the horror pack, which cards it directly.
entries.application: Decide which element resolves at the end, because that is the one your reader will treat as the subject. And where you are borrowing the fear/arousal interaction, know that you are working with a documented effect rather than an intuition. The fear-as-subject side is the horror pack's; the hand-off card for it is `subgenre-24`.

entries.name: Historical Erotica
entries.description: Two different things that share a shelf: erotica set in the past, and the historical erotic text as a source.
entries.principle: The first is a contemporary work using a period setting, and its craft problem is the ordinary historical-fiction problem of research and anachronism. The second is the period text itself, read as a model — and it is the more useful of the two to a working writer, because the older conventions were answers to constraints that no longer apply and are therefore available as technique rather than as habit.
entries.example: The frame narrative — the found manuscript, the letters, the confession, the deposition — is the clearest case: it was a deniability device under obscenity regimes, adopted for legal reasons and now available for structural ones.
entries.application: Be clear which of the two you are writing, because they have different failure modes. And when you borrow a period convention, find out what it was originally solving; a device adopted for a legal reason will not do structural work unless you give it some.

entries.name: Speculative Erotica
entries.description: Non-human, monstrous and science-fictional bodies, as a continuous tradition rather than a recent market.
entries.principle: The domain's craft advantage is that an unfamiliar body makes description necessary again: the reader has no default to fill in, so the writing has to specify, and specification is what the form's prose most often lacks. Its characteristic failure is the inverse — cataloguing the difference instead of dramatising what the difference costs or permits.
entries.example: The tradition is old and continuous, and is not to be confused with the short, platform-native commercial form that emerged after 2013 and was then reshaped by a retailer's content policy — that is a market formation, and it is carded separately.
entries.application: Make the unfamiliarity structural rather than decorative: if the body's difference does not change what the characters can do, want or fear, you have written a costume. And separate the tradition from the market moment when you look for models.

entries.name: The Courtship Promise and the Guaranteed Ending
entries.description: The sex scene inside a courtship, and heat as a reader contract.
entries.principle: Where the sexual material serves a relationship arc that is promised to resolve, the craft question changes completely: every scene is measured against what it does to the couple's state, and the heat level functions as a contract with the reader rather than as a property of the prose. That whole apparatus belongs to the romance pack, which cards it in detail.
entries.example: The receiving pack owns the sex scene as a state change, the closed door as a technique, escalation as emotional rather than explicit, point of view inside the scene, the vocabulary problem, negotiation before the act, specific bodies, the scene that fails, scene frequency, writing desire without sex, and a full block on consent, power and safety.
entries.application: If your book guarantees its ending, work from that pack rather than this one — its craft rules assume the guarantee and ours do not. This subject is handed off to the `romance-reference` pack.

entries.name: Intimacy in Period
entries.description: Period-accurate depiction of intimacy, and the consent history that goes with it.
entries.principle: Depicting intimacy inside a historical setting raises a problem this pack does not own: how to render a period's actual constraints accurately without adopting its position on them. That is a historical-fiction craft question and the historical pack cards it directly, together with the screen for checking it.
entries.example: The receiving pack owns both the craft card on intimacy and sex in period and the checklist that audits a draft against the period's consent history.
entries.application: Use this pack for what desire is doing structurally and that pack for whether the period would have permitted it, in those words, to those people. This subject is handed off to the `historical-reference` pack.

entries.name: The Adult Comics System
entries.description: The Japanese adult-comics tradition, its magazines, its circuit and its jurisdiction.
entries.principle: The largest adult-comics market in the world is a complete publishing system — demographic magazines, a serialisation economy, an amateur circuit that feeds it, and its own censorship jurisdiction — and it is owned entire by the manga pack, which cards all four. This pack cards no manga at all and declares that medium a zero.
entries.example: The receiving pack owns the transgressive line in that tradition, the amateur circuit as a talent pipeline, the demographic categories and the card on jurisdiction and ordinance.
entries.application: Do not treat that tradition as a variant of the Anglophone one; its constraints, its formats and its legal position are different at every level. This subject is handed off to the `manga-reference` pack.

entries.name: The Obscenity Trial as a Writer's Biography
entries.description: Prosecution as a fact about a life and a movement, rather than as a fact about the law.
entries.principle: The obscenity trials appear twice in this library and the split is clean. Where the prosecution is a fact about an author's life or about a literary movement's circulation, it belongs to the literary pack, which cards it that way. Where the legal test itself shaped a compositional convention, it stays here.
entries.example: The receiving pack cards the little magazine prosecuted over its serialisation, and cards prosecuted authors as prosecuted authors — the biography, the movement and the circulation history.
entries.application: Use that pack for what happened to the writer and this one for what the ruling did to the writing. This subject is handed off to the `literary-reference` pack.

entries.name: Horror as the Register, Not the Subject
entries.description: Dread, revulsion, the reader's consent, and the craft of extremity.
entries.principle: Where fear is the organising subject, the work is horror's, and so is a substantial apparatus this pack must not restate: the argument for what unmediated extremity achieves, the mechanism by which arousal outlasts its cause, the standing critique of sexual violence as a device, and the technique of writing a body through what it can no longer do.
entries.example: The receiving pack owns transgression as craft, excitation transfer, the field's standing failure on sexual violence, and the body written through lost function — four cards this pack was drafting toward before the seam was read.
entries.application: Take the atmosphere from that pack and the organising question from this one. If you cannot say which element resolves at the end, you do not yet know which pack you are writing in. This subject is handed off to the `horror-reference` pack.

entries.name: The Joke as the Organising Purpose
entries.description: Sexual material whose organising purpose is the laugh, and obscenity as a register.
entries.principle: Where the sexual content exists to produce a laugh, the craft apparatus is comedy's — timing, target, register and the mechanics of the joke — and the comedy pack owns it. What that pack does not own, and what stays here, is the bawdy canon itself: it carries no card for the tradition, and this pack's pre-modern inheritance includes the writers usually filed under it.
entries.example: The receiving pack owns obscenity as a register held against a borrowed vocabulary, and the register slip that exposes what a position is made of — both genuinely comic techniques rather than erotic ones.
entries.application: Borrow the joke mechanics from that pack; keep the canon here. And note the asymmetry deliberately: this is a hand-off of technique, not of tradition. This subject is handed off to the `comedy-reference` pack.

entries.name: The Clandestine Trade
entries.description: A distribution system built entirely around not being caught, and the conventions it produced.
entries.principle: For most of the form's printed history the market was illegal, which made distribution rather than composition the binding constraint. The resulting conventions — the false imprint, the subscription list, the small print run, the anonymous or pseudonymous byline — are not stylistic choices but operational ones, and several of them survive as literary devices long after the risk that produced them disappeared.
entries.example: The Victorian trade ran on part-issue publication, private subscription and a concentrated bookselling district, and its authorship is largely unrecoverable by design.
entries.application: When you find an old convention that seems arbitrary, check whether it was a distribution solution. And treat the anonymity of this period as evidence rather than as a gap: the record is thin because it was built to be.

entries.name: The Paris Model: Jurisdictional Arbitrage
entries.description: Publishing in one jurisdiction to sell into another — and the model's eventual failure.
entries.principle: A market formation built on the fact that obscenity law is national while readers are not. English-language work that could not be published in Britain or the United States was printed in Paris and carried across borders by individual readers, which made the constraint a matter of customs enforcement rather than of publishing law.
entries.example: The model is routinely confused with the American litigation strategy that followed it, and they are opposites: this one avoided the courts and that one sought them. It also failed on its own terms, with French seizures from the late 1950s and its principal publisher out of the country by 1963.
entries.application: Read this as the pattern rather than the period — the same arbitrage recurs wherever a platform is domiciled in one jurisdiction and read in others. And do not cite it as a success story; it was a holding action that ran out.

entries.name: The Trial as Strategy
entries.description: Publishing in order to be prosecuted, and winning.
entries.principle: The inverse of arbitrage: a publisher selects a title precisely because it will be challenged, litigates deliberately, and converts a defeat of the censor into a permanent expansion of what may be printed. The strategy requires a legal test that admits a defence — which is why it becomes available only after literary merit becomes arguable in court.
entries.example: The American strategy is the clearest case, and it depended on a statutory and case-law environment in which serious literary intent could be advanced as a defence rather than dismissed as irrelevant.
entries.application: Note what this formation costs: it requires a publisher willing to be the defendant, and it produces a canon selected for litigability rather than for quality. The books that won the cases are not necessarily the best books of their moment.

entries.name: Black Lace and the By-Women, For-Women List
entries.description: A mass-market erotica imprint with an editorial position about who was writing it.
entries.principle: A market formation defined by an authorship policy rather than by content: an imprint publishing erotica written by women for women, operating at mass-market scale in print rather than in the specialist trade. Its significance is that it demonstrated the readership existed at that scale, which the general trade had not believed.
entries.example: Launched in the United Kingdom in 1993, it organised its output into contemporary, historical and paranormal lines — a mass-market erotica list, given a free hand, reaching for the same three-way setting split that romance uses.
entries.application: Read the by-women, for-women position as a formation that has been taken up at least three times under different market conditions, not as a continuous tradition. The label is the same each time; the economics, the distribution and the editorial control are not.

entries.name: The KDP Short-Form Boom and the 2013 Purge
entries.description: A genre that platform economics created, and that a moral panic then reshaped.
entries.principle: The clearest case in the form of a market formation producing a genre rather than carrying one. Platform self-publishing made very short, rapidly produced erotic fiction economically viable for the first time, a recognisable commercial form emerged inside those economics, and a subsequent retailer and press reaction reshaped what could be listed — none of it by any change in law.
entries.example: The 2013 retailer removals are the best-documented event in the form's market history, and nothing removed in them was found unlawful by any court.
entries.application: Treat platform economics as a genre-forming force rather than a distribution detail. And when a commercial form appears very suddenly, look for the pricing or discovery rule that made it viable before you look for a change in taste.

entries.name: The Queer Small Press
entries.description: A publishing infrastructure built because the general trade would not carry the work.
entries.principle: A formation defined by necessity rather than by preference: presses founded to publish queer erotic writing when mainstream houses would not, operating their own distribution, their own periodicals and their own review culture. Because they were the whole apparatus rather than one part of it, they shaped the writing far more directly than a trade imprint does — an editor who is also the distributor and the reviewer sets conventions unopposed.
entries.example: The gay men's and sapphic lines built substantially separate press ecosystems that barely touched, each with its own founders, its own list logic and its own award structures — two parallel infrastructures rather than one queer market.
entries.application: When you read a work from this formation, find out which press carried it before you draw conclusions about convention, because the conventions are house conventions. And note that the two ecosystems are not interchangeable evidence about "queer erotica" as a single thing.

entries.name: The Illustrated Book as a Publishing Form
entries.description: A publishing form rather than a comics form — the plate book, the private folio, the double edition.
entries.principle: Distinct from comics, and distinguished by the relationship between image and text: here the images accompany a text that stands without them, in an edition whose physical form is the commercial proposition. It is the format in which the expurgated and unexpurgated versions of the same work most often coexisted, because the expensive edition could carry what the cheap one could not.
entries.example: The double edition — one text sold openly and a fuller one sold privately — is the form's characteristic artefact, and it is a distribution mechanism wearing the appearance of a bibliographic curiosity.
entries.application: Treat the physical edition as part of the work's meaning in this formation, because it was part of its legal position. And do not read the illustrated tradition as an ancestor of erotic comics; the two solve different problems and have different lineages.

entries.name: Platform Fiction and the Archive Economy
entries.description: Where most erotic writing is now actually produced, and it is neither a press nor a prize.
entries.principle: The dominant contemporary site of erotic composition is not a publisher at all: it is a set of archives and platforms that are free to read, free to publish into, and governed by terms of service rather than by editorial judgement. The economics invert the commercial form's — no gatekeeper, no advance, no scarcity — so status is carried by engagement metrics and the work's shape adapts to them.
entries.example: The formation has its own ending grammar, which the commercial form has no equivalent for: the series that continues indefinitely, the work marked complete, and the abandoned work-in-progress, which is a real and common terminal state rather than a failure of one.
entries.application: If you write here, understand that the platform's terms of service are your censorship regime and your only one, and that they change without notice. And take the ending grammar seriously — a reader of this formation reads an unfinished work differently from a reader of a published one.

entries.name: The Transgressive Stance as a Market Position
entries.description: A stance available to any mode, which the market has learned to sell as if it were a genre.
entries.principle: Transgression is not a content domain — it is a position a work takes toward its own material, and it can be taken in any mode and any domain. The market nonetheless packages it as a category, because a stated intention to offend is a legible proposition to a buyer in a way that a craft argument is not.
entries.example: The stance has an institution: a prize founded in 2001 explicitly to honour contemporary literature and contemporary libertinism, which has gone to essayists, documentary writers and novelists alike — awarding a position rather than a form, and one of its laureates refused it.
entries.application: Decide whether you are taking a stance or occupying a category, because they have different obligations. A stance has to be defensible inside the book; a category only has to be signalled on the cover. The craft argument for what unmediated extremity achieves that mediation does not is the horror pack's, carded at `subgenre-24`.

entries.name: The Cut Test
entries.description: If this scene were removed, what would the book lose?
entries.principle: A specific and significant answer means the scene is earned; a vague one means it is decoration.
entries.example: The test is the form's most transferable diagnostic because it survives the absence of a courtship — a romance can answer "the couple would not have changed", and a work with no couple has to name something else: a decision, a limit found, a self-understanding revoked.
entries.application: Answer in one sentence naming a thing that is different afterwards. If the honest answer is "the reader would have had one fewer scene", cut it or give it a job.

entries.name: What Changes, If Not the Relationship
entries.description: The state-change test, rewritten for a form with no relationship state to change.
entries.principle: Every scene must alter something the reader can name, and in this form that something is rarely the couple.
entries.example: The romance pack's version of this test asks what the couple now know or owe each other, and it is the right test there; here the candidates are different — what the protagonist will now agree to, what they have stopped being able to pretend, what the arrangement now costs, what is no longer available.
entries.application: Name the changed thing before you draft the scene. The scene-that-changes-a-relationship version of this rule is `romance-reference`'s and it does not transfer, because the object it acts on may not exist here.

entries.name: The Repetition Audit
entries.description: Three scenes doing one job is one scene printed three times.
entries.principle: Count the scenes, name each one's job, and cut or merge any two whose jobs are the same.
entries.example: Repetition is the form's characteristic failure and the reason it is most often dismissed, and it is a structural failure rather than a stylistic one — the prose can be excellent in all three.
entries.application: Do the count on a list, not in your head. A drafter who can hold the list in memory has usually stopped noticing the duplication.

entries.name: Which Imported Ending Is This
entries.description: The form cannot end from inside its own logic, so the ending is always brought in.
entries.principle: Name which ending you are importing before you draft the last movement, because the choice determines what the preceding third has to establish.
entries.example: The available endings are a short list — exhaustion, transformation, return, catastrophe, catalogue completion, interruption, and the imported commitment that makes a work read as romance instead.
entries.application: Write the chosen ending's precondition early. An ending by transformation needs a before-state on the page; an ending by exhaustion needs the earlier encounters to have been larger.

entries.name: The Consequence Test
entries.description: Does anything in this book cost anything?
entries.principle: A world with no fatigue, no scarcity, no injury and no economic drag reads as weightless, whatever happens in it.
entries.example: The critical account of the form's ideal type describes exactly that weightlessness as its defining property; the counter-argument holds that the actual historical texts are full of failure, decay and mortality. Both positions are live and the pack carries both.
entries.application: Give one thing in the book a real cost and let it persist. The cost does not have to be moral — time, money, sleep, a job, a friendship and a body that is tired all work.

entries.name: The Interiority Check
entries.description: Is anything happening in the head?
entries.principle: Read any scene with the physical description deleted and see whether anything remains.
entries.example: Practitioners are near-unanimous that the differentiator in this form is what is happening in the mind rather than on the body, and the test makes that checkable rather than aspirational.
entries.application: If nothing remains, the scene is choreography. Add what the point-of-view character is deciding, resisting, noticing about themselves, or getting used to.

entries.name: The Register Hold
entries.description: One register, chosen deliberately, held to the end of the passage.
entries.principle: A single lapse into a different register collapses the effect for everything that follows it.
entries.example: English offers clinical, coarse, euphemistic and lyric vocabularies and nothing neutral, which means every choice is marked — there is no default to fall back on when the writer's nerve goes.
entries.application: Mark the register at the top of the scene and reread only for lapses. The claim that register is characterisation belongs to `romance-reference`, which cards it for a courtship voice; here the register is also an address to the reader, which is `craft-19`.

entries.name: The Escalation Direction
entries.description: Is the rise in stakes, or only in detail?
entries.principle: A book that escalates in explicitness alone has nowhere to go after the third scene.
entries.example: The trap is structural rather than a matter of taste: detail saturates, and a reader who has been given the maximum in chapter four will read chapter eleven as a repetition regardless of what it contains.
entries.application: Plot the escalation as a list of what is being risked rather than what is being shown. If the list is flat, the book is flat, however the prose reads.

entries.name: The Anti-Climax Problem
entries.description: The largest scene, placed last, is followed by nothing.
entries.principle: The final movement usually has to be quieter than the penultimate one and take its force from meaning rather than intensity.
entries.example: A form built on escalation has a structural trap at its own ending: put the biggest scene last and the book stops rather than closes; put it earlier and it deflates everything after it.
entries.application: Decide where the largest scene sits, then write the ending to do a different kind of work. This is where an ending by transformation earns its place, because meaning is the only register that can follow intensity without competing with it.

entries.name: The Frame Audit
entries.description: What is the frame doing, if anything?
entries.principle: A frame that does not change how the enclosed material is read is a decoration with a cost.
entries.example: The found manuscript, the letters, the confession and the deposition entered the form as legal deniability devices rather than as structural ones, so a writer adopting one inherits a shape that was solving a problem they do not have.
entries.application: State what the frame changes — reliability, distance, the reader's complicity, the ending's availability. If it changes none of those, cut it and reclaim the pages.

entries.name: The Specificity Check
entries.description: Could this body, this room and this hour belong to anyone?
entries.principle: Generic particulars produce generic scenes, and the fix is one true detail rather than more detail.
entries.example: The failure is usually a symptom rather than a cause: a writer who has not decided who these people are cannot describe them specifically, and adds volume instead.
entries.application: Name one thing that could only be this person, this place or this time, and let it recur. The version of this rule that serves a courtship is `romance-reference`'s; here it is doing a different job, described at `craft-49`.

entries.name: The Signalling Check
entries.description: Does the front matter tell the reader what the book actually is?
entries.principle: State the ending contract and the content plainly where a reader sees them before purchase.
entries.example: In a form with no guaranteed ending, the most reliably reported complaint is not explicitness in either direction but a reader who inferred a promise the book never made.
entries.application: Write the note as information rather than as apology or as defence. The developed content-warning culture and its author-supplied conventions belong to `romance-reference`; what is yours is the ending contract, which that culture has no vocabulary for.

entries.name: Interiority Is the Differentiator
entries.description: The near-unanimous practitioner claim: it happens in the head, not on the body.
entries.principle: What distinguishes work in this form is the quality of attention, not the explicitness of the description.
entries.example: The claim is made independently across the field's craft literature, in the editorial guidance and by practitioners in interviews, and it is the one point on which sources that agree on nothing else converge.
entries.application: Budget your sentences accordingly. If the physical and the mental are running at one to one, the scene is probably twice as long as it needs to be in one of the two.

entries.name: Attention as the Erotic Object
entries.description: Being noticed accurately is the effect most of this writing is actually producing.
entries.principle: Precise perception of one person by another reads as intimacy more reliably than any physical description does.
entries.example: The device works because it is difficult to fake in prose: a writer who has not decided what a character is like cannot show someone else noticing it correctly, so accurate perception doubles as evidence that the characterisation exists.
entries.application: Give the observer something specific to notice and let them be right. Then decide whether the observed person knows they have been seen, because that is a second beat and usually the stronger one.

entries.name: The Unspoken Calculation
entries.description: What the character is working out while the scene proceeds.
entries.principle: A point-of-view character who is not calculating something is not present in the scene.
entries.example: The calculation need not be strategic — whether to admit a preference, whether this is going where they thought, whether they mind — and its presence is what separates a participant from a camera.
entries.application: Give the calculation a wrong answer at least once in a book. A character who mis-reads a situation and proceeds anyway is the cheapest reliable source of consequence this form has.

entries.name: Wanting Against Oneself
entries.description: Desire that the character has an objection to is more legible than desire they endorse.
entries.principle: Internal contradiction gives the reader a position to occupy; uncontested wanting gives them nothing to do.
entries.example: The pattern is not a moral one — the objection can be practical, aesthetic, social or simply inconvenient — and its function is structural: it makes the wanting visible by giving it something to push against.
entries.application: Find the character's objection before you write the encounter. If they have none, either supply one or accept that the scene is doing less work than you think.

entries.name: The Thing Not Said
entries.description: The gap between what is thought and what is spoken, held open on purpose.
entries.principle: Let the reader hold one piece of information a character in the scene does not have.
entries.example: The device is the form's most efficient tension source in a work with no external plot: with no obstacle outside the room, the asymmetry inside it has to carry the scene.
entries.application: Decide who knows what at the top of the scene and do not let it drift. And close the gap deliberately at some point, because an asymmetry that never resolves reads as an oversight.

entries.name: Habituation, and Writing the Fourth Time
entries.description: What it is like when this is no longer new.
entries.principle: The interior register must change as the situation stops being unfamiliar, or the book stops being believable.
entries.example: This is the interior counterpart of the repetition problem: the prose can vary the events indefinitely, but a character who registers the fourth occasion exactly as they registered the first has not been written as a person.
entries.application: Write the shift explicitly once — the moment something stops being remarkable is a scene. After it, the interiority should be doing different work: comparison, boredom, expertise, unease at one's own ease.

entries.name: Register as Address
entries.description: The register is aimed at the reader as well as spoken by the narrator.
entries.principle: In this form the diction chooses a relationship with the reader, not only a voice for the narrator.
entries.example: A clinical register holds the reader at a distance and can read as either honesty or coldness; a coarse one assumes complicity; a euphemistic one asks the reader to supply what is withheld, which is a demand as much as a modesty. The characterisation reading of register is `romance-reference`'s and is correct there; it is incomplete here.
entries.application: Decide what you are asking the reader to do, then pick the register that asks it. A mismatch between the two is the most common reason a technically competent passage reads as embarrassing.

entries.name: The Second Person and the Present Tense
entries.description: A form unusually tolerant of both, and the reasons are structural.
entries.principle: Second person and present tense are conventional here rather than experimental, because both collapse the distance the form is trying to close.
entries.example: The tolerance is real and specific: readers of this form accept devices in it that would read as mannered in most others, which is a fact about the reading contract rather than about the prose.
entries.application: Use them deliberately rather than by default, and know their cost — second person forecloses the observed character's interiority almost entirely, and present tense makes retrospection expensive.

entries.name: Naming the Body Without a Catalogue
entries.description: What a body means to the person in it, before what it looks like.
entries.principle: Write the relationship to the body before the description of it.
entries.example: The parallel problem in horror was solved the same way and is carded there: detailed anatomy engages the reader as an observer of a specimen, while function and the character's relation to their own altered body is what registers and is renewable where description saturates.
entries.application: Give the character one thing they are aware of about their own body in this moment. The horror pack's version of this rule is about capability lost; yours is about attention paid, and the mechanism is the same.

entries.name: The Reader Is Doing Something
entries.description: The one craft objective this form has that most others do not state out loud.
entries.principle: The work is written to produce a bodily response in the reader, and that is a design constraint rather than an embarrassment.
entries.example: The distinctive thing is not that the form has that objective — horror, comedy, the thriller and the weepie all state it, and the critical literature groups them together as forms organised around involuntary response. What is distinctive is that this form's response is unadmitted, inaudible, and the only reliable measure of success it has.
entries.application: Accept that you are writing without a feedback loop: there is no laugh and no scream to tell you it landed. That is the argument for the diagnostic block rather than for instinct.

entries.name: No Feedback, So Instrument the Draft
entries.description: A form whose success condition cannot be observed needs checkable tests instead.
entries.principle: Where the effect is invisible, substitute structural questions you can answer without a reader in the room.
entries.example: A comic writer knows within a second whether a line worked, and rewrites accordingly; this form's writer gets nothing back, which is why the diagnostic block exists at all and why the field's craft advice is unusually rule-shaped.
entries.application: Run the diagnostics rather than reading for feel on a fourth pass. Your own arousal or boredom at that stage is measuring your familiarity with the text, not the text.

entries.name: Complicity and Its Limits
entries.description: The form positions the reader as a participant, and can position them badly.
entries.principle: Decide what the reader is being made complicit in, because the text assigns them a position whether or not you chose it.
entries.example: The question is sharpest at the transgressive end, where a work may be indicting a spectacle or supplying it, and where serious critics divide on individual works. The craft argument about unmediated extremity is carded in `horror-reference`; what is at stake here is the reader's assigned seat.
entries.application: Read your scene as the reader is positioned rather than as the characters experience it. Where those two readings diverge sharply and you did not intend it, that is the defect.

entries.name: Consent as the Reader's Contract
entries.description: The reader agreed to a book, and the front matter is where that agreement is made.
entries.principle: A reader who was told and chose is in a different relationship to difficult material than a reader who was not.
entries.example: Consent between characters is a large and well-developed craft area and it belongs to `romance-reference`, which cards eight rules on it. This card is about a different party: the person holding the book.
entries.application: Signal specifically rather than generally, and place the signal where it is seen before purchase rather than only in the front matter. Specificity protects the book as much as the reader.

entries.name: Distance, and When to Increase It
entries.description: Closing the distance is the form's default move, and the reason to reverse it.
entries.principle: Widening the distance at a chosen moment is the form's most under-used effect.
entries.example: A scene rendered from further away — summarised, overheard, remembered, reported by someone who was not present — reads with a different charge, and the shift is legible precisely because the form's default is proximity.
entries.application: Use it once, deliberately, and place it where the material would otherwise saturate. The closed-door version of this move belongs to `romance-reference`; this is the same lever used for effect rather than for heat level.

entries.name: Who Is Watching
entries.description: The observer inside the text, and what they do to the observer outside it.
entries.principle: An observing character reassigns the reader's position, usually by giving them somewhere safer to stand.
entries.example: The device recurs across the form's whole history and does consistent work: it converts the reader from participant to witness, which lowers the temperature and raises the reader's freedom to judge what they are seeing.
entries.application: Use the observer when you want the reader thinking rather than only feeling, and remove them when you do not. Do not leave one in place by accident, because they are never neutral.

entries.name: The Fade, and What It Costs
entries.description: Stopping short is a technique with a price, and the price is not modesty.
entries.principle: A break in the text redirects the reader's attention rather than removing it, and the redirection has to be built.
entries.example: The device is an inheritance from a legal test rather than a taste — a standard that judged a book by its most explicit page made the explicit page the unit of risk, and the euphemism and the cutaway were the compositional answers. `sanction` cards that causation directly.
entries.application: If you cut away, put something in the gap — an aftermath, a domestic detail, a changed arrangement — because the reader's attention does not stop at the break. The closed door as a market position belongs to `romance-reference`; this is the device rather than the promise.

entries.name: The Reader Who Is Not Aroused
entries.description: Most readers of most scenes are not, and the writing still has to work for them.
entries.principle: Write the scene so that it remains readable as prose when it is not doing its other job.
entries.example: The form's failure mode under this test is distinctive: a passage that is functional only for the reader it happens to reach reads, to everyone else, as an inventory. A passage carrying character, decision or consequence survives the miss.
entries.application: Reread one scene per book imagining a reader who is bored by it, and ask what is still holding them. If the answer is nothing, the scene has one function and one audience.

entries.name: Shame, and Who Is Carrying It
entries.description: The form's most common uninvited passenger, and it belongs to a character or to nobody.
entries.principle: Decide whether shame is in the book or only in the writing, because a reader can tell.
entries.example: Prose that flinches — abstraction arriving exactly at the difficult moment, a sudden rise in register, a joke — reads as the author's discomfort rather than the character's, and it breaks the address the rest of the book has established.
entries.application: If a character is ashamed, write it as theirs and give it a shape. If the flinch is yours, the fix is a decision about what kind of book this is, not a better sentence.

entries.name: The Reader's Prior Reading
entries.description: This audience arrives more practised in the form than almost any other genre's.
entries.principle: Assume a reader who has read a great deal of this and will recognise a convention on sight.
entries.example: The audience skews heavily toward repeat readers of the form, and the practical consequence is that a device presented as a discovery reads as a cliché to the people most likely to be holding the book.
entries.application: Name the convention in the text where you are using it straight, or bend it. The one thing that does not work is deploying a familiar structure as though the reader has never met it.

entries.name: Where the Reader Is Allowed to Judge
entries.description: Every book decides how much evaluative room the reader gets, whether or not the writer noticed.
entries.principle: Leave the reader somewhere to stand that is not identical with the protagonist's position.
entries.example: A work that offers no distance at all requires total identification and loses the reader completely when it fails; one that offers too much converts participation into assessment, which is a different and cooler experience.
entries.application: Place one moment where the text and the protagonist can be read apart. It does not have to be a criticism — a second character noticing something the protagonist has not is enough.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Found Manuscript
entries.description: The form's oldest frame, adopted for a legal reason and inherited as a structural one.
entries.principle: The found text buys deniability, distance and an excuse for incompleteness, and costs immediacy.
entries.example: The device entered the form under obscenity regimes, where an editor presenting a document is in a different position from an author presenting a fiction — `sanction` cards that causation. Its structural residue is that it licenses gaps, which is why the form's frames so often come with missing pages.
entries.application: If you use it, use the gaps. A found text that is complete and orderly has taken on the frame's costs and none of its advantages.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Letters
entries.description: Correspondence as a structure: alternating interiority with a built-in delay.
entries.principle: The epistolary frame gives every exchange a gap in time, and the gap is the device.
entries.example: What the letter form does that direct narration cannot is separate the wanting from the answer: a correspondent writes into uncertainty, and the reader holds both the letter and the silence after it before the reply arrives.
entries.application: Make the delay matter — a reply that arrives as if instantaneous wastes the form. And decide who is keeping the letters, because that question is the frame's second free gift.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Confession
entries.description: A narrator addressing an authority, real or imagined, who is entitled to judge.
entries.principle: The confessional frame installs a listener with standing, and the narrator's prose bends toward them.
entries.example: The frame's inheritance is religious and legal before it is literary, and it brings both a vocabulary of transgression and an expectation of consequence — which is why so many works using it end in punishment even when the author does not appear to want that.
entries.application: Decide who is being confessed to and whether they are owed anything. If the answer is nobody, the frame is decorative and the punishment ending it drags in will read as unearned.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Deposition and the Case File
entries.description: The document that exists because something went wrong.
entries.principle: A legal or clinical frame promises an outcome before the narrative begins, and the reader reads toward it.
entries.example: The frame is unusually efficient at supplying stakes to a form that often lacks external plot: a reader who knows there was an inquiry reads every ordinary scene as evidence.
entries.application: Decide early whether the outcome is disclosed or withheld, because the two produce different books from identical scenes. And keep the register of the document type, or the frame stops working by chapter three.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Editor's Apparatus
entries.description: Footnotes, prefaces and a hand that claims only to have arranged the material.
entries.principle: An editorial voice can say what the narrative cannot, including that it disapproves.
entries.example: The apparatus is the direct descendant of a defensive strategy: where literary merit or scholarly purpose was a defence, the scholarly frame was a legal instrument as much as a literary one. `sanction` cards the statute that made it useful.
entries.application: Give the apparatus a position of its own and let it be wrong about something. An editor who agrees with the text at every point is doing nothing the text was not already doing.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Frame That Never Closes
entries.description: Opening a frame and abandoning it, and when that is a choice rather than a fault.
entries.principle: A frame the reader has stopped noticing has become the book's voice, which may be the right outcome.
entries.example: The pattern is common enough in the form's history to be a convention rather than an error, and it usually happens because the frame was a permission device that stopped being needed once the writing got going.
entries.application: Decide deliberately. If the frame is load-bearing, close it; if it was scaffolding, cut it in revision rather than leaving a first chapter that promises a structure the book abandons.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: Nested Narration and the Deferred Scene
entries.description: A story told inside a story, which delays the thing the reader came for.
entries.principle: Nesting converts anticipation into structure, and the delay must be shorter than the reader's patience.
entries.example: The technique is ancient in the form and is the mechanism behind the classical frame collections: the telling is itself an occasion, and the listener's reaction is a second scene running alongside the first.
entries.application: Write the listener. A nested tale with no reaction from its audience is just a chapter with an extra layer of quotation marks around it.

entries.category: The Frame, the Found Text and the Document
entries.name: The Document as Evidence Against the Narrator
entries.description: The frame's strongest move: letting the reader see past the person writing.
entries.principle: A document frame lets the reader draw conclusions the narrator has not, and that gap is unavailable to direct narration.
entries.example: The effect requires the narrator to be recording faithfully and interpreting badly — the facts must be present and their meaning missed — which is a harder trick than unreliability and a more durable one.
entries.application: Plant one detail the narrator reports without understanding, early. If the reader catches it, every later page is read twice, which is the most economical effect this form has.

entries.name: Saturation
entries.description: Description stops registering long before the writer notices.
entries.principle: The reader's attention to physical description decays across a book, and no increase in intensity reverses it.
entries.example: This is why escalating in explicitness fails structurally rather than merely aesthetically: the fourth scene is being read by a reader whose threshold the first three have raised, and more detail is the one adjustment that cannot work.
entries.application: Vary the register, the distance, the length or the interiority instead. And spend your most explicit writing early or late, never in the middle, where it will be absorbed without registering.

entries.name: Each Scene Needs a Different Job
entries.description: Not a different position — a different reason to exist.
entries.principle: List the jobs before drafting and refuse to write two scenes with the same one.
entries.example: The distinction matters because varying the events is the obvious fix and it does not work: three scenes that differ in every particular and share a purpose still read as one scene occurring three times.
entries.application: Write the job in the margin of the outline. The scene-count version of this rule, keyed to a courtship's pacing, is `romance-reference`'s; this one is about purpose rather than frequency.

entries.name: The Sentence That Has Appeared Before
entries.description: The form's vocabulary is small, and a writer's personal vocabulary is smaller.
entries.principle: Track your own repeated constructions, because you will not hear them.
entries.example: The constraint is real: the available register is narrow, the physical vocabulary is narrower, and a full-length work in this form asks a writer to describe similar events more times than almost any other genre does.
entries.application: Build a list of your own tics during revision and search for them. This is mechanical work and it is the single highest-yield revision pass this form has.

entries.name: Compression as the Escape
entries.description: The later scene that is shorter is usually the better one.
entries.principle: As the book proceeds, the same material needs fewer words, not more.
entries.example: The pattern follows from saturation: what took a page in chapter two is already established by chapter nine, and rendering it at full length asks the reader to attend to something they have finished learning.
entries.application: Cut the later scenes hardest. If a late scene resists compression, that is evidence it is carrying new material — which is the thing you wanted to find out.

entries.name: Interruption as Structure
entries.description: The scene that does not complete, used deliberately rather than as a tease.
entries.principle: A withheld or broken scene resets the reader's attention more effectively than a bigger one.
entries.example: The device works because it restores uncertainty to a form whose outcomes are otherwise predictable, and it costs nothing except the writer's nerve.
entries.application: Use it once in a full-length work and place it after the point where the pattern has become legible. Twice reads as a system; three times reads as evasion.

entries.name: What the Book Does Between
entries.description: The connective material is where a work in this form usually fails.
entries.principle: The passages between encounters must carry their own reason to exist.
entries.example: The characteristic bad book in this form is not badly written in its scenes; it is empty between them, and the emptiness is what makes the scenes feel repetitive even when they are not.
entries.application: Give the between-material a plot of its own — logistics, money, work, a third party, a decision pending. The scenes will read as more varied without a word of them changing.

entries.name: Escalation That Is Not Physical
entries.description: What else can rise: disclosure, risk, dependence, cost, audience.
entries.principle: Choose an escalating variable that is not the body, and make it visible.
entries.example: Every one of these can be raised indefinitely without saturating, because none of them is a description — the reader's threshold does not adapt to a rising risk the way it adapts to rising detail.
entries.application: Pick one and chart it. The emotional-escalation version of this rule, in service of a courtship, is `romance-reference`'s; the variables here are wider and none of them has to be feeling.

entries.name: The Last Scene Problem
entries.description: By the end, the reader knows the vocabulary better than the writer does.
entries.principle: Write the final encounter for a reader who can predict it, and give them something they cannot.
entries.example: The reader of a full-length work in this form arrives at the last scene having read the pattern several times, which makes conventional execution there read as a failure of nerve rather than as a satisfying return.
entries.application: Change one structural element — the point of view, the distance, the tense, who is present, whether it is narrated at all. The change is the ending, more often than the content is.

entries.name: Specificity Without a Relationship to Reveal
entries.description: Detail must do a different job when there is no couple for it to characterise.
entries.principle: In this form the specific detail establishes attention rather than intimacy, and that is a different achievement.
entries.example: The courtship version of this rule holds that a particular body generates awkwardness and heat between two people who are learning each other — it is `romance-reference`'s and it is correct there. Here there may be no learning and no continuing pair, so specificity has to justify itself as perception rather than as revelation.
entries.application: Ask what the detail tells the reader about the person noticing, not about the person noticed. If the answer is nothing, the description is inventory.

entries.name: The Room, the Hour, the Weather
entries.description: Circumstance is the cheapest source of variation the form has, and the most neglected.
entries.principle: Put the encounter somewhere specific at a specific time, and let the place impose something.
entries.example: The form's critical literature identifies weightlessness as its ideal-typical failing — no season, no scarcity, no fatigue — and circumstance is the most direct correction: a cold room, a short hour, a thin wall and a last train all constrain a scene without any moral apparatus at all.
entries.application: Give each encounter one environmental constraint and let it change what happens. This is also the cheapest fix for repetition, because circumstance never saturates.

entries.name: The Unfamiliar Body
entries.description: When the reader has no default to fill in, the prose has to specify.
entries.principle: An unfamiliar body makes description necessary again, which is a craft opportunity rather than a genre novelty.
entries.example: The effect is why the speculative domain is more useful to a writer than its reputation suggests: with no default available, vagueness becomes visible, and the writing either specifies or fails audibly.
entries.application: Use the unfamiliarity structurally — what it permits, prevents or costs. A difference that changes nothing about what the characters can do is a costume, and the reader will treat it as one.

entries.name: Clothing, Removal and the Ordinary Object
entries.description: The objects around an encounter carry more than the encounter often does.
entries.principle: A named object gives the reader something to hold that is not the body.
entries.example: The technique is old and reliable across the form's whole history: the glove, the letter left on the table, the unfastened thing that takes a moment longer than expected. Its efficiency comes from being outside the saturating register.
entries.application: Choose objects that are already doing work in the book — something owned, borrowed, hidden or about to be returned. An object introduced only for this scene is set dressing.

entries.name: Duration and the Sense of Time
entries.description: How long a scene feels is a decision, and most of the form's scenes feel the same length.
entries.principle: Vary the relationship between page-time and story-time deliberately across a book.
entries.example: A form organised around a repeated event has an unusual need for this, because identical pacing across similar scenes is precisely what makes a reader experience them as one scene — the sameness is temporal before it is descriptive.
entries.application: Write one encounter in summary and one at full length in every book. The summary is not a lesser version; it is a different instrument, and it makes the extended scenes readable.

entries.name: Sound, Smell and the Underused Senses
entries.description: The form is overwhelmingly visual and has no particular reason to be.
entries.principle: Non-visual detail is less saturated in this form than visual detail, so it registers harder.
entries.example: The imbalance is inherited from a visual culture surrounding the written form rather than from anything in prose, which has no advantage in the visual at all and considerable advantage elsewhere.
entries.application: Audit a draft for the ratio. If ninety per cent of the sensory material is visual, you are competing with images on their ground rather than working on yours.

entries.name: What Is Not Described
entries.description: Omission is a technique, and it is not the same as the cutaway.
entries.principle: Choosing not to describe one specific thing, inside a scene you are otherwise rendering fully, focuses attention rather than deflecting it.
entries.example: The distinction from the fade is that the scene continues: the reader remains present and is simply not given one element, which they then supply and cannot stop supplying.
entries.application: Pick the omission deliberately and keep everything around it precise. Vagueness on all sides is not omission; it is the absence of decision, and it reads as one.

entries.name: The Aftermath
entries.description: What the book does in the minutes after is where most of its meaning is available.
entries.principle: Write the aftermath at length at least once, because it is the form's least-used and most legible register.
entries.example: Aftermath is where consequence becomes visible without being asserted — what is said, what is not, who leaves, what is arranged for next time, what is quietly not arranged. The courtship pack's version, in which the aftermath is owed after depicted harm, is `romance-reference`'s and is narrower than this.
entries.application: Give one aftermath the space you would give an encounter. It will do more for the book's weight than any escalation available to you.

entries.name: The Ending Audit
entries.description: Run before drafting the final third, not after. The form has no native ending, so the ending is a decision you make rather than one the material supplies.
items: Which of the imported endings is this — exhaustion, transformation, return, catastrophe, catalogue completion, or interruption?
Is that choice established anywhere in the first half, or does it arrive from outside the book?
If the ending is commitment, is this book actually a romance, and should it be signalled as one?
Where does the largest scene sit, and what follows it?
Does the final movement take its force from meaning rather than intensity?
What is different about the protagonist that was not different before?
Could the book stop two chapters earlier without loss? If yes, it probably should.

entries.name: The Repetition Audit
entries.description: Run on any draft with more than three encounters. Repetition is this form's characteristic failure and it is structural, not stylistic — the prose can be excellent in all three.
items: List every encounter and write one sentence naming its job.
Are any two jobs the same? Cut or merge.
Is anything escalating that is not the level of physical detail?
Do the later scenes get shorter, and if not, why not?
What happens between the encounters, and does it have its own reason to exist?
Search for your own repeated constructions. Name three and count them.
Does the last encounter differ structurally from the others, or only in content?

entries.name: The Content Handling Screen
entries.description: Run on every card and every scene. The pack's §5b test in question form — the difference between writing about the material and writing as it.
items: Is the content named plainly in the opening clause rather than approached obliquely?
Would a reader finish this better informed about how it works on the page?
Would they finish it better supplied with the thing itself? If yes, rewrite.
Is there a flinch — an abstraction, a joke, a rise in register — arriving exactly at the difficult moment?
If there is shame in the passage, does it belong to a character or to the writing?
Is anything here relished? Is anything here censored? Both are failures and they look different.

entries.name: The Exclusion Screen
entries.description: Run before any Authors or Works batch and again before release. The pack's categorical exclusion, which is an assembly screen rather than a drafting rule because a written rule is not a control.
items: Does any card name, describe or cite material depicting minors?
Where a carded figure's record includes such material, is the work named as excluded with no further detail?
Where such content is the substance of a work, has the work been left out entirely rather than carded with a caveat?
Has the term-list scan been run over every field, not only the description?
Is the exclusion stated once in the pack's own documentation and not repeated as a disclaimer on cards?

entries.name: The Boundary Audit
entries.description: Run on any subject that sits near another pack. Tests whether this pack should own the subject at all, which is a different question from whether it can.
items: Does the work guarantee its ending? If yes, it is the romance pack's.
Is the sexual material serving a relationship arc, or is it the subject?
