Is fear, the laugh, or the period the organising element? Each has an owner.
If deleting the neighbouring pack's collection would leave this card untouched, it is in the right place.
Does the destination pack actually carry a card that receives this subject? A hand-off to an empty destination is worse than none.
Have you read the destination pack, or only assumed its contents?

entries.name: The Register Audit
entries.description: Run on any scene before it is considered finished. English offers no neutral sexual register, so every choice here is marked and none is a default.
items: Which register is this — clinical, coarse, euphemistic or lyric?
Was it chosen, or did it arrive?
Is it held to the end of the passage, or is there a lapse?
What is the register asking the reader to do, and is that what you want?
Does the register match the frame? A confession and a case file do not sound alike.
If the register changed mid-scene, is the change doing work or is it a loss of nerve?

entries.name: The Interiority Audit
entries.description: Run on any scene that feels flat despite good sentences. The near-universal practitioner claim is that the differentiator is in the head, and this makes that checkable.
items: Delete the physical description. Does anything remain?
What is the point-of-view character working out during the scene?
Do they get anything wrong?
Is there something the reader knows that a character in the room does not?
Does the interior register change as the situation stops being unfamiliar?
Is the ratio of physical to mental material about one to one? If so, one of the two is too long.

entries.name: The Reader-Position Audit
entries.description: Run once per book, at structural revision. This form assigns the reader a seat whether or not the writer chose it.
items: Where is the reader standing — participant, witness, or judge?
Is there an observing character, and is their effect intended?
Is there anywhere the text and the protagonist can be read apart?
What is the reader being made complicit in?
Does the front matter tell them what the book is before they buy it?
Would the scene still be readable as prose for a reader it does not otherwise reach?

entries.name: The Frame Audit
entries.description: Run whenever a draft has a frame narrative. Most frames in this form are inherited legal devices rather than structural choices, so they arrive solving a problem you do not have.
items: What does the frame change — reliability, distance, complicity, or the ending's availability?
If it changes none of those, why is it there?
Does the frame close, and if not, is that a decision?
Is the document type's register held consistently?
Does the frame license gaps, and are you using them?
Is there one detail the narrator records without understanding?

entries.name: The Award-Claim Screen
entries.description: Run on every Works and Authors card carrying an award. This field has almost no award apparatus, so a credit here is more likely to be wrong than in any other pack in the library.
items: Is the awarding body named, with the category and the year?
Is the award named after a person, and has it been attributed to that person by mistake?
Is the body still operating, and if not, is the closing date stated?
Is this a juried prize or a popular vote?
Is it a prize for the writing, or for a performance, a production or an audiobook?
Is it the Bad Sex in Fiction Award? That is not a prize for erotic writing and it ended in 2019.
Is it the Rauxa Prize? Do not card it — every trace is author-side and no awarding body has been found.
If nothing is found, does the card say so in a way that names what was checked?

entries.name: The Contested-Canon Screen
entries.description: Run on any card touching a live dispute. The pack carries eleven of them and the method is fixed: name the contest, state both positions at full strength, take no side.
items: Is the contest named on the card, or only implied?
Is each position stated at its strongest, in the terms its own holders use?
Is only one side sourced? A contested card with one side sourced does not ship.
Who contests what, and is that recorded?
Read the last sentence on its own. Does it adjudicate?
Read the application field separately. A fix to the principle can leave the application deciding what the principle declined to.

entries.name: The Attribution and Pseudonym Screen
entries.description: Run on every Authors card. This pack exercises the pseudonym taxonomy harder than any before it, and at least one case exceeds all four of its types.
items: Which of the four types is this — personal, publisher-owned, rotating house-stable, or character persona?
Is there a second layer? A pen name over a pen name is not rare here.
Is the real identity established, disputed, or unknown, and does the card say which?
Is an anonymous work being attributed on the strength of tradition rather than evidence?
Does the author card and every works citation spell the name identically?
Does this person generate a line — a press, a school, a prosecution, imitators — or are they a single unpinnable alias?

entries.name: The Year and Translation Screen
entries.description: Run on every Works card. A large share of this canon reaches English late and through French, which makes the translation year the single most likely wrong number on the card.
items: Is this the year the work first appeared in the form it was written as?
For a novel: first book publication, with any serial named separately?
For a short work: first publication in any form, usually the magazine?
Is this an original-language year rather than a translation year?
If a source gave you a translation year, is that stated?
Do two sources disagree, and if so, are they using different conventions rather than one being wrong?
Is the year a string, including negative years?

entries.name: The Living-Status Screen
entries.description: Run on every Authors card, and again immediately before release, dated. Post-cutoff deaths look known and are wrong — that is the trap, not ignorance.
items: Has living status been checked for this person, and on what date?
Is a recent death being present-tensed anywhere on the card?
Is the check dated on the card or in the build record?
Has the whole roster been re-run since the last batch, or only the new names?
A pack whose instruments all report clean has proved internal consistency and nothing about the world.

entries.name: The Sellability Screen
entries.description: Run on any card making a claim about what may be published. In this form the binding constraint is almost never the law, and conflating the two is the pack's most likely factual error.
items: Is this a claim about law, about platform terms of service, or about payment-network rules?
Is the layer named explicitly, every time?
Is a voluntary industry practice being described as a legal requirement?
Is the claim dated? Platform policy moves on a timescale of months.
Is a removal being described as a finding of illegality? Nothing in the 2013 or 2025 sweeps was found unlawful by any court.
Does the card distinguish what is illegal from what is merely unsellable?

entries.name: The Verification-Gap Screen
entries.description: Run at the close of any Authors or Works batch. This pack has less external verification available to it than any other in the library, and the honest response is to say so rather than to sound confident.
items: Was this claim verified, or is it a candidate carried forward from research?
If it could not be verified, does the card say what was tried?
Is an absence being reported as a finding, when it may be an infrastructure limit?
Is "None" being used where "not researched" is the truth?
Would a reader be able to tell which parts of this card are established and which are inferred?
Is the roster itself verified against anything, or only against the pack's other documents?

entries.name: The Instructed Initiate
entries.description: The experienced party teaches the naive one, and the teaching is the erotic content.

examples.text: The founding instance: the whole book is one woman explaining to another, so the instruction carries every function a plot would otherwise carry — exposition, escalation and closure all arrive as answers to questions.
The instruction is doubled, sexual and philosophical, and the two curricula are taught by different characters; that separation is what stops the didactic frame from flattening into a single voice.

Sade shows what the device is structurally for by pushing it past its use: the instruction becomes argument, the pupil begins to reason back, and the seam between pedagogy and thesis is visible on the page. Study it for the seam, not for the content.

entries.name: The Threshold Crossed Once
entries.description: The first time treated as a gate that cannot be reopened, and the structural debt that creates.

examples.text: Jong sets the gate late and off the erotic axis — the crossing that matters is a decision about a life, not an act — which is how a book keeps a first time load-bearing after its narrator is long past inexperience.

The threshold is crossed in the opening movement and the rest of the book has to keep re-opening it under new scenery; a clean demonstration that a gate used early leaves the remaining chapters with nothing to gate.
Hollinghurst splits the threshold in two, one erotic and one historical, and lets the second re-read the first; the retrospective structure is what makes a single crossing keep paying.

entries.name: The Tutor Undone
entries.description: The instructor is the party changed by the instruction.

examples.text: Jelinek runs the reversal to a cold conclusion: the teacher's authority is the thing being dismantled, and the sexual scenes are the instrument of the dismantling rather than a reward inside it.
Šejić builds a long serial on the instructing party losing her footing first, and the comics form makes the reversal visible in posture several instalments before it is admitted in dialogue.

The reversal is announced rather than dramatised, the trainer declaring her own undoing before the text has produced it; the trope fails whenever the tutor narrates the change instead of suffering it.

entries.name: The Late First Time
entries.description: Adult inexperience, and the different clock it puts on the scene.

examples.text: Forster's delay is legal and social rather than temperamental, so the lateness carries a history; when the scene comes it has to discharge decades, and the prose deliberately refuses to hurry.
Winterson relocates lateness into language rather than biography — the narrator has done everything and named nothing — which makes the device portable to a character with any amount of experience.
Baker withholds nothing anywhere, and the book is a useful control: with no scarcity of experience in the world of the book, lateness cannot exist as a value and every encounter weighs the same.

entries.name: The Catalogue of Firsts
entries.description: Initiation serialised — an inventory of encounters, each nominally new.

examples.text: Saikaku numbers the encounters and lets the count itself be the form; the catalogue holds because each entry is a different social situation rather than a different act, which is the distinction most imitators miss.
The documentary register turns the catalogue into data, and eleven volumes demonstrate the failure mode exactly: enumeration without development produces quantity that reads as one page repeated.
Nin distributes the catalogue across separate stories, which solves the accumulation problem by refusing accumulation — the unit resets, and nothing is required to escalate.

entries.name: The Initiation That Disappoints
entries.description: The first time is a letdown, and the letdown is the point.

examples.text: Duras writes the encounter as already elegiac, so the disappointment is temporal rather than physical — the thing is a memory while it is happening — and that is why the scene survives its own anticlimax.
Baldwin puts the failure in the aftermath rather than the act; the withdrawal that follows is the actual event, which teaches that this trope needs its consequence scene more than it needs its scene.
The satire runs disappointment through every episode until it is the book's only joke; anticlimax repeated turns out to be structurally identical to climax repeated, and just as inert.

entries.name: The Training Arc
entries.description: Initiation into a practice rather than into a person, with stages, tests and a graduation.

examples.text: The stages are formal and named, and the book's force comes from a syllabus applied to a person; the curriculum supplies the ending that the erotic material cannot supply on its own.
Preston writes the arc for a subculture that had an actual curriculum, so the fiction is checkable against practice, and the serial origin shows in the episode-shaped stages.
Rice removes the world outside the training entirely, and the arc loses its gradient: with nothing to be trained away from, the stages become a sequence rather than a progression.

entries.name: The Second First Time
entries.description: Re-initiation — after a marriage, an injury, a bereavement or a long abstinence.

examples.text: Lawrence stages the return against an injury and a class line, so the second first time carries two arguments the first could not have carried.
Reyes compresses the re-entry into a job and a summer, and the brevity is the craft: a re-initiation needs no history told, only a former state the reader can infer.
The memoir frame makes the return irreversible in a way fiction has to work for, and the voice of someone already out the other side is what keeps the account from reading as a brochure.

entries.name: The Terms Agreed in Advance
entries.description: The negotiated first encounter, where the agreement is spoken or written before anything happens.

examples.text: The contract is on the page, dated and signed, and it establishes the form's oldest working discovery: writing terms down converts anticipation into suspense, because a document can be broken.

The negotiation is the book's best-known sequence and its clearest structural problem — the terms are debated at length and then largely set aside, so the document generates an expectation the plot declines to honour.
Califia writes negotiation as characterisation rather than as procedure; each clause reveals who is asking, which is the only reliable way to stop the scene reading as paperwork.

entries.name: The Retrospective Initiate
entries.description: The now-experienced narrator recounting the first time, and the gap between the two voices.

examples.work: Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure
examples.text: Cleland's book is that gap: an accomplished stylist reporting an ignorant former self, and the diction of the older voice is what makes the younger one legible without a single coarse word.
Saikaku frames the account as a confession made in old age, so every episode arrives pre-judged; the frame supplies a moral weather the episodes do not have on their own.

examples.work: La Vie sexuelle de Catherine M
examples.text: Millet reports without retrospective embarrassment, which removes the trope's usual engine and forces the prose to be interesting on description alone — the most instructive version precisely because the gap is refused.

entries.name: The Initiate Who Is Not One
entries.description: The apparent novice turns out to hold the expertise, and the hierarchy inverts.

examples.text: Aretino runs the reversal as comedy — the instructing voice is repeatedly outflanked by its listener — and the comedy is what keeps a didactic frame from hardening into a lecture.
The reversal is the architecture rather than a scene inside it, and the second telling re-reads every earlier gesture; the trope pays most when the reader is initiated alongside the character.
The apparently passive party is the one who sets the terms and closes the arrangement, and the film withholds that fact until the last movement without ever having concealed it.

entries.name: Entry Into the Scene
entries.description: Initiation into a community with its own vocabulary, etiquette and gatekeepers.

examples.text: The anthology is itself an initiation document — a community explaining itself to newcomers and to its critics at once — and the double address is why its pieces read as arguments as often as accounts.
Rechy's narrator learns a geography and a vocabulary before he learns anything else, which is the trope's true shape: a community is entered through its language, not through an act.
Townsend wrote a manual, and read as craft it shows what an entry scene owes the reader: a subculture has procedures, and a novice scene without procedures is only a party.

entries.name: The Concealed Observer
entries.description: Watching without being seen — the keyhole, the gap in the curtain, the room next door.

examples.text: Bataille keeps the observing eye an object inside the story rather than a position outside it, which is how the book makes watching horrifying instead of merely titillating.
The clandestine tradition's standard opening move, doing real structural work: an unseen watcher can describe an act nobody present would narrate, so the device is a permission slip for the prose.
Observation is so continuous that nothing is ever concealed from anyone and the charge disappears — a clean demonstration that this trope is powered by the risk of discovery rather than by the view.

entries.name: Performing for a Known Watcher
entries.description: The act staged deliberately for someone whose presence is acknowledged.

examples.text: The whole book is a demonstration arranged for a spectator, and the arrangement is what is being written about; the sexual content is subordinate to the question of whom the display is for.

examples.work: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
examples.text: The looking is professional before it is erotic, and the transfer of the gaze between the two women is the entire event — the best available model for writing reciprocal observation.
On a stage the watcher is structurally guaranteed, and the revue's problem is the one a written exhibition scene has: guaranteed attention is not the same as earned attention.

entries.name: The Recording Device
entries.description: The camera, the tape, the file — the act preserved, and therefore transferable.

examples.text: The recording is a confessional rather than a document, and the film's discovery is that the machine changes what people will say far more than what they will do.

Baker's medium is a telephone line, which is a recording device with no recording; the constraint forces every erotic effect into diction and pacing, and it is the cleanest study of that in the modern canon.
The footage is treated as evidence of a shared taste rather than as an object with consequences, so the trope's strongest lever — that a recording can be shown to a third party — is left unused.

entries.name: The Implicated Reader
entries.description: The text turning its own reader into the watcher, and saying so.

examples.text: Apollinaire escalates until the reader's continued attention becomes the joke, which is the mechanism in its purest form: address the reader's persistence rather than the reader's arousal.

Carter argues that a pornographic text always positions its reader and that the position is the political content; whatever a writer concludes about the argument, it is the most useful account available of what this device does.

Cooper builds the implication into an unreliable structure, so the reader who has been watching is told at the end what they were watching — the hard case, and the one to study for how far the device goes before it becomes a trick.

entries.name: The Watcher Caught
entries.description: Observation reversed — the concealed party is seen, and the scene reorganises around them.

examples.text: Haneke stages the discovery with no music and no cut to soften it, and the flatness of the reveal is the craft: shame plays better unaccompanied.
The household is full of listeners at doors and the engine of the book is that every one of them is eventually found out; the domestic architecture does the plotting.
Schnitzler's audience is the caught watcher, which is why the play was prosecuted rather than merely disliked — the trope can be aimed at a room instead of at a character.

entries.name: The Commanded Spectator
entries.description: Being made to watch — attention itself as the thing compelled.

examples.text: Sade's tableaux exist to be witnessed by someone with no option to leave, and the arrangement is the argument; the compelled watcher is how the philosophy gets stated inside the scene rather than beside it.
The masked ceremony is built so that the intruder must watch and must not participate, and the tension comes entirely from that separation rather than from anything shown.
The compelled watching is decorative and nobody's position changes as a result, which exposes the requirement: the spectator must be paying a cost the participants are not.

entries.name: The Mirror
entries.description: Watching oneself, and the split it puts in the point of view.

examples.text: Buñuel refuses to mark the boundary between the fantasy and the room, so a character watching herself is also a film watching itself; the ambiguity is deliberate and load-bearing.
Barnes writes self-observation as a condition rather than a moment, and the prose's famous difficulty follows directly: a narrator who cannot stop seeing herself cannot report simply.
Roche's narrator inspects herself with clinical attention, and the book is most instructive on how fast sustained self-observation converts an erotic register into a medical one.

entries.name: The Account Given to a Third Party
entries.description: The encounter reaches the reader through one person telling another about it.

examples.text: The telling is addressed and confessional, and the second person it implies does more work than any description in it — the shortest demonstration in the canon that report can outperform depiction.

Friday's book is entirely reported fantasy, and its structural discovery is available to novelists as readily as to interviewers: an account solicited from someone else licenses material a first person could not offer.
The sequel narrates at a further remove from an already distant original and the attenuation is visible; a second-hand account of a second-hand account has almost nothing left to withhold.

entries.name: Sight Withheld
entries.description: The blindfold, the darkness, the turned back — watching prevented, and what fills the gap.

examples.work: In the Realm of the Senses
examples.text: Ōshima shows almost everything and then withholds the one thing the film has been moving toward, which is the general rule stated in its hardest form: a work that shows everything must still reserve something.
Genet keeps the decisive acts just off the page and lets the reader assemble them from the aftermath, which is why the book reads as far more explicit than it is.
Carter uses darkness and the forbidden room as literal apparatus, and the collection is the best study available of how a withheld interior generates more pressure than an opened one.

entries.name: The Public Act
entries.description: Exposure in front of a crowd that was never a chosen audience.

examples.text: Houellebecq stages collective sexual scenes as consumer arrangements, and the coolness of the reporting is the craft point: publicness read as ordinary disturbs more than publicness read as transgression.
Despentes writes public sexual acts and public violence in the same flat register, which forces the reader to notice that it is publicness rather than content that the culture punishes.

The framing wager is public and the participants know it, and the nineteenth-century version already contains the whole device: consent to be watched by strangers is a separate consent, and the text has to earn it separately.

entries.name: The Gradient Itself
entries.description: Asymmetry as the engine — what a difference in standing does to a scene that would otherwise be flat.

examples.text: Sacher-Masoch isolates the variable: two people, one document, and a difference in standing they invent and can revoke. Study it for what happens to the prose when the gradient wavers — the sentences lose their subject and begin reporting weather and furniture, which is the reliable tell for a gradient that has stopped carrying the scene.

Losey and Pinter invert the gradient without a line announcing it, entirely through who enters a room first and who is standing when the other sits; the model for writing rank as blocking rather than as dialogue.
The gradient is fixed at maximum from the first page and never varies, so the book has no instrument left to play; a gradient that cannot change is a setting rather than an engine.

entries.name: The Master and the Servant
entries.description: Domestic rank — the household as a machine for producing asymmetry without anyone arranging it.

examples.text: Lawrence puts the gradient in accent and vocabulary rather than in orders given, so class does the work rank usually does; the dialect is the power structure, which is why the book cannot be translated without losing an argument.

Boccaccio's household tales run on servants out-manoeuvring masters, and the comic engine is the gradient's reversibility; the earliest systematic demonstration that rank is funniest when it is temporary.

The clandestine version flattens every rank into an opportunity and the gradient stops signifying — a control case showing that a power difference must cost somebody something before it reads as power.

entries.name: The Command That Is Obeyed
entries.description: The order as the basic erotic unit, and what obedience does to the sentence carrying it.

examples.text: The imperative is the book's smallest unit and its plainness is deliberate: an order written without adornment makes the reader supply the compliance, which is exactly why the prose can afford to stay so cool.

The written list of demands is an order issued upward, and the cruelty is that it is obeyed to the letter and destroys the person who issued it — the sharpest case in the canon that a command transfers responsibility, not only control.
The commands are frequent and consequence-free, which drains them of force; an order that cannot be disobeyed is a stage direction.

entries.name: The Order Refused
entries.description: Disobedience, and what the refusal costs the scene it interrupts.

examples.text: Genet's refusals are silences rather than speeches and the scenes reorganise around what a character declines to do; the model for writing refusal without staging a confrontation.

The refusal is procedural — an interview in which the questioned party declines to be positioned — and the film shows that a refusal read as flirtation destabilises far more than one read as resistance.
Refusals are absorbed rather than costed, the arrangement bending around each one, so the book can never show what disobedience is for.

entries.name: Ownership and the Collar
entries.description: Belonging stated as a relation, with an object or a formula that carries it.

examples.text: Preston makes belonging a stated, repeated and public relation rather than a private feeling, and the repetition is the craft — an ownership claim must be re-asserted in the text or the reader quietly stops believing it.

The contributors argue in print about what the object means and do not agree, which is the most useful thing a writer can read on it: the token is contested inside its own community, so a card or a scene that settles the question is describing something that does not exist.
The mark of ownership is decorative and transfers between owners without friction, so it never becomes an object anyone would fight over.

entries.name: The Reversal of Rank
entries.description: The party with standing gives it up, and the scene has to survive the exchange.

examples.text: Ives builds a two-hander in which an audition's power inverts and inverts again, and the stage form makes the mechanism legible: every reversal is a piece of paper or a garment changing hands.
Apuleius reverses rank by changing what the protagonist is, and the ancient version already knows the joke — a person stripped of standing sees more of everyone else's than they ever did before.

Saikaku's samurai stories and his townsman stories cross rank in opposite directions, and reading the two halves against each other is the clearest historical evidence in the pack that a gradient's meaning is local to its society.

entries.name: The Gradient That Is Not Chosen
entries.description: Structural asymmetry — money, employment, status — as distinct from asymmetry that is staged.

examples.text: Houellebecq writes economic asymmetry with no staging and no contract, and the discomfort is that the reader cannot locate a moment when anyone agreed; the unchosen gradient's defining feature is that it has no scene of consent to point at.

McQueen keeps every encounter formally consensual and materially unequal, and the method — long takes, no score, no explanation — is the one that makes an unchosen gradient visible without editorialising it.

The structural inequality is dressed as style and then resolved by departure, so the film raises the unchosen gradient and declines to account for it; a common evasion, and worth study for how smoothly it goes down.

entries.name: The Rival and the Audience of Peers
entries.description: Status competition leaking into the encounter, with the peer group as the real audience.

examples.text: Petronius's men perform for each other more than for their partners, and the comedy comes from status competition contaminating the erotic scene; the earliest clean case of a peer audience changing what participants do.
The ensemble authorship shows in scenes staged for a knowing circle, and the book is a document of a readership as much as of a plot — read it for how a coterie audience shapes what a text will risk.
The rivalries are asserted rather than dramatised and the peer audience never actually watches; with no witness, status competition collapses into boasting.

entries.name: The Punishment Scene
entries.description: Discipline as structure — the scene that has a stated reason, a duration and an end.

examples.text: Sade argues his punishments as well as staging them, and the interleaving is the structural lesson: a discipline scene without a stated rationale is choreography, and the rationale is what the reader is actually made to hold.

Califia writes the aftermath as part of the scene, and the inclusion changes the genre of the whole passage — the strongest single argument in the canon that where a writer stops determines what the scene means.

The discipline set pieces repeat across eighteen issues with almost no variation, which is the serial trade's characteristic failure and a standing reminder that repetition of situation reads as one page.

entries.name: Permission Granted
entries.description: The gradient exercised by allowing rather than by compelling.

examples.text: Rice makes permission the only currency in the world of the book, and the flatness of the result is instructive: where everything must be permitted, granting permission stops being an event.
Winterson's permissions are linguistic — the narrator is allowed to name a thing, and does — which relocates the device into diction and makes it available in any register, however unexplicit.

Hernandez times the granting with page-turn and panel break, and the comics version shows what prose has to simulate: permission is a question of when the reader is allowed to look, not of what anybody says.

entries.name: The Protocol
entries.description: Formalised address, ritual and etiquette — rank maintained by procedure.

examples.text: Strickland runs a household entirely on written protocol and then breaks it for ordinary reasons — fatigue, a bad back, boredom — and the breaking is the subject. Study it for how completely a formal apparatus depends on somebody remaining willing to keep it up, and for the decision to cost that willingness in scenes rather than assert it in dialogue.
Townsend records protocol as working practice with reasons attached, and it is reading the reasons rather than the rules that stops an invented protocol reading as invented etiquette.
The rituals escalate without ever being formalised, so nothing can be breached; a protocol that is never stated cannot generate the transgression the story is reaching for.

entries.name: The Withdrawal of Attention
entries.description: The gradient enforced by absence — attention as the thing rationed.

examples.text: Bataille's absences do more than his presences, and the withdrawal is written as a physical condition rather than an emotional one; the model for making inattention felt on the page.

Duras's lovers spend the book already leaving, and the withheld attention is what gives the physical description its charge — the strongest available case that scarcity rather than access is the erotic variable.
The long final movement is entirely about attention withdrawn and not recoverable, which demonstrates that this device pays most after the erotic material has stopped.

entries.name: The Superior Who Is Dependent
entries.description: The party with standing needs the arrangement more, and the text knows it before the characters do.

examples.text: Cavani's former officer needs the arrangement more than the person inside it, and cutting between past and present without marking either as the true one makes the dependency structural rather than psychological.

Li Yu's protagonist is nominally in command of every arrangement and materially at the mercy of all of them, and the satire runs on that gap; the comic version of the dependent superior, and the oldest.
The dependency is a plot revelation rather than a condition visible in the scenes, so nothing earlier can be re-read; this device works only when the audience could have seen it and did not.

entries.name: Rank Put Down
entries.description: The scene ends and the gradient has to be set aside — the descent, which is where this material's endings live.

examples.text: Bright's selections repeatedly end after the gradient is released rather than at its peak, and the collection is the best short-form demonstration that this material solves its ending problem in the descent rather than the climb.
Forster's ending puts down a class gradient permanently and costs both parties their positions; the rare case where the dissolution rather than the encounter is the book's payload.

The gradient is put down by conversion — one party simply stops wanting it — which resolves the book without ever addressing what the arrangement was for; a widely copied ending, and the one that leaves the least behind.

entries.name: The Mask
entries.description: The face covered, and what the covering licenses.

examples.text: Kubrick makes the mask an admission ticket rather than a concealment, and the reversal is the useful one: in a room where everyone is masked, removing it is the exposure and wearing it is the belonging.
Kessel's heroine wears a name rather than a face, and the novel is clearer than its adaptation about the mask being a timetable — two lives held apart by the clock rather than by a disguise.

Aretino attached text to images already circulating without attribution, and the sonnets work as cover for the engravings while the engravings work as cover for the sonnets; concealment achieved by pairing two forms rather than by hiding either.

entries.name: The Assumed Name
entries.description: The pseudonym inside the fiction, and the pseudonym on the cover, doing the same work.

examples.text: Genet's characters carry invented names that describe them, and the naming is the characterisation; in this tradition an assumed name is a claim rather than a disguise.
Steward wrote as a character who was himself a pen name, and the stories are the clearest working example of the persona pseudonym — the fiction of authorship is part of the fiction.

Louÿs published invented translations of an invented poet and supplied a scholarly apparatus to support her, which is instructive on how much of an erotic text's permission comes from its frame rather than its content.

entries.name: The Mistaken Body
entries.description: Disguise, dress and darkness — the encounter that proceeds on a wrong assumption.

examples.text: Hall's protagonist is legible to nobody in the book, and the novel was prosecuted while containing nothing explicit — the pack's clearest evidence that this trope's legal exposure has never tracked what is shown.

Marguerite de Navarre's tales run repeatedly on a body taken for another in the dark, and the frame discussions that follow each tale argue about what the mistake means; the earliest instance of a text supplying its own commentary on the device.

Baker's premise removes the other party's knowledge entirely, and the book spends its length noticing the problem without resolving it; a useful case for how fast this device stops being about disguise and becomes about consent.

entries.name: The Anonymous Encounter
entries.description: Neither party is identified, and the writing has to find something else to be specific about.

examples.text: Delany writes anonymity as an infrastructure with places, hours and rules, and that specificity is what stops the encounter reading as a fantasy of nobody in particular.

Miller's encounters are anonymous by economics rather than by design, and the flat reportorial register is why the book reads as a document; anonymity here is a fact of the city, not a choice anyone made.
The same material a second time with the reportage thinner, and the comparison is the lesson: anonymity without a specified place becomes interchangeable almost immediately.

entries.name: The Unsigned Letter
entries.description: Writing as concealment — the note, the tablet, the line that cannot be traced back.

examples.text: Diderot arranges for speech to come from where it cannot be attributed, and the satire is about what testimony is worth when nobody can be held to it; the eighteenth-century form of the anonymous account.

Ovid instructs on writing what cannot be signed and on the tablet that must be destroyed, and the practical detail is the point — concealment in this trope is a logistics problem before it is an emotional one.

Baker's callers are unsigned by construction, and the novel demonstrates that removing identity from an exchange concentrates it rather than diluting it, because everything then has to be established by voice.

entries.name: The Double Life
entries.description: Two lives kept apart, and the maintenance cost the text has to show.

examples.text: Hollinghurst runs two chronologies of concealment against each other and lets the older one explain the newer, so the double life becomes a historical argument rather than a personal secret.

Baldwin distributes the concealment across a group, each character hiding something different from a different person, and the network is what makes the double life structural rather than a plot device.

examples.work: Le bleu est une couleur chaude
examples.text: Maroh keeps the concealed and the disclosed on separate pages through the diary frame, and the comics form puts the cost of the separation into the colour rather than the dialogue.

entries.name: Speaking Without Seeing
entries.description: The grille, the partition, the darkened room — an exchange in which the parties cannot see each other.

examples.text: The convent dialogue puts its instruction through a grille, and the concealment licenses a frankness the same speech could not have face to face; the device is a permission structure before it is a setting.
Al-Nafzawi addresses a reader he cannot see and will never meet, and the encyclopedic register follows directly — a text that cannot read its audience has to cover every case.

Schnitzler replaces each encounter with a mark on the page, so every production has to decide what its audience is denied; the structure is built out of that gap, which makes the withheld view a formal device rather than a modesty.

entries.name: The Open Secret
entries.description: Everyone knows and nobody says, and the etiquette of not saying is the machinery.

examples.text: Murasaki's court knows everything and acknowledges none of it, and the etiquette of non-acknowledgement is the machinery of the whole book; the model for concealment maintained by a group rather than by a person.
The household's arrangements are common knowledge and formally unmentioned, and the satire lives in the distance between the two; the open secret is the domestic form of the gradient.

The secret is kept from the audience as well as the characters, which converts the trope into suspense and forfeits its actual subject — an open secret is only interesting when the reader is already inside it.

entries.name: The Carnival
entries.description: Sanctioned suspension of identity — the masked ball, the festival, the licensed interval.

examples.text: Apuleius sets his transformations against festivals and processions, and the licensed interval is what makes the impossible narratable; the oldest working version of the device.
Bertolucci's rule against names is a private carnival with two participants, and the film is a controlled experiment in how long a suspension of identity can hold before the world reinserts itself.

The revue suspends the ordinary rules by announcement rather than by agreement, and once the announcement is made there is nothing left to suspend; a carnival needs the rule it breaks to still be in force.

entries.name: The Unmasking
entries.description: Concealment ends — who does the revealing, and what the revelation costs them.

examples.text: Every revelation is also a re-concealment, and the structure makes unmasking a repeatable move rather than an ending; the study case for spending this device more than once in one story.
Genet unmasks his own invention repeatedly, reminding the reader the characters are being composed in a cell, and the disclosure increases the charge rather than dissolving it.
The novel ends on a demand to be recognised rather than on an exposure, and the difference is the useful one: an unmasking performed by the concealed party is a claim, not a defeat.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Closed World Itself
entries.description: The principle behind the category — a sealed institution supplies the constraint this material has no native source for.

examples.work: In the Realm of the Senses
examples.text: Ōshima's couple seal themselves into an inn and stop going out, and the principle is visible in its purest form: the enclosure is voluntary, total, and the only thing in the film supplying an end to a sequence that could otherwise run indefinitely.
Arsan's expatriate compound is a closed world made of distance and money rather than walls, which is instructive on how thin an enclosure can be before it stops generating anything.
Baker's resort has no rule that costs anything, so the enclosure yields nothing; a closed world is only useful when leaving it would be a loss.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Convent and the Cloister
entries.description: Enclosure by vow — the oldest institutional setting in the tradition, and the most argued over.

examples.text: Diderot writes enclosure as coercion and argues it politically, and the polemic is what keeps the material from being decorative; the convent book that most clearly refuses to be a fantasy.
The clandestine tradition's convent is a permission structure rather than a prison, and the contrast with Diderot a century later is the whole history of this trope in two books.
Lewis puts the enclosure inside Gothic machinery, and the scandal of the book was that the vow itself was doing the erotic work; the case study for enclosure written as suspense.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Ship
entries.description: A hierarchy with no appeal and no exit, moving.

examples.text: Melville's ship is a closed hierarchy with no appeal and no shore, and the charge is carried entirely by rank and proximity without a single scene; the model for writing desire a text never names.
Saikaku ends his catalogue by sailing for an island of women, and the voyage is the joke: a closed world entered on purpose is a different device from one that cannot be left.
The aircraft is used as a sealed space for one sequence and then abandoned, and nothing about the enclosure carries forward; a closed world used as scenery rather than as constraint.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Regiment and the Barracks
entries.description: Enforced proximity plus enforced silence — the institution that manufactures the desire and the prohibition together.

examples.text: McCullers puts the post's forced closeness and its forced silence in the same frame, and the novel is the best study available of an institution that produces both the wanting and the rule against naming it.

Steward's stories run on servicemen and the economy of encounters a garrison town creates, and the specificity of the arrangements — where, when, for how long — is what keeps them from being interchangeable.
Donleavy's institution has stopped enforcing anything, and the book shows what follows: the encounters lose their cost and the comedy has to carry the whole weight.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Prison
entries.description: Confinement with a ladder already in it, and desire organising itself along the ladder.

examples.text: Genet writes the prison as a hierarchy with its own aristocracy and its own honours, and the erotic system is inseparable from the disciplinary one; the definitive case that in a closed world desire arranges itself along whatever ladder is already standing.
The companion volume treats confinement as a vocation rather than a punishment, and reading the two together shows how much of this trope is the writer's stance rather than the setting.
Cooper's enclosures are private and chosen rather than institutional, and the comparison exposes what an institution supplies that a locked room cannot: other people with a stake in the rules.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Hospital and the Sanatorium
entries.description: Illness as the reason nobody leaves, and the clinical register that comes with it.

examples.text: Mann's sanatorium supplies what this material most often lacks — a reason nobody can go, a calendar, and a hierarchy that is not sexual in origin but governs every encounter inside it.
Ballard assembles the book's erotics in a ward and a rehabilitation unit, and the borrowed clinical vocabulary is the craft point: an institution supplies a register as well as a setting.
Roche sets the whole book in a hospital bed and takes a register from it but no constraint — nobody's position in the institution is at stake, so the enclosure never generates a scene.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Country House and Its Staff
entries.description: The household as an institution, with wages, notice periods and a hierarchy that predates anyone's desire.

examples.work: Le Journal d'une femme de chambre
examples.text: Mirbeau writes the household from below and makes the erotic material inseparable from wages, references and notice periods. Study it for the choice of vantage: giving the point of view to the person who can be dismissed converts every encounter into a calculation, and the calculation is what most country-house writing leaves out and then has to replace with atmosphere.
The house is the entire institution and a staff of one dismantles it from inside; the cleanest study available of a closed world with a population of two.
The household has no economy — nobody works and nobody can be dismissed — so the arrangement never acquires stakes; the failure shows that in this trope employment is the constraint.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Brothel as a Workplace
entries.description: The house written as a business rather than as a fantasy of one.

examples.text: Hollander writes the house with overheads, hours and a client book, and the commercial detail is exactly what makes it a workplace on the page.

Zola treats the trade as an economy running through an entire society and keeps the accounts relentlessly; the naturalist method supplies the register this trope needs and that most erotic writing declines to use.
Saikaku's narrator descends the licensed quarter's grades one at a time, and the structure is an occupational ladder rather than a moral one — the earliest workplace novel in the tradition.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Court
entries.description: Rank, access and procedure — the institution whose medium is who may be seen by whom.

examples.text: Laclos makes the salon a closed world with letters for infrastructure, and the campaign is legible only because every move is documented; the model for an institution whose medium is correspondence.

Murasaki's court runs on rank, screens and exchanged poems, and the constraint is wholly procedural — access is a question of who may be seen by whom, which is why the poems carry what the scenes cannot.
Aretino's speakers describe a court from outside it and the institution never becomes a place with rules; the dialogues get the economics right and the architecture wrong.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Club, the Society, the Lodge
entries.description: Membership, a threshold and a door policy — the closed world people choose and can be expelled from.

examples.text: Feinberg writes the bar as an institution with membership, protection and a door policed from outside as much as from within; the closed world that exists because the world around it is dangerous.

The ensemble text is a private society's product circulated to a membership of two hundred, and the staging assumes a room of initiates; here the club is in the publishing history as much as in the plot.
The society is a couple's private invention with no members and no door, so there is nothing to be admitted to or expelled from; a club needs a threshold or it is only a habit.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: The Retreat and the Weekend
entries.description: The temporary closed world, where the return date does the work walls do elsewhere.

examples.text: Ozon's house is a closed world on a fixed lease, and the deadline supplies the constraint; the enclosure is temporal rather than architectural and behaves identically.
Nin's stories repeatedly occupy a bounded stay, and the collection is a catalogue of what a temporary enclosure can hold before it has to end.
Cuarón's journey is a closed world in motion with a fixed destination, and the narration keeps announcing the future so the audience never forgets the enclosure is temporary.

entries.category: The Institution and the Closed World
entries.name: Leaving the Institution
entries.description: The return to the world, and what the institution's rules turn out to be worth outside it.

examples.text: The sequel exists because the first book's institution had nothing outside it, and it demonstrates the difficulty exactly: the rules prove unportable and nothing has been established that could replace them.
Rechy's narrator leaves and the last movement is about what the vocabulary is worth off its own ground; the departure is where the novel makes its argument.
The narrator carries the prison's hierarchy out with him and goes on ranking the free world by it, which is the trope's sharpest form: leaving is not the same as being released.

entries.name: The Price Named
entries.description: The figure said out loud, and what saying it does to the scene it is said in.

examples.text: Defoe itemises everything and the ledger is the book's structure; naming the price converts an encounter into a transaction the reader can audit, and this is the earliest sustained case in English.

Delacoste and Alexander put rates, conditions and disagreements side by side without resolving them, and the disagreement is the useful part — the contributors do not agree on what naming a price means, and a writer who settles it is writing about something simpler than the thing.
Southern and Hoffenberg's heroine gives everything away and is charged nothing, so no price is ever named and the satire has no ledger to work against; the joke needs an economy it declines to build.

entries.name: The Gift That Obliges
entries.description: The present that creates a claim, and the cover story that hides the claim.

examples.text: Ovid is explicit that a gift creates an obligation and advises on managing it, and the cynicism is instructive: the poem treats obligation as the mechanism and affection as the cover story.

Vatsyayana catalogues gifts, occasions and expected returns as part of a system of conduct rather than of seduction, and the contrast with Ovid is the pack's clearest evidence that a gift's meaning is set by its society.

The stories were written to a collector's standing order at a fixed rate a page, and nobody inside them owes anybody anything; the obligation is in the book's commissioning history rather than in its contents, which is where a reader should look.

entries.name: The Debt
entries.description: An obligation carried forward, settled in a currency it was not incurred in.

examples.text: Prévost keeps the price unspoken between the lovers and explicit everywhere else, and the gap is the tragedy; the model for a transaction the participants refuse to name while the reader counts.
Chaucer settles a cash debt with a sexual one and audits both, and the comedy is arithmetical; the earliest English case of the two ledgers being deliberately confused.
The debt is stated once and then abandoned in favour of jealousy, so the film raises a transaction and resolves an affair; a common substitution, and a clean specimen of it.

entries.name: The Contract of Employment
entries.description: The work written as work — hours, equipment, invoices and the difference between a career and a scene.

examples.text: Anderson writes the industry as a workplace with contracts, a payroll and a technological shock that ends careers, and the professional frame is what stops the sexual material becoming the subject.
Schroeder films a professional's working day — appointments, equipment, the room being tidied afterwards — and the ordinariness of the labour is the point.
The arrangement is never contractual and the narrator's actual employment stays offstage, so the book cannot ask what she is risking materially; the omission is what leaves it floating.

entries.name: The Marriage Settlement
entries.description: The arranged transaction that cannot be reopened, and the second economy that grows beside it.

examples.text: Wycherley builds the comedy on marriage as a property arrangement and on the deception required to work around it, and the stage form makes the accounting audible; the settlement is the plot.
Kessel's marriage is a completed transaction that cannot be renegotiated, and the afternoons are a second economy running alongside it; the novel is precise about which of the two has a contract.
Li Yu's marriages are negotiated between families and the satire tracks the clauses, with a reckoning at the end that is arithmetical rather than moral — the settlement is what the book audits.

entries.name: The Barter
entries.description: Exchange in a currency that is not money — favours, secrets, standing, silence.

examples.text: Boccaccio's exchanges are of favours, secrets and reputation rather than coin, and the tales are precise about the rate; barter is where the collection's realism lives.
Marguerite de Navarre's frame debates put a value on each exchange after the tale rather than inside it, so the reader receives the transaction and the argument about it as separate objects.
Jong's exchanges are of attention and self-regard and the book says so, but nothing is ever actually surrendered, so the barter has no consideration on either side.

entries.name: The Patron and the Kept
entries.description: Maintenance as a standing arrangement, with two ledgers that never agree.

examples.text: Dumas fils makes the paperwork visible — the furniture, the creditors, the settlement after her death — and the melodrama is carried entirely by the accounting beneath it.
Nin records being kept and keeping in the same pages, and the double position is the useful one: the patron's ledger and the kept party's are both hers and they do not agree.

The arrangement is total and its collapse is announced in the first chapter, so nothing about it is ever in question; the naturalist certainty that makes the economics legible also removes the suspense.

entries.name: The Wager
entries.description: A stake placed on an outcome, which is what makes a seduction narratable.

examples.text: The wager is stated, minuted and enforced by correspondence, and the cruelty comes from both parties keeping accurate records; the definitive case that a stake converts pursuit into plot.
The frame is a bet made in company and the book never lets it lapse, which is what keeps a series of set pieces attached to a structure.
The two-sisters design is a demonstration wager — a proposition to be proved by outcome — and reading it as a bet rather than as a story explains why the ending has to be arbitrary.

entries.name: The Refusal of Payment
entries.description: The transaction declined, which is a move inside the economy rather than an exit from it.

examples.text: Aristophanes turns collective refusal into a bargaining position, and the play is the oldest surviving argument that withholding is a transaction rather than the absence of one.

Dworkin argues that what is presented as a transaction cannot be one where the buyer sets the terms, and the case is made at full strength; the opposing position is carded separately in this pack, and a writer working in this territory has reason to read both at their strongest.
Despentes answers the transaction with violence rather than with refusal, which is a different move; the book sits here to mark the distinction, because the two are frequently run together.

entries.name: The Broker
entries.description: The intermediary who arranges the exchange and takes a cut of it.

examples.text: Chaucer gives the go-between his own motives, his own risk and his own disappointment, and the poem is the reason the name became the word; a broker with nothing at stake is only a device, and this one has everything at stake.

Prévost's brother-broker keeps the arrangements running while pretending to be a bystander, and the pretence is the trope's characteristic move — the intermediary insists on being outside the transaction he is inside.

The brokerage is described as frictionless and disinterested, which is the one part of the business the book romanticises; a broker who takes no cut and carries no exposure is not being written, only mentioned.

entries.name: The Marked Body
entries.description: Scars, brands and tattoos — the alteration that does not come off.

examples.text: Kafka's machine writes the sentence into the body, and the story is the extreme statement of what a mark is for: it removes the possibility of the event being denied later, which is the whole reason this trope exists.
Genet reads tattoos as a legible social record — who owns whom, who has served what — so the marks carry information rather than atmosphere, which is what stops them being decoration.
The marks are applied and gone by the following chapter, so nothing is permanent and nothing is at risk; a mark that heals on schedule is a costume change.

entries.name: The Body Trained
entries.description: Change over time — endurance, habit and the physical learning curve.

examples.text: Šejić lets the training take instalments rather than a montage, and the serial form makes the curve visible: what is difficult early is ordinary later, and the reader has watched the interval.

Colette writes about what long practice does to appetite rather than to capability, and the distinction is the useful one — this trope is usually written as skill acquired when the interesting change is in what is still wanted.
The training is a sequence of scenes with no interval between them, so nothing accumulates; a body cannot be shown to change in a form that refuses to show time passing.

entries.name: The Body in Costume
entries.description: Clothing as alteration — the garment that changes what a body is taken to be.

examples.text: Ives makes a single coat carry the entire transformation and puts it on and off in front of the audience, and the staging is the argument: the costume is not concealing a body, it is producing one.
Gautier treats dress as the thing that determines who may be desired by whom, and the novel's long digressions on clothing are the theory rather than an interruption of it.
The costuming is styling: it signals a category to the audience without altering what anyone in the film can do, which is exactly the substitution the novel's constraint refuses.

entries.name: The Body Restrained
entries.description: Restraint as a change to what a body can do, rather than as an image of one.

examples.text: Cavani writes restraint as a resumed arrangement between two people who both know the terms from before, and the history is what makes the physical constraint mean anything.

Breillat films restraint clinically and without arousal in the frame, which isolates the mechanism: the interest is in what the restrained party can no longer initiate, and the camera declines to supply anything else.
The restraint is described at length and costed at nothing — the narrator's circumstances outside the scene are unaffected — so the alteration is temporary in a way that empties it.

entries.name: The Body as Terrain
entries.description: Description that maps the body onto landscape or architecture, and what the map leaves out.

examples.text: The source of the whole convention in the Western line: the body is given as orchard, tower and city, and the figures are specific to a place and a trade rather than generic, which is why they still read as description rather than as euphemism.

Aragon sustains a single topographical description far past the point where it should exhaust itself, and the achievement is that the terrain keeps acquiring new features; the demonstration that this figure fails from repetition, not from length.
The stories reach for the same small set of landscapes across the collection, and the recurrence shows how quickly the device becomes a vocabulary rather than an act of seeing.

entries.name: The Aging Body
entries.description: Time as the alteration nobody chose, and the asymmetry it creates.

examples.text: Colette makes the age difference the structure rather than the situation, and the novel's cruelty is arithmetical — the gap is fixed and both parties can calculate it, which is what neither can stop doing.

examples.work: La Vie sexuelle de Catherine M
examples.text: Millet writes a retrospective account without either nostalgia or apology, and the refusal of both is what makes the passage of time legible instead of sentimental.
The older body is a symbol before it is a body, and the novel's interest in it is metaphysical, so nothing about age as a physical fact reaches the page.

entries.name: The Injured Body
entries.description: Illness, disability and the body that will not do what the scene requires.

examples.text: Ballard reorganises desire around damage and writes the injuries with borrowed medical precision, and the borrowed register is the craft point: the vocabulary decides whether the reader is looking at a wound or a fetish.
Mann's invalids have their bodies measured and charted daily, and the erotic charge runs through the chart — the institution's instruments become the language of attention.

Campion removes speech and lets a single joint of a finger carry a consequence, and the film is the strongest available case that a body's limits can be the source of the erotic material rather than an obstacle to it.

entries.name: The Transformed Body
entries.description: Metamorphosis — the alteration that is not gradual and cannot be undone.

examples.text: Ovid supplies the tradition its grammar for this, and what to study is the timing: the change lands mid-pursuit, so the transformation is a consequence of desire rather than a setting for it, and the pursuer is left holding something else. Nearly every later use of the trope either follows that ordering or quietly reverses it, and the reversal is why so many modern versions feel decorative.

Carter runs the transformation in both directions across the collection and lets the reader compare, so the device is examined rather than deployed; the clearest modern demonstration that which party changes is the whole meaning.
Carter makes the transformation surgical and institutional rather than magical, and grounding it in a procedure with a location and an operator is what keeps the allegory arguable.

entries.name: The Body Made Strange
entries.description: Defamiliarisation — the clinical, zoological or object-like gaze that makes a familiar body unrecognisable.

examples.text: Bataille's account of the body as a discontinuity that eroticism breaches is the theory behind the device, and it explains why estrangement intensifies rather than cools: what is made strange can be crossed again.
The substitutions between objects and body parts are systematic rather than incidental, and following the chain is the exercise; the book is the practical companion to the essay above.
Cooper's estrangement is total from the first page, so nothing is available to become strange; the device needs a familiar body to work on, and this one never supplies it.

entries.name: The Body Between Categories
entries.description: Androgyny, transition and the body read wrongly — written as craft rather than as a position.

examples.text: Woolf changes her subject without explanation and then spends the book on the social consequences rather than the physical fact, and the allocation of attention is the technique: what alters in the writing is who may address the character and how.

Feinberg writes the body through the institutions that read it — bars, factories, hospitals, police — so the reader gets a sequence of readings rather than a definition, and the disagreement between them is the material.

Barnes refuses to resolve her characters into categories and lets the prose stay difficult in consequence, which is one available answer to the problem: a body the sentence will not settle keeps the reader in the act of looking.

entries.name: The Interruption
entries.description: Somebody comes in, and the scene has to become something else at speed.

examples.text: Wycherley builds entire sequences on people arriving at the wrong moment and on the double meanings that survive their arrival, and the stage form makes the timing exact; interruption here is a metrical device.
Petronius structures his set pieces by intrusion — the episode does not end, it is ended — and the technique is why the book reads as a sequence of collisions rather than a plot.

Miller reports interruptions rather than staging them, so the reader learns afterwards that something was cut short; the device needs to happen in the present tense of the scene or it is only information.

entries.name: The Near Miss
entries.description: Almost discovered — the tension of a consequence that does not arrive.

examples.text: The afternoons are structured by the risk of overlap between two lives, and Buñuel keeps the near misses ambiguous enough that the audience cannot be sure a discovery has not already happened.
Lee lets one unobserved near miss become the story's whole engine by revealing much later that it was not unobserved, which is the device's strongest form: a near miss that was a hit.
The near misses carry no attached consequence, so nothing tightens; without a stated cost of discovery, proximity to it is not suspense.

entries.name: The Letter Found
entries.description: The written trace that reaches the wrong reader.

examples.text: Lyne makes the discovery an object handled on screen rather than a fact announced, and the physical business of finding, reading and putting back is what generates the sequence's pressure.

The recording is made for a custody hearing, so the discovery has a legal destination from the moment it exists; the strongest available demonstration that a found trace is only as sharp as the use waiting for it.
Ovid treats discovery as a recurring inconvenience to be managed rather than an event with a consequence, so nothing in the poems can turn on it; a trace that costs nothing when found is only a prop.

entries.name: The Pregnancy
entries.description: The consequence the form most often declines to write, and what its absence does.

examples.text: Defoe keeps the arithmetic — the costs, the arrangements, the intervals out of circulation — and the accounting is why the book reads as a life rather than a series of episodes.
The contributors treat contraception, pregnancy and health as working conditions rather than as plot, and reading them that way is the correction most fiction in this territory needs.

examples.work: Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure
examples.text: Cleland's world produces almost no consequences of this kind at all, and the absence is systematic rather than accidental; it is the clearest single measure of how far the book's realism actually extends.

entries.name: The Disease
entries.description: Transmissible consequence — a subject the tradition handled badly for a century and then had to learn.

examples.text: Delany writes the epidemic into the infrastructure of the encounters rather than into a subplot, so risk is a property of the world instead of a punishment attached to a character; the book is contested and its own preface argues with the reader, which is part of what makes it worth study.

Dumas fils makes illness the terminus of the economy the novel has been auditing, and the nineteenth-century convention is visible in the join: the disease arrives on schedule and does the moral work the plot has been deferring.
Bataille's illness is symbolic and cannot be transmitted, so it carries none of the trope's weight; a consequence nobody else can catch is a metaphor with a temperature.

entries.name: The Scandal
entries.description: The consequence that is social rather than personal — reputation as the thing that is spent.

examples.text: The scandal is the film's actual subject and the affair its pretext, and the structure makes that visible: the encounters are brief and the fallout is long.
McCullers has the institution absorb the scandal rather than release it, which is the rarer version and the more frightening one — nothing becomes public and everything is known.
Brown writes expulsion and disgrace as the engine of the first half and keeps the tone comic, and the comedy is what makes the consequence legible as unjust rather than deserved.

entries.name: The Blackmail
entries.description: Discovery converted into leverage and held rather than spent.

examples.text: The leverage is informational and the film never settles who holds it, so every scene is played by two people each of whom may be the one being managed.

Clerical blackmail is the clandestine novel's only structural device and it drives every episode, which makes the book a useful specimen: the trope can carry a whole plot, and here it carries one badly.
Leverage is offered and then withdrawn before anyone is held to anything, so the film raises blackmail and declines to run it.

entries.name: The Confession
entries.description: Voluntary disclosure — the party who was not caught and tells anyway.

examples.text: Nin discloses to several people in sequence and shapes the account differently for each, and the differences are readable side by side; the sharpest available lesson that a confession is composed for its listener.

Friday's contributors disclose to an intermediary who has promised anonymity, and the promise is what the material depends on; the confession's content is inseparable from the conditions under which it was given.
Lorde's disclosures are shaped toward a stated purpose and the book says so on the page, which is worth reading against the confessional mode's usual claim to be unshaped by anything at all.

entries.name: The Investigation
entries.description: A third party assembling the evidence, and becoming part of what they assemble.

examples.text: Campion's investigator is a participant before she knows it, and the film keeps the audience's information identical to hers; the design decision that separates this trope from a procedural.
The interviews are an investigation whose investigator is inside the case, and the method is exactly what generates the material — every answer changes his position rather than only his knowledge.
The record is compiled by its own subject, so there is no independent party and nothing can be corroborated; an investigation with only one witness is a deposition.

entries.name: The Cost Falling on Someone Else
entries.description: The consequence lands on a person who was not in the room.

examples.text: Baldwin places the heaviest cost on the character furthest from the encounter that caused it, and the distance is the point; the novel's structure is an argument about who actually pays.
Diderot has the consequences fall on a family and an order rather than on the participants, which converts a personal story into an institutional indictment without changing a single scene.
The lives around the summer are sketched and never billed, so nothing outside the pair is affected; a consequence that stops at the edge of the scene is not a consequence.

entries.name: The Consequence Refused
entries.description: The text that declines to punish, and what it has to supply instead.

examples.text: Ovid systematically refuses to attach a penalty to anything he advises, and the refusal is a position rather than an oversight; the poem's own author was relegated, which is the tradition's first demonstration that declining to write a consequence does not prevent one.

Sade's design punishes the virtuous sister and spares the other, and reading it as an argument against consequence as a narrative law explains why the ending has to be arbitrary — a refused consequence leaves the writer holding the ending problem directly.
Consequences reset between instalments, which is the serial's habit rather than a refusal; the distinction matters, because a text that forgets is doing something different from a text that declines.

entries.name: The Aftermath
entries.description: The scene after the scene — where this material's endings are actually found.

examples.text: Bright's editing repeatedly keeps the last page for the return to ordinary time rather than for the peak, and the collection is the best short-form training available in it. Study the endings against each other: the pieces that stop at the climax have to import a conclusion from outside, and the ones that stay for the aftermath end on something the story itself produced. This is the pack's organising problem in miniature, in the shortest form it occurs in.
The entire novel is an aftermath narrated from a single room on a single night, and the frame converts every earlier scene into evidence; the extreme case of letting the aftermath hold the book.

The ending replaces the aftermath with a further event, which is the commonest substitution in the form — the scene that would have to account for what happened is displaced by one more thing happening.

entries.name: The Hicklin Test and the Isolated Passage
entries.description: A standard that judged a book by its worst page, and the prose habit that followed from it.
entries.principle: R v Hicklin (1868) asked whether the tendency of the matter charged was to deprave and corrupt those into whose hands it might fall, and the operative words are the matter charged: a prosecutor could excerpt. Once the unit of legal risk is the passage rather than the book, the unit of composition becomes the passage too, and the safe sexual scene is one that does not survive excerption as a self-contained thing.
entries.example: *Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure* was already a century old when the test arrived, and its metaphor-dense manner — no coarse vocabulary anywhere in it — is the shape that a passage-by-passage standard rewards, whatever Cleland's own reasons were.
entries.application: The general observation that a legal regime shapes a literary form is old and is made elsewhere; what this collection offers is the specific mapping from a named test to a named habit. So read the fade as an inherited legal artefact before you read it as taste, and then decide whether you are using it or repeating it.
entries._label: The Legal Test and the Craft It Produced

entries.name: The Most Susceptible Reader and the Expensive Book
entries.description: Limiting who can obtain the book was a legal argument before it was a marketing one.
entries.principle: Hicklin's standard reader was the most corruptible hypothetical person into whose hands the work might fall, not the actual purchaser. That makes restricting the hands a defence, and it is the doctrinal engine behind the privately printed, subscription-only, deliberately expensive edition — a commercial form with a legal cause.
entries.example: *The Pearl* was mail-order, limited to a small print run and priced where only the wealthy could reach it, and the limitation was part of the design rather than a consequence of demand.
entries.application: If you are writing about this period, treat price, print run and imprint as plot facts rather than bibliography. A book that could only be bought by subscription was making an argument about its readership, and characters inside that trade knew it.
entries._label: The Legal Test and the Craft It Produced

entries.name: Motive Is Not a Defence
entries.description: The instinct that a serious purpose protects the work is exactly what Hicklin foreclosed.
entries.principle: Hicklin was decided on a religious-political pamphlet, and its actual innovation was to make the publisher's purpose irrelevant. With merit and motive both outside the test, seriousness could not be pleaded; it had to be built into the object as framing — the warning preface, the cautionary structure, the closing punishment that presents the book as a document rather than an entertainment.
entries.example: *My Secret Life* wears the documentary register throughout — dated, enumerated, quantified — and the register is doing framing work whether or not its compiler thought of it that way.
entries.application: When you write a moral frame, know which of the two jobs it is doing: making an argument to a reader, or making one to a hypothetical prosecutor. They produce different sentences, and a frame built for the second reads as insincere to the first.
entries._label: The Legal Test and the Craft It Produced

entries.name: Lord Campbell's Act and the Sanction Against Stock
