entries.example: *The Perfumed Garden* is Arabic and North African rather than Persian, a distinction routinely collapsed, and translations made directly from the Arabic did not appear until the second half of the twentieth century.
entries.application: When a writer reaches for an ancient-wisdom voice, the thing usually being reached for is this register at two removes. If you want it, go to a translation made from the original language and check which state of the text you are holding.

entries.name: Commercial Erotic Publishing Before Europe
entries.description: A mass paying readership for erotic prose existed seventy years before the first English case, in a market with no obscenity-law antagonist.
entries.principle: The prose of the floating world was written for and about an urban merchant class, sold in a functioning book trade, in colloquial language, and it developed without the European kind of legal opponent. This matters to periodisation and not only to the roster: a history that presents Europe as the origin of commercial erotic publishing is wrong on the dates, and it also mistakes a legal antagonism for a necessary condition.
entries.example: *Kōshoku Ichidai Otoko* appeared in 1682 and was followed within five years by three further titles from the same author, a body of work with a market rather than a scandal behind it.
entries.application: If your period story assumes that erotic writing must be clandestine, check the jurisdiction and the century. In some of them it was a trade with a shop, and a trade with a shop produces entirely different characters from a trade with a warehouse.

entries.category: Print, the Libertine Century and the Clandestine Trade
entries.name: The Press Changes Everything, and Keeps Changing It
entries.description: Mechanical reproduction produces a panic and then an apparatus, and the sequence has repeated identically ever since.
entries.principle: When sexual images and text became cheap, reproducible and hard to trace, an institutional response followed, and the pattern established then has recurred with every subsequent reproduction technology: the photograph, the paperback, the videotape, the network. The technology is new each time and the shape of the response is not, which is the most reliably predictive fact in this history.
entries.example: *Sonetti Lussuriosi* was written to accompany engravings already circulating without attribution; the dating is contested between conventions that count from the first engravings and from the first illustrated-with-sonnets edition, and its author's complete works were placed on the Index in 1559.
entries.application: If you are writing about a new medium and a moral panic, you are writing a story that has a known shape. Use the shape deliberately or subvert it deliberately, but do not present it as unprecedented, because your reader has seen it four times.

entries.category: Print, the Libertine Century and the Clandestine Trade
entries.name: The Whore's Education Is Invented
entries.description: The genre's most durable structure arrives in the seventeenth century and is still the armature of the initiation narrative.
entries.principle: The experienced woman instructing the naive one is a pedagogical frame wrapped around narrative — the ancient instructional voice folded into the newer fiction — and once invented it never leaves. It supplies exposition, escalation and a reason for the telling in a single device, which is why it survives every change of regime, medium and market that follows.
entries.example: *L'École des filles* is the founding instance and is one of a small group of seventeenth-century dialogues whose dates and attribution frames both need checking against a source rather than repeating, since several of them carry false attributions as part of their design.
entries.application: If you use the structure, remember that its power comes from the gap closing. An instructor who remains permanently ahead produces a lecture; the device works while the pupil is catching up.

entries.category: Print, the Libertine Century and the Clandestine Trade
entries.name: Respectable Prose for an Unrespectable Subject
entries.description: The founding demonstration that this genre's central problem is a problem of diction.
entries.principle: The most influential English erotic novel is written in elevated, metaphor-dense literary prose with no coarse vocabulary anywhere in it, and its influence established the two poles between which every subsequent writer has had to choose: figurative or clinical, with nothing comfortable in between. The choice is not about explicitness, since either pole can be entirely explicit; it is about which vocabulary the reader is asked to think in.
entries.example: *Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure* appeared in two instalments in 1748 and 1749, its author and publisher were arrested the following November, and the book was withdrawn after its author renounced it in court.
entries.application: Pick your pole consciously and hold it. Most failures of erotic prose are not failures of nerve or of taste but of consistency, a sentence that starts in one vocabulary and finishes in the other.

entries.category: Print, the Libertine Century and the Clandestine Trade
entries.name: The Erotic Becomes an Argument
entries.description: The point at which sexual writing acquires a thesis, and the contest that has surrounded it ever since.
entries.principle: In the libertine philosophical mode the sexual scenes are interleaved with expository dissertation, and the book's form is a treatise wearing a novel. The mode is genuinely contested and both positions are held by serious readers: that treating such work as philosophy launders what it depicts, and that it is the one body of writing that refuses to make desire consoling and is therefore diagnostically valuable.
entries.example: *La Philosophie dans le boudoir* appeared in 1795, in a sequence of publications running from 1791 to the end of the decade, and its structure alternates demonstration with debate as a matter of design rather than of padding.
entries.application: If you write erotic material with an argument in it, the argument has to be contestable inside the book. A demonstration no character can answer is a lecture, and readers of the mode arrive expecting the answering.

entries.category: Print, the Libertine Century and the Clandestine Trade
entries.name: The Supply Chain Is the Story
entries.description: What changed in the Victorian trade was not the writing but the distribution, and the writing changed because of it.
entries.principle: Cheap steam printing, a reliable postal service and a concentrated physical market produced a trade organised around not being found: small numbered runs, mail order, no shop window, false imprints. The literary consequence is the arrival of the documentary register — the enumerated, dated, quantified first-person record that presents itself as data rather than as art — and everything from the later confessional to the contemporary true-account framing descends from it.
entries.example: *The Pearl* ran eighteen issues between 1879 and 1880, limited to a small run and priced beyond ordinary reach, with its editor also its publisher and part of its authorship.
entries.application: Read the documentary register as a claim about purpose rather than as a style. It was doing legal work; it now does something else entirely, and knowing the difference is what stops you from using it as mere flatness.

entries.category: Print, the Libertine Century and the Clandestine Trade
entries.name: The Writer's Name Becomes a Diagnosis
entries.description: For the first time a novelist's surname is converted into a clinical category on the evidence of his fiction.
entries.principle: In 1886 a psychiatrist coined a diagnostic term from a living novelist's name, justifying it explicitly by the content of the novels. The earlier figure whose name had already become an adjective had been dead for seventy-two years; this one was alive and objected. That is the historical root of the still-current confusion between depicting a desire and having it, and it is the origin of the question every erotic writer is eventually asked.
entries.example: *Venus im Pelz* appeared in 1870 as part of a projected cycle, and the term derived from its author's name has long since detached from both the book and the man.
entries.application: When you are asked whether your fiction is autobiography, the question has a history and it is not a compliment or an insult. Knowing where it comes from is more useful than having a witty answer to it.

entries.name: Two Verdicts in One Year, and the Moral Frame Is French
entries.description: The punished-transgression ending is eleven years older than the English test it is usually credited to.
entries.principle: In 1857 a single French court acquitted a novel in February and convicted a book of poems in August, and the difference turned on form: a novel can be read as delivering a consequence and a lyric sequence has nowhere to put one. The moral-warning frame is therefore French and pre-Hicklin, and its cleanest proof is a controlled comparison inside one year and one jurisdiction rather than an inference from English practice.
entries.example: *Les Fleurs du mal* carried the suppression of six poems for the rest of its author's life, and the conviction was annulled only in 1949, under a statute passed in 1946 specifically to permit such revisions; the fine's amount is given differently by different official sources and should not be carded from memory.
entries.application: Attribute conventions to the regime that actually produced them. Getting this one right also gets the mechanism right — it was the shape of the book rather than the quantity of its content that decided the outcome.

entries.name: Hicklin, and the Century It Set
entries.description: One sentence in 1868 organised English-language erotic writing for a hundred years, and outlived its own jurisdiction.
entries.principle: The test asked whether the tendency of the matter charged was to deprave those into whose hands it might fall, and each clause produced a habit: the isolated-passage rule produced the unexcerptable scene, the most-susceptible-reader rule produced the expensive limited edition, and the irrelevance of motive produced the moral frame. It was received into American federal practice, survived there for decades, and remained good law in at least one other jurisdiction into the present century.
entries.example: The pamphlet the case actually concerned was an anti-Catholic polemic rather than an erotic work, and the decision's real innovation was the elimination of purpose as a defence.
entries.application: A writer's instinct is to say that the intention was serious. That is precisely the argument this test foreclosed, and its long afterlife is why seriousness had to be built into books as an object rather than pleaded as a state of mind.

entries.name: Modernism Collides with Procedure
entries.description: The mechanism was customs and the post office, and the defence changed shape in response.
entries.principle: Modernist novels were stopped at borders and in mail sorting rooms rather than pursued through general policing, and the resulting cases forced courts to invent the tests of the work as a whole and of redeeming value. In doing so the defence made a permanent trade: it stopped arguing that the book was not sexual and started arguing that it was literature. Every subsequent defence has made the same trade, which is why literary merit became a legally operative concept.
entries.example: *Lady Chatterley's Lover* was privately printed in Florence in 1928 and in Paris the following year, with expurgated commercial editions appearing in 1932, and its two best-known proceedings — an American postal case and an English criminal prosecution — are separate matters a year apart and are constantly merged.
entries.application: If your plot uses a famous obscenity case, find out which door the book was stopped at. Postal, customs and criminal proceedings put different people in danger and produce different scenes.

entries.name: A Separate Legal History
entries.description: For a century the threshold for same-sex material sat far below the threshold for everything else, and that produced a parallel tradition rather than a subset.
entries.principle: The clearest evidence is a novel containing no explicit content whatever that was ordered destroyed for the existence of its subject, banned in its home country for two decades while being cleared in another within months. A different threshold produces different institutions: separate presses, separate distribution, separate coding, and a line that runs alongside the main one rather than inside it. Treating it as a subset breaks the periodisation and not merely the roster.
entries.example: *The Well of Loneliness* was ruled obscene in London in November 1928 with an appeal dismissed in minutes, and was cleared in New York the following April after an initial finding against it.
entries.application: If you write this history, do not merge the two lines. The dates do not match, the mechanisms do not match, and the crafts that developed under them are not the same craft.

entries.name: The Arbitrage, and Why It Failed
entries.description: Publishing in English in a country whose censors did not read English was a business model with a specific expiry.
entries.principle: Books unpublishable in English-speaking countries could be printed in France for readers who would carry them home, and the arrangement produced the genre's densest concentration of publisher-owned pseudonyms, commissioned to specification. It is usually told as a story about a haven. It was an arbitrage, it was closed by the French authorities from the late 1950s, its principal publisher was out of the country by 1963, and it created no precedent whatsoever.
entries.example: *The Ginger Man* came out of this list, where writing to a commercial specification and remaining permanently canonical overlap more heavily than anywhere else in the tradition — which is the strongest argument available against treating commissioned erotica as automatically inferior.
entries.application: Distinguish evasion from confrontation when you write a publisher. Evasion produces a business that ends quietly and changes nothing; confrontation produces a precedent that protects everybody afterwards, and the two make opposite kinds of character.

entries.name: Merit Becomes a Statutory Defence
entries.description: A legislature wrote down that literary value is a defence and that witnesses may prove it, and post-war erotic writing is downstream of that sentence.
entries.principle: The English statute of 1959 admitted publication for the public good on grounds of literature, science, art or learning, and expressly made expert evidence admissible. In the United States a plurality decision seven years later required that material be utterly without redeeming social value before it could be condemned, which for seven years made any demonstrable value a complete answer. Between them, these two instruments made seriousness worth building into the object.
entries.example: *Naked Lunch* was found not obscene in Massachusetts in 1966 on precisely that ground — that a substantial and intelligent group in the community believed it to have literary significance — four months after the test it was decided under was handed down.
entries.application: The apparatus of that period, the critic's foreword and the note on the text, was an element-by-element answer to a legal test rather than authorial vanity. Read it that way before you either adopt it or mock it.

entries.name: Theory Arrives
entries.description: Eroticism becomes something a book can be about rather than only something a book can contain.
entries.principle: The post-war French line supplied the form its first sustained theory — eroticism as an assent to life extending into death, continuity purchased by the violation of the discrete self — and once such an account exists it becomes possible to write erotica that is about eroticism rather than merely composed of it. That is a change in what the material can be for, and it is the origin of the literary mode's claim to be doing something other than performing a service.
entries.example: *L'Érotisme* appeared in 1957, three decades after the same author's founding erotic fiction, so the theory follows the practice rather than producing it — a chronology that the usual account of this tradition reverses.
entries.application: If you write in the theoretical mode, keep the fiction ahead of the argument as this line did. A book written to illustrate a theory of desire tends to read as an illustration, and readers of the mode can tell within a page.

entries.name: The Authorship Contest
entries.description: The most-discussed attribution in the form's history, unresolved for forty years and contested in its meaning even after it was resolved.
entries.principle: A book published in 1954 under a pen name, prefaced by an established man of letters who professed not to know its author while being both its addressee and its instigator, was acknowledged by its author only in 1994. The identification settles a fact and not the argument. One reading holds that the book's power and its scandal both depend on a woman having written it. The other holds that it was written to and for its prefacer, in answer to his provocation, and shaped by his hand, so that single-author attribution flattens a genuinely asymmetrical production. Both are held by serious scholars.
entries.example: *Histoire d'O* is also the pack's hardest pseudonym case, running a dedicated pen name over a professional one over a legal name, so its author appears in the record under three names of three different kinds.
entries.application: When you research an attribution, separate the factual question from the interpretive one. Establishing who held the pen very often leaves the argument about what that means exactly where it was, and a card or an essay that treats the first as settling the second has stopped reporting.

entries.name: The Sex Wars
entries.description: The argument that split feminism over pornography, and the reason two words for this material still mean different things to different readers.
entries.principle: Between the late 1970s and the early 1990s two positions were set out at full strength and neither prevailed. One held that pornography is not speech about subordination but an act of it, produced through coercion and consumed as training in contempt, and framed its remedy as a civil rights claim giving harmed individuals a private action rather than as criminal obscenity law. The other held that any machinery built to suppress it would be turned first on feminist, lesbian and sexually dissident material, and that sexuality requires a theory of its own rather than a derivative one.
entries.example: An ordinance embodying the first position was enacted in 1984, struck down by a federal appellate court in 1985 and summarily affirmed against in 1986, so the argument was decided as constitutional law and not as a question about what pornography does.
entries.application: This is why the words erotica and pornography are two names for one thing to some readers and a crucial distinction to others. Whichever you use, you are taking a position in an argument that has not ended, and it is better to know that than to discover it in a review.

entries.name: The Chain Disappears
entries.description: Text-only distribution removed the printer, the customs officer and the bookshop in a single move.
entries.principle: Every constraint in the preceding two centuries of this history operated on a physical object passing through identifiable hands. Networked text has no printer to raid, no border to cross and no shop to close, so the entire apparatus described in this pack's legal collection became inapplicable at once — not repealed, simply bypassed. What replaced it was not freedom but a different chokehold, and the rest of this collection is about where that chokehold moved.
entries.example: The archives and newsgroups of the 1990s carried an enormous body of erotic writing under no publisher's imprint at all, which is the first time in this history that a large erotic literature existed with no commercial intermediary anywhere in it.
entries.application: When you write about censorship in a networked setting, find the new choke point rather than assuming the old one. The interesting scene is no longer the raid; it is the account suspension, and it has no warrant, no hearing and no appeal.

entries.name: The Unpaid Apprenticeship
entries.description: A vast non-commercial training system with real-time reader feedback, and where a large share of working writers learned pacing.
entries.principle: Fan communities produced the largest body of erotic writing currently being made, outside the market entirely, with no gatekeeper, no advance and no scarcity — so the shaping constraints became social and infrastructural rather than editorial. The tag, the comment and the platform's terms of service replaced the editor, and writers learned pacing from immediate response at a volume no commercial apprenticeship has ever offered.
entries.example: The content-tagging vocabularies these communities developed are materially more granular than any retailer's classification scheme and are applied by authors rather than imposed, which makes them the most detailed public record that exists of what readers of this form seek and avoid.
entries.application: Read the tag vocabulary as craft information. It is a working taxonomy built by readers describing what they actually want, and there is nothing else like it available to a writer in this form.

entries.name: The Cover Disappears
entries.description: The most underrated economic fact in the form's history: the purchasing friction had always been social visibility rather than price.
entries.principle: For two centuries the constraint on buying erotic books was being seen buying, carrying and owning them, and every commercial form the trade developed — the plain wrapper, the mail order, the discreet imprint — was an answer to that single problem. The e-reader solved it completely and by accident, and the resulting demand was not created by the technology so much as released by it.
entries.example: The commercial breakout of the early 2010s is unintelligible without this fact, since the same material had been continuously available in print and had never reached that scale.
entries.application: If your story turns on a character's embarrassment about reading something, place it before this change. After it, the emotion is available but the mechanism is not, and the mechanism is what made the emotion dramatic.

entries.name: The Gatekeeper Goes, and the Economics Invert
entries.description: Direct publishing removed the acquiring editor and replaced an advance economy with a velocity economy.
entries.principle: Self-publishing platforms removed the person who decided what existed, and with them the advance, the print run and the two-year cycle. What replaced them rewards series over standalones, speed over polish, and a direct relationship with readers over a relationship with a house. That is a craft constraint and not merely a commercial one: it selects for a sustained relationship rather than a completed arc, which is why so much recent work is structurally serial where the entire earlier canon is episodic or closed.
entries.example: A dedicated erotic-romance publisher whose founding year is given variously as 1999, 2000 and 2001 by different sources — one trade account resolving it as selling from 2000 and incorporating in 2001 — was selling roughly two hundred thousand books a month by 2012, attributed its decline to the direct-publishing platform rather than to any censorship, and ceased operations at the end of 2016.
entries.application: If you are writing to this market, the structural decision is series or standalone, and it is made before the first chapter. Retrofitting a series onto a finished standalone is the most expensive mistake available in this form.

entries.name: The Enforcement Unit Is the Shelf
entries.description: When a retailer responds to a content panic it does not filter, it suspends a category.
entries.principle: A press investigation in October 2013 became a national newspaper story about self-published material on sale at a high-street retailer, and the retailers responded within days. One shut its entire website behind a holding page until every self-published ebook could be removed; another suspended sale of all self-published titles in one market and then in two more; a third closed its ebook store altogether. Both of the sources documenting it are emphatic that the purge did not land on its target: authors who do not write erotica lost titles, and compliant erotica was deleted anyway.
entries.example: Roughly 7,883 self-published titles were removed through a single distribution channel during the episode, and that is the point rather than the number — the retailers acted on the channel and not on the content, which is exactly why compliant work and work that was not erotica at all disappeared together.
entries.application: Understand that in this form you are exposed to the conduct of writers you have never read. The practical consequences are unglamorous and real: keep your files, keep your reader list off the platform, and do not let a single storefront be the only place your work exists.

entries.name: The Private Chokehold
entries.description: The operative constraint on this material is now contractual and financial, and it has no jurisdiction, no hearing and no appeal.
entries.principle: Payment networks set acceptable-use standards for the banks and merchants they serve, and those standards reach any seller anywhere, applying a single commercial rule across every legal system at once. Nothing removed under them has been found unlawful by anybody. The layer is tighter than any statute in this pack's legal collection, its criteria are not published in usable form, and there is no procedure by which a writer can contest an outcome.
entries.example: A card network's public statement of August 2022 reinforcing its adult-content standards is the point at which this constraint became written policy rather than case-by-case pressure, and it is the single most citable document in the sequence.
entries.application: If you sell directly, read your processor's acceptable-use policy before you read any retailer's content guidelines. It is the document that actually governs, and most writers in this form have never seen it.

entries.name: The Mechanism, and Its Portability
entries.description: A small advocacy body petitions the processors, the processors press the platforms, and the platforms suspend a category.
entries.principle: The sequence has a stable shape and it does not require a law, a court or a finding of any kind. In mid-2025 a games platform removed hundreds of titles citing processor pressure after a campaign that had first written to the company directly; on 24 July 2025 another platform deindexed everything tagged as adult and said it was complying with processor requirements in order to remain viable, and from 1 August it began reindexing free adult content while paid content remained pending. The widely quoted before-and-after search counts for that action are not carried here: they circulate without a source and the platform's own posts give no figure.
entries.example: The second platform hosts a large body of text-based work, so written material was inside a tag-level sweep aimed at something else — the precise exposure of text in that action is not established here, but tag-level enforcement cannot have exempted it.
entries.application: This mechanism is portable to any bookseller, and nothing about it is specific to games. Assume it applies to you, and note that the pressure point is three steps removed from anyone who has read your book.

entries.name: The Filter Rather Than the Gate
entries.description: The modern sanction is not removal but unfindability, and it has no official name.
entries.principle: A title flagged as adult at the largest retailer remains purchasable at its direct address and disappears from search, browse and category listings, which makes it effectively invisible to anyone not already looking for it. The authors it happens to have a name for it and the retailer does not; there is no notification, no stated criterion and no appeal, and the affected writer usually infers the state from a collapse in sales.
entries.example: The condition is discussed continuously in author forums, in author blogs and on commercial advice sites under the community's own term for it, and the absence of any official terminology is itself the finding.
entries.application: Metadata is now a craft surface in this form. Title, subtitle, cover, category and keyword choices determine whether a book is discoverable at all, and they are made after the writing but they are not separable from it.

entries.name: A Payment Model Changed and a Literature Ended
entries.description: The best-documented case in the library of a market structure operating directly as a craft constraint.
entries.principle: A subscription programme launched in July 2014 paying per borrow regardless of length made short erotica briefly and extraordinarily profitable. The payment model was announced in June 2015 and took effect that July, switching to payment per page read; a standardised page count was already in force at that point and was revised, with a cap, in February 2016. Under a per-page model there is no break-even length at all, only a rate, and the effect on short work was immediate and severe.
entries.example: One reported title earning roughly a hundred and fifty dollars a day under the first model earned three hundred and sixty-four dollars across its entire lifetime under the second, a comparison of one work against itself rather than a market figure.
entries.application: Notice what the change actually did. Rewarding length at that scale did not merely make short erotica unprofitable — it pushed its writers across the boundary this pack is built on, from a form with no guaranteed ending and a short natural length into one with both. A payment model made for unrelated reasons selected for a different genre.

entries.name: Velocity as a Formal Pressure
entries.description: Release cadence became a structural constraint on the writing rather than a business practice around it.
entries.principle: Where discovery depends on recency and on series momentum, the schedule enters the composition: books are planned to a length that can be delivered on a cycle, hooks are front-loaded because a sample decides the sale, and instalments end on escalation because the next one is already listed. These are the serial's old habits arriving through an economic door rather than a legal one, and they produce the same characteristic weakness.
entries.example: The rapid-release pattern reproduces the Victorian part-issue's formal signature — the recap, the threshold ending, the indefinitely extensible cast — a century and a half later and for entirely different reasons.
entries.application: If you write to a cadence, budget one thing per instalment that changes permanently. That is the single discipline that separates a series from a treadmill, and it costs nothing but planning.

entries.name: Discovery Replaced Censorship as the Binding Constraint
entries.description: The present-day problem for a writer in this form is not being stopped, it is not being found.
entries.principle: In the Anglophone jurisdictions the legal exposure of written erotic material has largely fallen away, and what constrains a working writer now is a stack of private layers — processor rules, storefront policy, the adult filter, category and keyword systems, and the recommendation engine. None of them is a censor in the sense this pack's legal collection describes, and together they determine whether a book has readers, which is the outcome censorship was aiming at.
entries.example: The two large disruptions of the platform era, in 2013 and in 2025, were both triggered by campaigns rather than by proceedings, and in neither case was anything removed found unlawful by any authority.
entries.application: Plan for invisibility rather than for prosecution. The historical anxiety of this form is the raid; the actual one is a silent change to a ranking, and the defences against the two have nothing in common.

entries.name: The Continuity Nobody Names
entries.description: The private distribution chokehold is not new; it is the oldest mechanism in this history wearing current clothes.
entries.principle: A body with no legal power to ban anything, whose force comes entirely from distributors declining to carry unclassified or unapproved material, is the structure of a film industry's self-regulation, of a wholesaler's refusal to stock, and of a payment network's acceptable-use standard. In each case nothing is unlawful, no authority has ruled, and the material is unobtainable. Reading the present arrangement as unprecedented misses that the state has usually been the weaker of the two constraints on this material.
entries.example: The classification body most often described as a censor in one major market is a private foundation with no power to prohibit anything, and its practical authority rests on venue owners refusing unclassified work — the same shape as a processor standard, arrived at seventy years earlier.
entries.application: When you research a constraint, ask who can actually stop the object reaching a reader. It is usually not the person with the statute, and this has been true for most of the period this pack covers.

entries.name: Two Purges, One Shape
entries.description: The 2013 retailer purge and the 2025 processor sweep are the same event with different actors, and carding them as a pair is what makes the pattern visible.
entries.principle: In the first, a newspaper triggers retailers and retailers suspend a category. In the second, an advocacy group triggers processors, processors pressure platforms, and platforms suspend a category. In neither case was the enforcement unit the individual book, in both cases the collateral damage exceeded the stated target, and in both the affected writers had no forum in which to be heard. A twelve-year interval and an added intermediary are the only differences.
entries.example: The second episode's decisive moment is a whole tag being deindexed in a day on a policy change announced as compliance rather than as judgement, and the fact that its scale is quoted everywhere from no traceable source is itself part of what carding it teaches.
entries.application: Expect a third. The shape is stable enough to plan against, and the planning is the same each time: own your list, keep your files, and do not be single-homed.

entries.name: What This Pack Does Not Know About the Present
entries.description: The closing card, naming the live gaps rather than covering them.
entries.principle: This collection's account of the present is uneven and says so. The subscription economics are researched and load-bearing; the retailer purge is well documented; the processor sequence is dated but several of its individual events are recorded here as partial rather than confirmed. What is not established is how the adult filter interacts with subscription discovery, whether short-form work is eligible on the same terms as long, and the current state of the most recent platform restorations.
entries.example: The single most consequential live question for a working writer in this form — how short erotica fares under per-page subscription economics and under the adult filter simultaneously — is unresearched here, and a pack that implied otherwise would be more useful only in the sense that a wrong answer is faster than none.
entries.application: Treat the platform cards as a map of mechanisms rather than as current operating detail, and check any specific policy against the platform itself before acting on it. Mechanisms in this territory have proved stable for a century and a half; the policies change quarterly.

entries.name: Nothing Here Was Designed to Answer a Question About Prose
entries.description: The first card, because it conditions every other card in the collection.
entries.principle: Almost the entire empirical literature on desire and arousal uses film or audio material presented in a laboratory. A writer taking guidance from it is extrapolating across a medium boundary the studies did not test, and no study located for this pack was built to say anything about reading. Robustness tier: robust as a description of the literature's own design, since it is a statement about what the studies used rather than about what they found.
entries.example: The closest thing to a text-relevant study in the modern literature uses audio narratives rather than prose, and its authors describe its samples as small.
entries.application: Read the rest of this collection as background on human beings rather than as instruction about pages. Where a finding seems to imply a craft rule, the implication is yours and not the study's, and it should be held that loosely.

entries.name: The Outcome Measure Is Not Agreed
entries.description: There are at least three incompatible ways of measuring arousal and no principled basis for preferring one.
entries.principle: Arousal is measured by genital vasocongestion, by self-report on a dial or a scale, and more recently by neuroimaging. These do not agree with each other, and no argument establishes any of them as the criterion the others should be judged against. One of the instruments also yields a signal in arbitrary units, which supports comparison within a person but not between people. Robustness tier: robust, since the disagreement between measures is the best-established fact in the field.
entries.example: The most-cited quantitative result in the whole area is a number describing how poorly two of these measures agree, which is a finding about instruments as much as about people.
entries.application: Whenever you meet a claim about arousal, ask which instrument produced it. Two studies reporting opposite things frequently measured different quantities and are not in conflict at all.

entries.name: Who Volunteers, and Who Is Sampled
entries.description: The people in these studies are not a cross-section of anybody, and the field says so itself.
entries.principle: Volunteer bias in this area is severe and specific: people who agree to genital measurement in a laboratory or to detailed fantasy questionnaires differ systematically from those who decline, in sexual experience, attitude and sensation-seeking. Samples are also overwhelmingly undergraduate and drawn from a narrow set of wealthy Western societies, in a domain where cultural variation should be expected to be large. Robustness tier: robust, and it is the most cited limitation in the field's own reviews.
entries.example: The volunteer problem is not hypothetical or theoretical; it is stated as a limitation by the reviewers of this literature rather than by its critics.
entries.application: Treat every number here as a fact about a particular set of volunteers. That is not a reason to dismiss the work, and it is a reason to refuse any sentence beginning with a claim about people in general.

entries.name: What This Pack Refuses to Card
entries.description: Seven claims commonly found in craft writing about this genre, and why none of them appears here.
entries.principle: This pack declines to card the following: that the body contradicts the mind; that one desire pattern belongs to one sex and another to the other; any prevalence figure for force or non-consent fantasy; erotic plasticity as an established finding; any claim that reading arouses differently from viewing; trade-book survey percentages as population rates; and anything phrased as what women want. Each is either a mis-statement of a real result, a comparison across studies that define their terms differently, or a contested position presented as settled. Robustness tier: not applicable, since this card states policy rather than reporting a finding.
entries.example: The best known of the seven inverts an actual result, restating a weaker average correlation as though it were a contradiction between two things, which is a different claim entirely.
entries.application: When a craft book states any of these as fact, it is not that the underlying research is bad; it is that the sentence is not what the research says. Go to what was measured, and you will usually find a smaller and more interesting claim.

entries.name: Responsive and Spontaneous Desire
entries.description: A real and useful distinction that has been popularised into something the literature does not support.
entries.principle: The model holds that desire frequently follows arousal rather than preceding it, so that a person may begin from neutrality, be moved by a stimulus into arousal, and experience desire as a consequence. The existence of that pattern is well supported. What is not supported is the popular version in which one pattern belongs to women and the other to men: both occur in both, and leading researchers in the area explicitly deny that any single model describes all women. Robustness tier: contested, with the existence of the pattern well supported and its distribution disputed.
entries.example: The model was proposed against earlier linear sequences that put desire first, and the argument between them concerns the ordering of stages rather than whether either pattern is real.
entries.application: The craft use is structural rather than descriptive. A scene in which desire arrives after arousal has a different shape from one where it arrives first — the decision, and the character's surprise at herself, land in different places — and both scenes are available to any character.

entries.name: Desire and Arousal May Not Be Separable in Experience
entries.description: A strong minority position holds that the distinction the research relies on is not one people actually make.
entries.principle: Researchers in the area have argued that subjective arousal and desire may not be distinguishable from the inside, and diagnostic frameworks have moved toward combining them rather than separating them. If that is right, a substantial body of work has been asking respondents to separate two things they do not experience as two. Robustness tier: contested, and it is a live disagreement among researchers rather than a criticism from outside the field.
entries.example: One study of a clinical population found that a large majority of participants did not distinguish the two in the way the instruments assumed.
entries.application: On the page this is a permission rather than a constraint. A character need not know which of the two she is feeling, and writing the confusion is more accurate to the literature than writing a clean separation would be.

entries.name: Non-Concordance
entries.description: The field's most solid quantitative result, and it is a statement about correlation.
entries.principle: A meta-analysis of a hundred and thirty-two laboratory studies, covering several thousand participants, found a significant sex difference in the agreement between self-reported and genital arousal, with men's correlation around two-thirds and women's around a quarter. The authors themselves identified moderators — how variable the stimulus was, and when the self-report was taken — so part of the difference is a function of how the studies were built. Robustness tier: robust as a description, contested as to cause.
entries.example: The result has held for fifteen years as a description and its interpretation has not converged in that time, which is an unusual and informative combination.
entries.application: This is the single finding in the collection most often converted into a craft rule, and it will not bear one. It says that two measurements agree less than expected, and it says nothing about what a reader experiences.

entries.name: What Non-Concordance Does Not Mean
entries.description: A weak correlation is not an anti-correlation, and the popular restatement is the opposite of the finding.
entries.principle: The result above is widely restated as the body saying yes while the mind says no. That is not what was measured. A lower average correlation means the two measures track each other less closely, not that they systematically oppose each other, and the restatement converts a quantitative finding into a claim about a person overruling herself. Robustness tier: not applicable, since this card corrects a mis-statement rather than reporting a finding.
entries.example: The figures involved are a correlation of about two-thirds against one of about a quarter, and a correlation of a quarter is a weak positive relationship rather than a negative one.
entries.application: The mis-statement is common in craft writing and it is doing real damage, because a scene built on it is a scene about a body overruling a person's stated wishes. Whatever a writer thinks of that as material, it should not be adopted on the authority of a study that did not find it.

entries.name: Three Live Interpretations, None Settled
entries.description: What the concordance difference means is genuinely open, and the three candidates imply different things.
entries.principle: The first candidate holds that one genital response is relatively non-discriminating because its function is protective rather than appetitive; a recent review by researchers sympathetic to it calls the evidence favourable but not entirely convincing. The second holds that the instruments measure different physical quantities with different signal properties, so part of the difference may be instrumental; work on a new instrument is early-stage. The third points to attention and to how accurately internal states are read. Robustness tier: contested, with the first two actively argued and the third not classifiable from the material available here.
entries.example: Each interpretation has published support and published contradiction, and the review most favourable to the first candidate declines to declare it established.
entries.application: If a scene turns on why a body responded, you are writing inside an open scientific question and the honest thing is to let the character be uncertain too. Certainty on this point is available only to writers who have not read the argument.

entries.name: Averages Are Not Categories
entries.description: The differences in this literature are differences between group means with enormous overlap.
entries.principle: Every sex difference reported in this area is a difference in average, measured across narrow self-selected samples, with variation inside each group far larger than the distance between the groups. Later work reports substantial within-group variation in exactly the specificity that the headline results describe. A mean difference licenses no statement about any individual. Robustness tier: robust, since it is a property of the statistics rather than a finding about people.
entries.example: The best-known result in the field is a difference between two correlation coefficients, and a correlation coefficient is a summary of a scatter that includes people at every point in it.
entries.application: This is why any sentence beginning with what women want is refused in this pack. Write the character, not the mean, and if a reader recognises herself it will be because the character is specific rather than because she is average.

entries.name: Habituation
entries.description: Response to a repeated stimulus declines, which is the empirical basis of this pack's escalation problem.
entries.principle: Repeated presentation of the same material produces a declining response, and this is among the better-established observations in the area. It is a property of attention rather than a fact about anybody's character, and it operates within a session and within a work. This is the mechanism underneath the structural claim made elsewhere in this pack: that a sequence of similar encounters loses the reader regardless of how good any individual one is. Robustness tier: robust as an observation, with the parameters — how fast, under what conditions, for how long — largely unestablished.
entries.example: Habituation appears in this literature as a supporting finding for other arguments rather than as a subject in its own right, and no study located for this pack measured it on prose.
entries.application: Assume the effect and design against it, but do not assume any particular rate. The craft response — vary kind rather than degree, and let consequence rather than intensity carry the sequence — does not depend on knowing the numbers.

entries.name: Context in Narrative Material
entries.description: The one study closest to what this pack is about, and it is small.
entries.principle: A study using audio narratives varied the relationship context between the participants described and measured genital and subjective response, which makes it the nearest thing in the modern literature to a test of narrative rather than image. Its samples were small and its authors describe one of them as underpowered by their own account. Robustness tier: unreplicated, and the authors themselves flag the sample sizes.
entries.example: That this is the closest available study to the question a writer would actually ask is itself the more useful finding, and it is a finding about the literature rather than about readers.
entries.application: Do not build anything on it, and do note what it suggests: that the described relation between characters is a variable the body responds to. Every writer in this form already assumed that, which is a reason to be suspicious of how readily one agrees with it.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: Fantasy Does Not Predict Behaviour
entries.description: The one robust finding in this area that a writer in this form most needs, and the one most often left unsaid.
entries.principle: The literature does not support inference from what a person imagines to what a person wants to happen, seeks out or would consent to. The two are separately measured and are not the same variable, and the assumption that they run together is a folk theory rather than a research finding. Robustness tier: robust, in the sense that the predictive link is not established rather than that its absence has been proved.
entries.example: The point recurs across reviews of the fantasy literature and is one of the few places where the field's reviewers converge.
entries.application: This is the answer to the question every writer in this form is eventually asked about their own work, and it is also a constraint on the work: a character's fantasies tell the reader what she imagines and not what she will do, which makes them a poor engine for plot and an excellent one for interiority.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: There Is No Standard Definition of Fantasy
entries.description: Studies mean at least four different things by the word, so their numbers cannot be compared.
entries.principle: Across this literature sexual fantasy variously means a deliberate daydream, an involuntary intrusive image, a masturbatory script, or any sexual thought at all. These are not the same object and they do not produce comparable prevalence figures, a criticism made by the field's own reviewers rather than by outsiders. Robustness tier: robust as a criticism, and it is stated inside the literature it applies to.
entries.example: A figure derived from questionnaires about deliberate daydreaming and one derived from questionnaires about any sexual thought are routinely quoted side by side as if they measured a single thing.
entries.application: When you meet a percentage about fantasy, find the definition before you find the number. In practice the definition is usually not given, which is itself the answer about how much weight the number will bear.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: Force and Non-Consent Fantasy
entries.description: What is established here is narrow, and what circulates is much wider.
entries.principle: Two things are reasonably well supported: such fantasies are not rare, and fantasy of this kind does not predict any corresponding wish, behaviour or consent. What is not supported is any specific prevalence figure, because the studies define the category differently and their numbers are not comparable. The distinction between an imagined scenario and a wanted event is the whole of what the literature establishes here, and it is enough. Robustness tier: robust as to non-rarity and non-prediction, unclassifiable as to prevalence.
entries.example: Reviews in this area state the definitional problem explicitly before reporting any figure, and the figures nonetheless circulate detached from the caveat that was printed above them.
entries.application: The material is available to a writer and it is analysed here as craft rather than either promoted or deplored. What is not available is a statistic, and a scene that leans on one has borrowed authority it cannot support.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: Why No Prevalence Figures Appear in This Pack
entries.description: The refusal stated as its own card, so that a later reader can see it was a decision.
entries.principle: Prevalence numbers for fantasy content are omitted from this pack throughout, not because they are unavailable but because they are not comparable: differing definitions, self-selected samples, and instruments that ask about different objects. A number carried into a craft reference acquires an authority its source did not have, and the acquisition is silent. Robustness tier: not applicable, since this card states policy rather than reporting a finding.
entries.example: The same underlying survey material is quoted at widely different figures in different craft books, which is what a definitional problem looks like from outside the literature.
entries.application: If you want a figure for a scene, write the character instead. A percentage tells your reader nothing about the person on the page, and it will be wrong in a way that a reader who knows the field will notice.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: Trade-Book Percentages Are Not Population Rates
entries.description: A large and useful survey is not a census, and the difference is where most misuse happens.
entries.principle: A widely cited trade book reporting a large online survey of fantasy content is a real body of data and a poor basis for statements about how common anything is, because its respondents recruited themselves. Large samples do not correct for self-selection; they make the resulting figures more precise about the wrong population. Robustness tier: contested as to generalisability, with the underlying data itself not in dispute.
entries.example: The book's percentages appear throughout craft writing about this genre as population rates, which is a use its own methodology section does not support.
entries.application: Read it for the taxonomy rather than the arithmetic. Its value to a writer is the range of things people report imagining, and the range is informative regardless of what proportion imagines each.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: Content and Function
entries.description: What a fantasy is about and what it is doing are different questions, and the second is the writer's.
entries.principle: The literature largely catalogues content, because content is what a questionnaire can capture. Function — what the imagined scenario accomplishes for the person imagining it, whether relief, rehearsal, escape, control, or something with no available name — is much less studied and much harder to measure. That asymmetry means the research is strongest exactly where a writer needs it least. Robustness tier: unclassifiable, since function is under-studied rather than contested.
entries.example: The available taxonomies sort by theme rather than by purpose, so two people whose fantasies are recorded identically may be doing entirely different things with them.
entries.application: Write the function. Two characters with the same fantasy and different reasons for it are two characters; two characters with the same fantasy and no stated reason are one character described twice.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: The Scenario Nobody Wants to Happen
entries.description: The gap between imagining and wanting is not a paradox to be explained away.
entries.principle: A person may repeatedly imagine an event they would refuse, fear, or be harmed by. Nothing in the literature makes that anomalous, and the folk instinct to resolve it — by deciding the person secretly wants it, or that the fantasy must be about something else — is an inference the research does not license in either direction. Robustness tier: robust as to the gap's existence, unclassifiable as to its explanation.
entries.example: The non-prediction finding is precisely a statement that this gap is ordinary, and treating it as a puzzle requiring resolution is where most confident writing about fantasy goes wrong.
entries.application: On the page the gap is the material, and a character who cannot account for her own imagination is more truthful than one who can. What a writer should resist is the pressure, from readers and from editors, to explain it.

entries.category: Fantasy and What It Does Not Predict
entries.name: What a Writer Can Actually Take From This
entries.description: The short list, after everything the collection has refused.
entries.principle: Four things survive: response to repetition declines; imagining does not predict wanting; the various measures of arousal disagree with one another and no one of them is authoritative; and every group difference reported here is an average across narrow samples with large overlap. Everything else in this collection is either contested, unreplicated, or a statement about the literature rather than about people. Robustness tier: not applicable, since this card summarises the collection rather than reporting a finding.
entries.example: A list of four is a small return from a large literature, and that is the honest size of it for a writer's purposes.
entries.application: Those four are worth having and are enough to work with. The rest of what a writer needs about desire is not in this literature at all, and is in the reading, the noticing and the drafting.

entries.name: The Medium Boundary
entries.description: Every finding here was produced with film or audio, and prose is a different object.
entries.principle: Prose supplies no image, no voice and no timing; the reader supplies all three, at a pace they control and can stop. Whatever is true of a supplied moving image under laboratory conditions has not been shown to hold of a constructed one under a reading lamp, and no study located for this pack tested the difference. Robustness tier: not applicable, since this card states a limit on the evidence rather than a finding.
entries.example: The closest available study substituted audio narrative for image, which narrows the gap by one step and does not close it.
entries.application: This is the single most important caveat in the collection and it applies to every card in it. A writer who forgets it will end up with craft rules derived from an experiment nobody ran.

entries.name: The Genuine Negative Result
entries.description: There is no locatable research on prose style and arousal at all, and that is worth carding.
entries.principle: Register, point of view, tense, sentence length, paragraph shape, the choice between figurative and clinical vocabulary — none of these has been studied against any measure of response that this pack could locate. The absence is total rather than partial, and a craft reference implying otherwise is inventing a literature. Robustness tier: not applicable, since a documented absence of evidence is not a finding with a tier.
entries.example: The entire craft tradition on erotic prose style, including the material carded elsewhere in this pack, rests on practitioner judgement and critical argument rather than on measurement.
entries.application: Treat this pack's craft collection as accumulated practitioner knowledge, which is what it is, and treat anyone who claims empirical backing for a prose rule in this area as having something to show you. Ask to see it.

entries.name: Erotic Plasticity
entries.description: A widely repeated idea that has been contested since the month it was published.
entries.principle: The proposal that one sex's sexuality is more responsive to social and cultural influence than the other's originated in a review article rather than an experiment, drew a published objection almost immediately, and later received a direct disconfirmation in the literature. It circulates in craft writing as established. Robustness tier: contested, with a published direct disconfirmation on the record.
entries.example: The objection appeared in the same year as the original and the disconfirmation eight years later, so the idea has never at any point been uncontested.
entries.application: The pack declines to card it as a finding and records it here as a live argument. If you want to use the underlying observation in a novel, use it as a thing a character believes, which is what it currently is.

entries.name: Attention, and What a Reader Notices
entries.description: One of the three live explanations for the concordance result is about attention, and it is the one a writer can act on.
entries.principle: If part of the disagreement between measures involves how much attention is paid to internal signals and how accurately they are read, then attention is a variable, and directing a reader's attention is precisely what prose does. That is a plausible bridge between this literature and the page, and it is a bridge nobody has tested. Robustness tier: unclassifiable, since this explanation is proposed rather than established and its extension to reading is inference.
entries.example: The other two explanations for the same result concern physiology and instrumentation, neither of which a writer can do anything about, which is why this one attracts craft attention disproportionately.
entries.application: Notice that the interpretation most useful to writers is also the least established, and that this is not a coincidence but a warning. Use it as a hypothesis about your own drafting rather than as a fact about readers.

entries.name: The Laboratory Is Not the Armchair
entries.description: External validity in this field is assumed rather than demonstrated, and the assumption is large.
entries.principle: Being instrumented in a cubicle and shown supplied material is not the condition under which anybody reads erotica: the setting is public, the material is not chosen, the timing is not controlled by the participant, and the participant knows they are being measured. The field acknowledges this as a limitation; the size of the resulting distortion has not been estimated. Robustness tier: robust as a limitation, unclassifiable as to magnitude.
entries.example: The conditions under which this material is normally read — private, self-selected, self-paced, re-readable, and stopped at will — differ from the laboratory in every one of those respects at once.
entries.application: The gap between the two settings is not a reason to dismiss the work; it is a reason to treat it as evidence about human beings under one specific condition. What happens in an armchair remains unmeasured, and a writer's own observation is currently the better instrument for it.

entries.name: How to Use This Collection
entries.description: The closing card, on what a collection this cautious is for.
entries.principle: This collection contains four usable findings, a set of refusals, and a description of a literature that was not built to answer the question a writer is asking. Its value is not that it tells you how to write; it is that it tells you what a great deal of confident craft advice about this genre is standing on, which in several well-known cases is a mis-statement of a real result. Robustness tier: not applicable, since this card describes the collection rather than reporting a finding.
entries.example: Of the seven claims this pack refuses to card, at least four appear routinely in books that advise writers on how to write about sex.
entries.application: Use it defensively. When you meet a psychological claim in a craft context, ask what was measured, on whom, with which instrument, and whether the sentence in front of you is the finding or a summary of it. That question is the collection's actual deliverable.

entries.name: Ovid
entries.description: The instructional voice invented as a fiction, and the manual that turns on itself.
entries.meta: Roman, 43 BCE – 17 or 18 CE, with reference works giving the death year both ways. Relegated to the Black Sea in 8 CE in a way he himself connected to the erotic poem, which makes him the first recorded case in the Western line of an erotic text costing its author a career.
entries.knownFor: The only surviving didactic erotic poem from antiquity that is a manual in form — instruction delivered in elegiac couplets by a self-appointed teacher of love.
entries.signature: The instructional voice as a fiction. The teacher-narrator is a character rather than the poet, and both the comedy and the erotics come from the gap between the confidence of the advice and its manifest inadequacy. The second move is the reversal book: the third book addresses women and systematically undoes the first two, which is a manual turning on itself and has no equivalent in this period.

works.title: Ars Amatoria
works.note: two dating conventions circulate and neither is settled

works.title: Amores
works.note: a lost five-book first edition survives as a three-book second

works.title: Remedia Amoris
works.note: the sequel that unsells the manual

entries.name: Ihara Saikaku
entries.description: The first large body of erotic prose written for a paying urban readership, seventy years before Cleland.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1642 – 9 September 1693. An Osaka merchant-class writer out of the haikai schools whose legal name was Hirayama Togo, working in a functioning commercial book trade with no obscenity-law antagonist of the European kind.
entries.knownFor: Creating the floating-world prose genre and, inside it, the tales of amorous life that are the earliest large commercial erotic literature anywhere.
entries.signature: The episodic sexual life told as an accounting ledger. Encounters are enumerated with running totals, so a life is measured in incidents. This is the strongest pre-modern answer in the pack to the ending problem: Saikaku does not find a native terminus, he substitutes an arithmetical one, and the reader feels the substitution being made.

works.title: Koshoku Ichidai Otoko
works.note: the numbered catalogue that founds the genre

works.title: Koshoku Nidai Otoko
works.note: also transmitted as Shoen Okagami

works.title: Koshoku Ichidai Onna
works.note: the confession frame that bounds a catalogue

entries.name: Pietro Aretino
entries.description: The first European writer to make erotic publication a commercial and political instrument.
entries.meta: Italian, 19 or 20 April 1492 – 21 October 1556, the birth day given as a two-day alternative by the sources. Born at Arezzo and operating from Venice; the name is a toponymic byname rather than a pen name, which is a standing misreading.
entries.knownFor: Satirist, playwright and blackmailer, nicknamed the Scourge of Princes, whose complete works went onto the Index in 1559.
entries.signature: The dialogue between professionals. The sexual material arrives as shop talk between women who work, with the economics visible and the instruction passed downward, so it has a speaker, a purpose and an addressee and therefore a shape. The second move is text written to accompany images, which makes him the one clean case in the tradition of erotic writing built as a caption system rather than as narrative.

works.title: Ragionamenti
works.note: the first part; the second followed in 1536

works.title: Sonetti Lussuriosi
works.note: the year is contested against a 1527 convention

works.title: I Modi
works.note: with Giulio Romano and Marcantonio Raimondi; a second state is dated 1527

entries.name: Vatsyayana
entries.description: Sexual conduct treated as a legitimate field of systematic knowledge rather than as transgression.
entries.meta: Indian, writing in Sanskrit; life dates unresolved, and the standard modern reference states plainly that little is known of him. Dated by internal evidence to the second half of the third century by its leading translator, on which dynasties the text names and which it does not.
entries.knownFor: The foundational Sanskrit treatise on kama, of which the sexual-technique material is one part of a much larger work on social conduct.
entries.signature: Taxonomy as erotic structure. The method is exhaustive classification of persons, situations and acts, in a condensed aphoristic form that needs a commentary to be usable at all. What a writer takes from it is not content but the demonstration that enumeration is itself a rhetorical mode with an erotic effect — and that its characteristic failure is the list that stops meaning anything, which is this pack's repetition problem stated in the third century.

works.title: Kama Sutra
works.note: the outer scholarly range runs from 400 BCE to 300 CE

entries.name: al-Nafzawi
entries.description: The commissioned manual with a named patron, and the earliest clean case of the apparatus of permission.
entries.meta: Born in southern Tunisia under the Hafsids; life dates unresolved, and he is known only through the commission itself. The work was compiled at the request of the ruler Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz al-Mutawakkil, which is a firmer dating anchor than the bare century usually printed.
entries.knownFor: The best known work of Arabic erotology in Europe, written inside a religious framework that treated pleasure as licit within marriage.
entries.signature: The defensive frame that precedes the instruction. The work justifies itself religiously and structurally before it teaches anything, which is the earliest clean instance of the apparatus — preface, dedication, medical or devotional framing — that erotic writing has used to reach print in every period since. Its European transmission is also a case study in translation as distortion: it reached English through a French version rather than the Arabic, and one chapter was omitted from both without disclosure.

works.title: Al-Rawd al-Atir fi Nuzhat al-Khatir
works.note: commonly known as The Perfumed Garden

entries.name: Catullus
entries.description: Obscene invective and tender erotic address inside one book, at the same register level.
entries.meta: Roman, c. 84 – c. 54 BCE, both endpoints inferred from Jerome's chronicle and approximate; a death as late as 53 BCE is also carried in the literature. Born at Verona in Cisalpine Gaul.
entries.knownFor: A transmitted collection of poems whose numbering conventions vary between editions, in which the coarse and the lyric sit adjacent by design.
entries.signature: Register collision as structure. A poem of extreme metrical polish is placed beside one of deliberate coarseness and the juxtaposition does the work, so the obscenity is not a lapse from the lyric but its structural partner. This is the most transferable classical technique in the pack: it is the answer to the diction problem, and the answer is to control the distance between registers rather than to pick one. Note also that the beloved is pseudonymous inside the work, which is a persona applied to a subject rather than to an author and which the pack's four-type taxonomy has no slot for.

works.title: Carmina
works.note: whether he arranged the collection or it was assembled after his death is unsettled

works.title: Carmen 16
works.note: the programmatic defence of obscene writing

entries.name: Petronius
entries.description: Sexual failure as a sustained subject, in the earliest surviving European prose fiction to attempt it.
entries.meta: Roman, c. 27 – 66 CE, born at Massalia and dead at Cumae. The transmitted name may be a traditional attribution to a possibly wrong historical person rather than an author's own, which is a status the pack's pseudonym taxonomy does not cover and which recurs across this period.
entries.knownFor: The earliest surviving European prose fiction in which sexual incident is narrated in a low comic register by a first-person narrator who is himself the joke.
entries.signature: The unreliable narrator whose unreliability is sexual. The narrator reports his own humiliations without recognising them as humiliations, and the reader's pleasure lives in the gap. The surviving text contains a sustained treatment of failure as a subject, which is the hardest thing for the modern form to do and precisely what the pack's central claim has been said to exclude, so this card is load-bearing for a contest the pack does not settle.

works.title: Satyricon
works.note: survives in fragments; the conventional assignment to a longer original is unconfirmed

entries.name: Sappho
entries.description: Desire written as a physiological event with symptoms, and analysed rather than declared.
entries.meta: Greek, c. 630 – c. 570 BCE, both dates conventional reconstructions rather than documentary, with an exile to Sicily around 600 BCE. Roughly 650 lines survive of an estimated ten thousand composed, and exactly one poem survives complete.
entries.knownFor: The surviving body of archaic Greek monodic lyric in which erotic feeling is treated as an object of analysis.
entries.signature: The symptom catalogue. Desire is rendered as a sequence of discrete bodily failures — hearing, sight, speech, temperature, motor control — reported in the first person and in order, so the reader infers the emotion from the inventory rather than being told it. It is the ancestor of every physiological-register technique the modern form uses, and it works precisely because it describes the autonomic nervous system rather than the act. The second move is an addressed second person who is not the reader: the erotic lyric is overheard rather than delivered.

works.title: Ode to Aphrodite
works.note: the only complete surviving poem; the date is a convention

works.title: Fragment 31
works.note: the symptom catalogue in its clearest form

works.title: Tithonus Poem
works.note: recovered in 2004

works.title: Brothers Poem
works.note: recovered in 2014

entries.name: Li Yu
entries.description: A doctrinal ending imported into erotic material from outside the Western tradition entirely.
entries.meta: Chinese, 1610 or 1611 – 1680, with the death implied by an attribution note recorded some thirty-five years afterwards and the birth year unverified. A dramatist, critic and commercial publisher to whom the erotic novel is attributed rather than signed.
entries.knownFor: Drama, criticism and commercial publishing, and by contested attribution the best known Chinese erotic novel.
entries.signature: A moral frame that is structurally rather than decoratively attached. A retribution architecture is installed and the erotic episodes are made to serve it, so the ending is doctrinally supplied rather than narratively earned. That is the pack's imported-ending mechanism appearing in a non-Western tradition with a non-romance import, and the comparison is the whole reason to card him.

works.title: Rou Putuan
works.note: written 1657 and published 1693; the attribution is disputed

entries.name: Marquis de Sade
entries.description: The point at which erotic writing acquires a thesis, and the eighteenth-century original of the pen-name argument.
entries.meta: French, 2 June 1740 – 2 December 1814, exact at both ends. Most of the work appeared anonymously or posthumously, and material excluded from this pack on its categorical ground is not listed here.
entries.knownFor: The libertine philosophical mode in its extreme form, in which sexual scenes are interleaved with expository dissertation and the book is a treatise wearing a novel.
entries.signature: Systematic exhaustion as structure. A combinatorial space is enumerated and then argued from in set-piece discourses, which makes this the extreme case of the pack's repetition problem embraced rather than avoided. He is worth carding as the demonstration of what the form looks like when nothing is withheld, and he should be read against Crebillon, who is the opposite pole. The publication history is the other card: anonymous for the libertine work and signed for the respectable work, with the signature proving legally costly.

works.title: La Philosophie dans le boudoir
works.note: published anonymously

works.title: Justine
works.note: published anonymously

works.title: Aline et Valcour
works.note: published anonymously

works.title: Histoire de Juliette
works.note: the run is given as 1797–99 and also as 1797–1801

works.title: Les Crimes de l'amour
works.note: published under his own name, and the signature had consequences

entries.name: John Cleland
entries.description: A whole long book of erotic prose with no coarse word in it, and the cost that choice carries.
entries.meta: English, 24 September 1709 – 23 January 1789, exact at both ends. Arrested with his publisher in November 1749 and charged with corrupting the King's subjects; he renounced the book in court and it was withdrawn, which is a disavowal under legal pressure rather than a pseudonym.
entries.knownFor: The first English prose novel of sustained erotic content, and the longest-running obscenity case in the language.
entries.signature: The euphemistic system. An entire long book is written without the Anglo-Saxon vocabulary, substituting an extended and internally consistent figurative register. It is the pack's most important technical card because the choice has measurable costs: the euphemism buys legality and elevation and pays in monotony, since the same metaphor family deployed dozens of times produces exactly the repetition failure the form is prone to. Card it as a solved problem that created the next problem. The second move is the retrospective epistolary frame, in which a settled narrator reports her own past and thereby imports the ending the erotic material could not supply.

works.title: Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure
works.note: the first volume November 1748, the second February 1749

entries.name: Crébillon fils
entries.description: The counter-case for the whole pack — what the form looks like when the explicit content is systematically withheld.
entries.meta: French, 13 February 1707 – 12 April 1777, exact at both ends. The suffix distinguishes him from his father the tragedian and is not a pen name, which is a standing misreading.
