entries.knownFor: The psychological libertine novel, in which seduction is rendered as a social and conversational process rather than as physical incident.
entries.signature: The ellipsis at the moment of consummation. The dialogue runs up to the act and breaks off, so the erotic charge lives entirely in the negotiation. For a pack whose central problem is that explicit sequence has no native terminus, he is the counter-case: the tension improves under withholding. He is the most useful author in the period for teaching restraint as a technique rather than as timidity, and he should be read against Sade.

works.title: Les Egarements du coeur et de l'esprit
works.note: issued across 1736 to 1738 and left incomplete

works.title: Tanzai et Neadarne
works.note: frequently and incorrectly listed under a later title

works.title: La Nuit et le moment
works.note: a dialogue in prose rather than a work for performance

works.title: Le Hasard du coin du feu

entries.name: Nicolas Chorier
entries.description: The most elaborate false-attribution frame in the tradition, and learned Latin used as a disinhibitor.
entries.meta: French, 1 September 1612 – 14 August 1692, exact at both ends. A lawyer, historian and prosecutor at Grenoble under Louis XIV.
entries.knownFor: The seventeenth century's most influential Latin erotic dialogue, and the conduit by which the Aretine dialogue form reached the eighteenth century.
entries.signature: Learned Latin as a permission technology. Writing obscenity in humanist Latin restricts the audience, signals status and supplies a rhetorical armature at once, so the erudition is not a disguise over the content but the thing that makes the content sayable. The attribution frame is doubled and is the canonical case: the work claims to be by a real historical poet and translated by a real humanist professor, and both claims are fabrications — a persona applied to living or historical third parties without consent, which is a different act from inventing one.

works.title: Satyra Sotadica
works.note: the full transmitted title runs to a line and a half

entries.name: Restif de la Bretonne
entries.description: Erotic writing as a direct critical argument with another erotic writer.
entries.meta: French, 23 October 1734 – 3 February 1806, born at Sacy and dead in Paris. Card the spelling Restif, which is his own print form and the standard authority heading, with the alternative as a see-also.
entries.knownFor: An enormous body of low-life realist and libertine writing, and a book written explicitly against Sade.
entries.signature: The rival book. The anti-Sade novel is an attempt to prove that the explicit register can carry pleasure without cruelty, which makes it the only clear pre-1900 instance of erotic writing conducted as an argument with another erotic writer — a practice that is entirely live now in the response, the corrective and the reclamation, and which has no other example in the period. He also set much of his own work in type himself, so the author and the compositor are the same person.

works.title: L'Anti-Justine
works.note: the year is contested against 1798, and the work appeared pseudonymously

works.title: Monsieur Nicolas
works.note: sixteen volumes issued to 1797

entries.name: Andrea de Nerciat
entries.description: The proof that the explicit register can be played for farce rather than for philosophy, politics or sentiment.
entries.meta: French, 1739–1800. A soldier and agent whose double life is as well attested as his bibliography is not; the works were published anonymously and their dating is a genuine minefield.
entries.knownFor: Comic libertine fiction at full explicitness, written against the seriousness of the philosophical mode.
entries.signature: Comic tone at full explicitness. The ensemble scene is handled as stage comedy, with entrances, timing and misfires, so the humour comes from choreography rather than from mockery of the material. It is the clearest demonstration in the tradition that explicitness and comedy are compatible, and the pack's comedy seam takes this card rather than a bawdy one.

works.title: Felicia ou Mes fredaines
works.note: the year is unverified and should be checked before use

works.title: Le Diable au corps
works.note: also dated 1803, and the two are not reconciled

entries.name: Denis Diderot
entries.description: A magical device that forces testimony, and an ending supplied by the depositions running out.
entries.meta: French, 1713–1784. The erotic novel was published anonymously in 1748, early and for money, before the encyclopaedia that he is otherwise known for.
entries.knownFor: The Encyclopedie, and within this pack the one licentious novel written before it and the political calculation attached to it.
entries.signature: The device that compels testimony. A conceit forces sexual truth-telling from parties who would not otherwise speak, which converts an unstructured subject into a sequence of depositions — a genuine formal solution to the ending problem, because a testimony sequence ends when the testimonies run out. That is an imported terminus of a third distinct kind, alongside the doctrinal and the marital.

works.title: Les Bijoux indiscrets
works.note: published anonymously

works.title: La Religieuse
works.note: written around 1760 and published posthumously, and the gap is the point

entries.name: Boyer d'Argens (attributed)
entries.description: The purest instance of erotica as a delivery system for a proposition, and a better teaching case than Sade.
entries.meta: French, 1704–1771, unverified in the second research pass and to be checked before release. The work was published anonymously and the attribution is not settled; the pack cards the attribution rather than asserting the man.
entries.knownFor: The materialist philosophical novel that is the direct ancestor of Sade's method.
entries.signature: The philosophical dialogue running underneath the erotic scene, with the two doing the same argumentative work. The materialist argument is not a frame around the sexual content; the sexual content is the demonstration of it. That makes this the purest case in the period of erotica as an argument, and a better card for teaching the technique than Sade because the content problem does not come attached.

works.title: Therese philosophe
works.note: published anonymously; a much longer transmitted title also circulates

entries.name: Jean-Charles Gervaise de Latouche (attributed)
entries.description: The boundary rule's hardest case — erotic writing that is primarily political.
entries.meta: French, 26 November 1715 – 28 November 1782, born at Amiens. A lawyer at the Parlement of Paris; the work was published anonymously and the attribution, while standard, is an attribution.
entries.knownFor: The eighteenth century's most durable anticlerical libertine novel.
entries.signature: The first-person career narrative with an anticlerical spine. The libertine memoir is organised as a working life inside an institution, so the episodes acquire a professional progression rather than remaining a sequence — the same structural answer Saikaku reaches by arithmetic, reached instead by a career ladder. It is also the clearest case of erotic writing whose sexual content is the vehicle for a political argument, which inverts this pack's own boundary rule and is worth carding as the boundary's hardest case.

works.title: Histoire de Dom Bougre, Portier des Chartreux
works.note: also circulates under the short title Le Portier des Chartreux

entries.name: Abbé du Prat (attributed)
entries.description: The enclosed setting as an intensifier, and the book behind the first obscenity conviction in England.
entries.meta: French, life dates unresolved, because the name is a clerical persona and the actual author remains unknown. Two candidates are on the record and the standard reference declines to choose between them, so the pack cards neither.
entries.knownFor: The convent dialogue that carried the Aretine form into a specifically institutional setting, and whose English translation produced a landmark prosecution.
entries.signature: The enclosed setting as an intensifier. A convent supplies confinement, hierarchy, a vow to be violated, and a devotional vocabulary available for reuse — four things the form otherwise has to manufacture. This is the origin of the institution-as-pressure-vessel move that modern erotica still runs in workplaces, ships and monasteries without knowing where it came from. Its legal afterlife is why it is carded ahead of better-written books: the English translation led to a prosecution, a King's Bench ruling that selling such material was a misdemeanour, and a sentence of a fine and an hour in the pillory.

works.title: Venus dans le cloitre
works.note: an English translation of 1724 produced the prosecution

entries.name: Michel Millot
entries.description: The instruction-dialogue machine that every later work in the tradition runs on.
entries.meta: French, life dates unresolved; catalogue metadata offers only an active year, which is a cataloguer's flourish rather than a date. The work was published anonymously, and a second man is named alongside him in the attribution without either being settled.
entries.knownFor: The founding French instruction dialogue, and the two-hander form it established.
entries.signature: The two-hander instruction dialogue with an age and knowledge gap. An experienced cousin instructs an inexperienced one, and the gap is the engine: it supplies a reason for exposition, a built-in reader surrogate, and a natural escalation ladder in a single device. Every later work in the libertine line is a variation on that machine, which is why the card is here despite the author being barely a person in the record.

works.title: L'Ecole des filles
works.note: published anonymously in Paris

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: William Lazenby
entries.description: The periodical as the delivery form for erotica, and the imprint name worn to defeat prosecution.
entries.meta: English, died around 1888, with no firm birth year located and the biographical record consisting of an encyclopaedia stub and commercial reprint listings. Prosecuted in 1871 and again in 1881, and trading through both.
entries.knownFor: The four great Victorian clandestine periodicals, published, edited and part-written by the same man.
entries.signature: Serial architecture. A magazine number mixes a serialised novel instalment, standalone short fiction, parodic verse, songs and a correspondence column, so the reader's appetite is renewed monthly rather than spent in one volume; every modern erotic anthology with a house voice descends from it. He also standardised the pastiche mode — erotic parody of a recognisable respectable form, which lets the sexual content ride on a structure the reader already knows how to read. His trade aliases are a publisher's evasion imprints rather than pen names, and the distinction matters: a publisher-owned name normally protects the house from the writer, and a clandestine one protects the house from the state.

works.title: The Pearl
works.note: eighteen issues to 1880, with a Christmas supplement; the run years are conventional rather than sourced

works.title: The Cremorne
works.note: the year is conventional rather than sourced

works.title: The Boudoir
works.note: the year is conventional rather than sourced

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: Walter (unidentified)
entries.description: The pack's canonical persona case, and the one where nobody can perform the unmasking.
entries.meta: Presumed English and presumed nineteenth century; life dates unresolved, because the identity is unresolved. Four candidates are on the record with named proposers across four decades and there is no scholarly consensus for any of them.
entries.knownFor: An eleven-volume sexual autobiography that is either the period's most detailed private record or its most sustained invention, and the argument about which is unsettled.
entries.signature: The exhaustive, unselective first person. The technique is a refusal to edit: failures, boredom, expense, illness and repetition are recorded at the same weight as consummation, and that flatness is what produces the documentary effect. Modern erotic memoir and autofiction inherit it directly, because the credibility comes from what the narrator declines to make interesting. The persona is the pack's canonical instance of a fictional author who claims to have written his own life, and its distinguishing feature is that no one can collapse it — the unmasking that would end the effect is unavailable, which is why the second dispute, over how much of it is record and how much invention, is the more useful one for writers.

works.title: My Secret Life
works.note: eleven volumes issued to about 1894; the first edition was probably printed in Brussels or Amsterdam in a very small run

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: Henry Spencer Ashbee
entries.description: The founding bibliography of Anglophone erotica, and a pen name designed to be solved.
entries.meta: British, 21 April 1834 – 29 July 1900, born in Southwark. Three privately printed volumes of 250 copies each, and the most commonly proposed candidate for an authorship this pack records as unresolved.
entries.knownFor: The first systematic bibliography of erotic literature in English, compiled and issued privately under a Latin cryptonym.
entries.signature: The annotated bibliography as covert criticism. Full title-page transcription, collation and provenance are followed by an extended descriptive note that quotes and evaluates, which let him write serious critical prose about material no Victorian journal would review. The apparatus is the alibi and the criticism is the payload, and a writer can steal the move directly: a scholarly frame licenses content the frame's own audience would refuse. His pen name is a personal one that announces rather than hides — a Latin pun on his own surname, solvable by anybody with a little Latin.

works.title: Index Librorum Prohibitorum
works.note: privately printed, 250 copies

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: Leonard Smithers
entries.description: The hinge between clandestine pornography and the aesthetic avant-garde, and the production-values defence.
entries.meta: British, 19 December 1861 – 19 December 1907, dead on his forty-sixth birthday of cirrhosis. A qualified solicitor who turned bookseller and publisher, bankrupt in 1900, buried in an unmarked grave paid for by Lord Alfred Douglas.
entries.knownFor: Publishing Beardsley, Dowson and Wilde alongside a clandestine erotica list, and taking The Ballad of Reading Gaol when no respectable house would.
entries.signature: The production-values argument. He published transgressive matter in limited, subscriber-only, beautifully made editions on fine paper with numbered copies, so that the object's expense and scarcity did the legitimating work the content could not do for itself. That is the origin of a durable strategy — material prosecutable as a cheap pamphlet passes as a collector's item. He also edited: he is recorded as having moved the setting of one anonymous novel from London to Paris. His imprint was a house name rather than a pen name, and the imprint carried the identity.

works.title: Priapeia
works.note: a translation issued with Richard Francis Burton

works.title: Teleny
works.note: published under the Erotika Biblion Society imprint

works.title: The Savoy
works.note: eight issues, co-founded with Arthur Symons and Beardsley

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: H. S. Nichols
entries.description: The clandestine trade as an international logistics problem, and a career that is a map of it.
entries.meta: English, 14 August 1865 – 30 November 1941, born at Wortley near Leeds and dead in a New York mental hospital to which he had been committed in 1939. Exiled to Paris from 1900, threatened with extradition in 1908, and publishing from Connecticut until 1939.
entries.knownFor: Co-founding the Erotika Biblion Society with Smithers, and running the clandestine business across three countries and half a century.
entries.signature: Jurisdictional arbitrage plus the subscription list. Print where the law is loose, sell by post into where it is tight, and keep a private list of named subscribers so that no copy is ever offered to the public and the publication element of the offence is contestable. His career demonstrates that the enabling technology of Victorian and Edwardian erotica was distribution rather than printing, and every later paperback operation and Paris house runs the same play.

works.title: Priapeia
works.note: issued jointly with Smithers under the society imprint

works.title: Teleny
works.note: the imprint's best known title

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: Charles Carrington
entries.description: The legitimacy veil — a catalogue made too respectable to raid.
entries.meta: British, born Paul Harry Ferdinando on 11 November 1867 in Bethnal Green and died in 1921 at Ivry-sur-Seine, with the exact death date not established. Moved from London to Paris in 1895 and traded there and briefly from Brussels; blinded by syphilis, robbed of his rare-book collection, placed in an asylum and dead in poverty.
entries.knownFor: The leading publisher of English-language erotica in Europe from the mid-1890s to the First World War.
entries.signature: The legitimacy veil. He deliberately published classical texts, translations and reputable authors so that the erotica travelled inside a respectable list — the structural counterpart to the production-values play, since one made the object too fine to prosecute and the other made the catalogue too respectable to raid. He also standardised the pseudo-documentary erotic novel, the memoir, the confession and the translated-from-the-French frame, which is the commercial ancestor of the whole first-person erotic novel line. The trade name is the house's rather than a writer's, and the man behind it is deliberately absent from the title page.

works.title: Suburban Souls
works.note: the year needs checking against a source before it is relied on

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: William Dugdale
entries.description: The pre-1857 generation, and the man the forfeiture statute was effectively written against.
entries.meta: English, c. 1800 – 1868, both dates carried from the second research pass as candidates rather than verified and to be checked before release. The dominant Holywell Street pornographer-publisher of the generation before Lazenby.
entries.knownFor: Running the largest clandestine publishing operation in London in the decades when the trade's legal exposure was being defined.
entries.signature: The pre-statutory operating model, which is worth carding precisely because it is the thing the law was designed to end. Dugdale worked before the sanction ran against stock, so his exposure sat differently and his methods did too, and the difference between his practice and Lazenby's thirty years later is a direct readout of what a change in enforcement mechanism does to a business. He supplies the generation this section otherwise lacks and ties the pack to the Holywell Street address the trade operated from until the street's loss around 1900.

works.title: The Exquisite
works.note: a periodical; the year is carried as a candidate and needs verification

entries.category: The Clandestine Trade and Its Anonymities
entries.name: Edward Sellon
entries.description: A named Victorian erotic writer with a life, against a section otherwise made of imprints.
entries.meta: English, 1818–1866, both dates carried from the second research pass as candidates rather than verified and to be checked before release. A soldier, hack writer and translator rather than a publisher.
entries.knownFor: Writing rather than issuing — the clandestine trade's rare case of an identifiable author with a biography attached.
entries.signature: The professional hand working across registers. Sellon wrote erotica, translations and antiquarian material for the same trade and often for the same customers, which is the working condition of the Victorian clandestine writer and is invisible in a section composed of publishers. Carding him is a corrective to the standard picture in which the period's erotica appears to have no authors at all, and the correction matters because it changes what a writer of the period is imagined to have been.

works.title: The Ups and Downs of Life
works.note: a memoir; the year is carried as a candidate and needs verification

entries.name: Leopold von Sacher-Masoch
entries.description: The contract as erotic structure, and the writer whose surname was taken from him and made a diagnosis.
entries.meta: Austrian, 27 January 1836 – 9 March 1895, born at Lemberg and dead at Lindheim. Most of his work remains untranslated into English, so the Anglophone picture of him is a one-book picture by accident of translation rather than by the shape of the career.
entries.knownFor: A single novella that supplied the tradition its contract device, and for having a clinical term coined from his name in 1886 while he was alive and objecting.
entries.signature: The contract as erotic structure. The arrangement is made explicit, written, negotiated and legally formatted inside the fiction, so the terms precede the scene and the scene executes the terms; everything in modern erotic writing that turns on negotiated consent, formalised roles and stated limits is downstream of it. The second move is the frame of aesthetic contemplation — a painting, a statue, a fur — mediating desire, so that the erotic object is encountered first as an image and only then as a person. He is also the pack's clearest case of the eponym hazard, where a surname is absorbed into clinical vocabulary and the work is thereafter read only as symptom.

works.title: Venus im Pelz
works.note: issued inside the first volume of a projected story cycle

entries.name: Rachilde
entries.description: The scandal carried by who holds the verbs, and a pen name that is a personal one in law and a persona in rhetoric.
entries.meta: French, 11 February 1860 – 4 April 1953. Convicted of pornography in her absence in Belgium, where the first editions of her best-known novel appeared, and sentenced to two years' imprisonment.
entries.knownFor: Decadent fiction of inverted and unstable gender, written across seventy years under a name she chose and kept.
entries.signature: Systematic inversion of the gendered grammar of desire. The female character occupies the sentence positions the period's prose reserves for men — agent, sculptor, purchaser, describer — and the male body is placed in the syntactic position of the described object, so the scandal is carried by who holds the verbs rather than by explicit content. The second move is eroticism routed through artifice, waxwork and doll and statue and costume, so that the desired body is always partly a manufactured thing. Her account of the pen name is that it belonged to a long-dead Swedish lord who reached her at a seance, which frames a personal name as a possessing character and lets authorship be disclaimed; the taxonomy's categories are functions rather than labels, and this is the proof.

works.title: Monsieur Venus
works.note: first published in Belgium, where it was prosecuted

works.title: Pourquoi je ne suis pas feministe

entries.name: Pierre Louÿs
entries.description: The forged apparatus, and the literary hoax whose exposure improved its reputation.
entries.meta: Born 10 December 1870 in Ghent and died 4 June 1925 in Paris; Belgian by birth and French by residence and career. One posthumous title falls under this pack's categorical exclusion and is not listed.
entries.knownFor: Presenting a sequence of prose poems as the work of an ancient Greek courtesan contemporary with Sappho, casting himself only as the translator.
entries.signature: The forged apparatus. He supplies the scholarly furniture of a translated ancient text — an attribution, a biography of the invented author, notes, and deliberately missing poems — so that the erotic content arrives pre-authorised by philology. It is the same manoeuvre as the bibliographic alibi run in the opposite direction, and the hoax's rapid exposure enhanced rather than damaged the work, which is the standing counter-example to the assumption that an unmasked literary hoax has failed. The second move is the short self-contained prose-poem unit, which lets an erotic sequence accumulate by juxtaposition rather than by plot.

works.title: Les Chansons de Bilitis
works.note: presented as translations from an invented poet

works.title: Trois filles de leur mere
works.note: written much earlier and published posthumously

entries.name: Guillaume Apollinaire
entries.description: Obscenity as a comic-picaresque engine, and one name kept off the work it could not survive.
entries.meta: Polish-French, 26 August 1880 – 9 November 1918, born Wilhelm Albert Wlodzimierz Aleksander Apolinary Kostrowicki in Rome and dead in Paris of influenza in the 1918 pandemic, weakened by a head wound of 1916. One 1911 title falls under this pack's categorical exclusion and is not listed.
entries.knownFor: Coining the terms cubism and surrealism, the removal of punctuation from his verse, and an anonymous erotic novel that runs on velocity.
entries.signature: Velocity and cataloguing. The erotic prose runs on relentless forward motion, comic escalation and geographic sprawl with almost no interiority and no psychology, which is the opposite of the Victorian confessional mode and is why the book reads as farce rather than as arousal. The poetic signature is the removal of punctuation so that syntactic units are cut by line and image alone and the reader supplies the breath. Note the split: he carried his chosen name across every register he wrote in, from art criticism to verse, and the clandestine erotica did not carry it.

works.title: Les Onze Mille Verges
works.note: published anonymously

works.title: Calligrammes
works.note: described as posthumous by some sources; it appeared in the year of his death

entries.name: Georges Bataille
entries.description: The displaced object, and a persona whose name insults the reader and the institution of authorship at once.
entries.meta: French, 10 September 1897 – 9 July 1962, the dates carried as candidates from the second research pass and to be verified before release. His founding erotic text is pre-war, which the usual placement of him inside the post-war tradition obscures.
entries.knownFor: A short novel published under an obscene invented byline, and a body of theory that made it possible to write erotica about eroticism.
entries.signature: The displaced object. An erotic sequence is built around a repeating physical form that migrates between incompatible registers — food, body, sacrament — so the transgressive charge is carried by metaphor substitution rather than by description of acts. The second move is flat, unhurried declarative sentences describing extremity with the affect withheld: the prose refuses to be excited by its own material, and the reader's discomfort comes from that refusal. The third is eroticism written as continuous with death and the sacred rather than opposed to them, which is why the fiction reads as argument. His pseudonym is a character rather than a cover, and it demonstrates that a persona need not be a plausible person.

works.title: Histoire de l'oeil
works.note: published under an invented and deliberately obscene byline

works.title: Madame Edwarda
works.note: under a second invented name, bearing a false earlier imprint date

works.title: Le Bleu du ciel
works.note: written around 1935; card the publication year

works.title: Ma Mere
works.note: posthumous

entries.name: Louis Aragon
entries.description: Erotica structured as lyric address rather than as scene, and the model of register-partitioned identity.
entries.meta: French, 3 October 1897 – 24 December 1982, the dates carried as candidates from the second research pass and to be verified before release. A 1968 republication of his erotic text was seized as pornography, forty years after it first appeared.
entries.knownFor: Surrealism and then Communist-aligned realism under his own name, and a single erotic prose work under an invented aristocratic one.
entries.signature: Metaphysical rhapsody applied to a body. The erotic text is written as invocation and cosmology — an extended apostrophe in which anatomical attention escalates until it becomes a theory of the universe — with almost no narrative at all. It is the strongest example in the pack of erotica structured as lyric address rather than as scene, and it is the technique literary erotica most often reaches for when it wants to escape the choreography problem. He is also the pack's model of register-partitioned identity: one writer, two names, the second reserved for material the first could not survive.

works.title: Le Con d'Irene
works.note: published under an invented aristocratic byline

entries.name: Colette
entries.description: Desire registered as heightened perception, and the pack's clearest case of a house name taking a writer's royalties.
entries.meta: French, 28 January 1873 – 3 August 1954. Elected to the Academie Goncourt in 1945 and its president in 1949, and given a state funeral in 1954, the first French woman of letters so honoured.
entries.knownFor: The early novel sequence published under her first husband's byline, the later fiction under her own, and a body of work that made the ageing woman's desire structurally central.
entries.signature: Erotic writing carried entirely by non-genital sensory precision — light, fabric, temperature, fruit, animal presence, the exact texture of a room — so that desire is registered as heightened perception rather than as described act. The second move is the ageing body as erotic subject, handled without pathos or apology. The third is free indirect style holding irony and tenderness in one sentence about one character. Her first four novels appeared under a byline her husband owned and operated as a stable of ghostwriters, and her authorship was uncredited during his lifetime; against a persona that hides an author who may not exist, this is a house name that hides an author who demonstrably does and takes her money.

works.title: Claudine a l'ecole
works.note: published under a byline owned by her first husband

entries.name: Radclyffe Hall
entries.description: A novel with no explicit content at all, suppressed for the existence of its subject.
entries.meta: English, born Marguerite Antonia Radclyffe Hall on 12 August 1880 and died 7 October 1943. Known personally as John, a name she lived under rather than published under, which marks the outer boundary of this pack's pseudonym taxonomy.
entries.knownFor: The novel whose English destruction order and eventual American clearance are the cleanest demonstration in the tradition that obscenity law of the period policed category rather than description.
entries.signature: The sincere case-history novel. She deliberately borrows the shape of sexological life-writing — childhood signs, family, formation, vocation, exile — and writes it with unironic high seriousness, so the book argues for tolerance in the register of testimony. The technique is withholding the explicit: the most famous sentence about consummation is a single elliptical clause, and the restraint is the argument, because it depends on the reader granting dignity. The trade-off is available to any writer and is stated plainly by the case — suppressing description buys moral authority and costs erotic force.

works.title: The Well of Loneliness
works.note: ruled obscene in London within a week of trial and ordered destroyed

entries.name: D. H. Lawrence
entries.description: The repetition-and-intensification sentence, and dialect used as an erotic register.
entries.meta: English, 11 September 1885 – 2 March 1930, dead at Vence in France. An earlier novel was suppressed and investigated for obscenity in 1915, with wartime suspicion of his German wife a contributing factor, and his last was unpublishable in Britain in full text for thirty-two years.
entries.knownFor: The novel of sexual relation as metaphysics, and two suppressions thirteen years apart.
entries.signature: The repetition-and-intensification sentence. A key noun or adjective is deliberately repeated within a paragraph rather than varied, driving the prose toward incantation and moving a scene out of observed description into felt state. The second move is an abstract-physical vocabulary of dark, flame and blood that avoids both the clinical and the euphemistic pole, and is the most imitated and most parodied erotic style in English. The third is dialect as an erotic register: the gamekeeper's shift into Derbyshire speech marks a change in relation rather than in class, so intimacy is signalled by a change of language rather than a change of act.

works.title: Lady Chatterley's Lover
works.note: privately printed in Florence, with an expurgated commercial edition in 1932

works.title: The First Lady Chatterley
works.note: an earlier version, first published in English in 1972 and a separate work

works.title: John Thomas and Lady Jane
works.note: the second version, likewise first published in 1972

entries.name: Henry Miller
entries.description: The first-person rant, and the erotic scene deliberately deflated by returning to money and weather.
entries.meta: American, 26 December 1891 – 7 June 1980, born in New York and dead at Pacific Palisades. Published in Paris in 1934 and not in the United States until 1961, with the obscenity findings overturned in 1964.
entries.knownFor: The autobiographical novel as sustained obscenity, and the second great legal chain in the Anglophone tradition after the modernist customs cases.
entries.signature: The first-person present-tense rant — long, unparagraphed, syntactically escalating passages fusing squalor, hunger, cityscape and sex into one undifferentiated stream, with appetite rather than plot as the organising principle. The second move abolishes the distinction between the obscene word and the literary sentence by refusing to mark the transition, so the four-letter word arrives inside an otherwise high-rhetorical clause, which is exactly what made the books legally indefensible until the standard changed. The third is the erotic scene as anti-climax: encounters are recorded and then immediately deflated by a return to money, lice, food or weather.

works.title: Tropic of Cancer
works.note: published in Paris; not published in the United States until 1961

works.title: Sexus
works.note: the first volume of a trilogy completed in 1959

entries.name: Anais Nin
entries.description: Erotica written as portraiture with a withheld centre, and the bridge from the paid-anonymous trade to literary erotica.
entries.meta: French-born American, 21 February 1903 – 14 January 1977, dead in Los Angeles. The erotic narratives were written in the 1940s for an anonymous private collector at a dollar a page, which is commissioned work for hire and is the fact that places her.
entries.knownFor: The diary as a literary form, and the only body of mid-century erotica by a woman with a settled canonical place.
entries.signature: Erotica written as portraiture with a withheld centre. Each piece builds a character and a milieu at full novelistic density and treats the sexual event as the occasion for revealing temperament, so the reader's attention is redirected from act to person. She is explicit in the diaries that this was a deliberate counter-method to the commission she was fulfilling, which makes the collection a documented argument with its own patron. The second move is a surreal, image-led prose in the uncommissioned work, in which psychological states are given landscape form rather than being analysed.

works.title: Delta of Venus
works.note: written in the 1940s and published posthumously

works.title: Little Birds
works.note: the remainder of the same commission

works.title: The Diary of Anais Nin, volume 1

entries.name: Anne Desclos
entries.description: The pack's hardest pseudonym case — a personal pen name laid over a personal pen name over a legal name.
entries.meta: French, 23 September 1907 – 27 April 1998. An editor at Gallimard and a critic at the Nouvelle Revue Francaise for fifty years under one name, the author of a single novel under another, and unacknowledged as its author for forty years until an interview in 1994.
entries.knownFor: The most consequential post-war erotic novel in French, and the authorship contest that outlived its own resolution.
entries.signature: The calm declarative register applied without variation to escalating material, so the sentence rhythm never registers what the content does and the gap between the two is the engine. The second move is the removal of interiority as an erotic device: the protagonist's consciousness is reported in the same neutral third person as the furniture, so the reader must supply the inner life the prose withholds. The third is an allegorical scaffolding of chateau, ring and mask that keeps the book at one remove from naturalism and lets it read as a system rather than as an incident. Both pen names are her own and neither is a publisher's, which makes this a personal name stacked twice rather than a house arrangement.

works.title: Histoire d'O
works.note: published under a name laid over the pen name she already worked under

works.title: Retour a Roissy
works.note: the attribution is contested and her biographer states she did not write it

entries.name: Jean Paulhan
entries.description: The paratext as an authorship claim — a preface that does argumentative work on the book it introduces.
entries.meta: French, 2 December 1884 – 9 October 1968, the dates carried as candidates from the second research pass and to be verified before release. Director of the Nouvelle Revue Francaise, and the addressee, instigator and public defender of a book he professed not to know the author of.
entries.knownFor: The provocation that produced the century's most discussed French erotic novel, and the preface attached to its first edition.
entries.signature: The paratext as an authorship claim. The preface asserts the author's sex, the book's sincerity and its philosophical seriousness in one move, and it is the cleanest example in the pack of a frame doing argumentative work on the text it introduces rather than merely introducing it. Any writer studying how to license transgressive material by framing should read it as a technique. His position in the authorship contest is the reason the contest is live: one reading has him as the reason the book exists, the other as the reason its single-author attribution flattens what was an asymmetrical production, and this pack settles neither.

works.title: Le bonheur dans l'esclavage
works.note: the preface, and the object the authorship contest turns on

entries.name: Maurice Girodias
entries.description: The house-name commissioning model, and the economic reason the Olympia pen names were the house's property.
entries.meta: French, 1919–1990, dead of a heart attack in Paris at seventy-one. His surname is a legal name change made under duress rather than a pen name, and it should not be carded as one; the distinction is exactly what the pack's taxonomy exists to protect.
entries.knownFor: Founding Olympia Press in 1953 on his father's Obelisk Press, the numbered Traveller's Companion series of ninety-four titles, and publishing Beckett, Burroughs, Donleavy, Miller and Bataille in English.
entries.signature: The house-name commissioning model. He paid flat fees to English-speaking expatriates in Paris to write to order under names the house controlled, which is the origin of the distinction between a name a writer owns and a name a publisher does. The record also states that he reprinted successful titles under other imprints without permission to avoid royalties and frequently failed to pay his writers, and that is not colour: it is the economic reason those names are house property rather than author property, and it is why the arbitrage produced no precedent and left nothing behind when it closed.

works.title: The Olympia Press list
works.note: the imprint itself is the work; it ran to 1965

works.title: Une journee sur la terre
works.note: memoirs in two volumes

entries.name: Catherine Robbe-Grillet
entries.description: The nouveau roman method turned on erotic material, and one evolving persona across a masculine and a feminine name.
entries.meta: French, born 1930; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated item of January 2025 and nothing later — the thinnest confirmation in this pack, and the one to re-run first. A practising dominatrix and the organiser of Parisian ceremonies for six decades, the widow of Alain Robbe-Grillet, and the subject of a documentary film about her practice.
entries.knownFor: A short novel published in 1956 under a masculine pen name, and two later books under the feminine form of the same name.
entries.signature: The nouveau roman method turned on erotic material — flat, measured, obsessively exact visual description with the narrator's judgement removed, so the scene is presented as a photographic record rather than as an experience. The novel is narrated by an observer, which relocates the erotics from participation to looking, and the technique a writer can take is an erotic scene built entirely from ordered visual detail with affect deliberately absent from the syntax. Both pen names are hers: the masculine form was a concealment and the later feminine form an avowal, and the pair should be read as one evolving persona rather than as two names.

works.title: L'Image
works.note: published under a masculine form of the pen name

works.title: Ceremonies de femmes
works.note: under the feminine form

entries.name: Emmanuelle Arsan
entries.description: The erotic novel as pedagogy, and a contested attribution the pack cards as the fact.
entries.meta: Thai-French, died 2005, life dates unresolved beyond that; born into an aristocratic Siamese family and married to a French diplomat in 1956. Whether the name belongs to a personal pen name or fronts a different or shared writer is contested, and this pack records the contest rather than choosing.
entries.knownFor: The francophone bestseller that became the 1974 film and the template for mainstream tasteful erotic cinema.
entries.signature: The erotic novel as pedagogy. The narrative is structured as a sequence of instructions and initiations delivered by mentor figures, with argumentative dialogue about desire carrying as much page space as the scenes. The technique to learn is scene as lesson: each encounter advances a stated doctrine, so the book has forward motion without conventional plot. The attribution is the second card: one position holds the name to be the writer's own and portable across her later titles, the other holds that the real author was her husband, and the claim postdates her death. Neither is adjudicated here.

works.title: Emmanuelle
works.note: clandestine and unsigned; do not card the 1967 signed edition or the 1971 translation

entries.name: Jean-Jacques Pauvert
entries.description: The open imprint — forcing the state to prosecute literature rather than seize anonymous contraband.
entries.meta: French, 8 April 1926 – 27 September 2014, born in Paris and dead at Toulon at eighty-eight. A publisher rather than an author, and carded for what the imprint did.
entries.knownFor: The first open publication of Sade in France under a real name and address, and the first publisher of the century's most discussed French erotic novel.
entries.signature: The open imprint strategy. Suppressed erotic material is published under a real name and address with full scholarly apparatus, which forces the state to prosecute literature rather than to seize anonymous contraband — and a prosecution of literature is a prosecution that can be won. It is the structural opposite of the Paris arbitrage model, which evaded the question entirely and left no precedent behind it, and the difference between the two publishers is the difference between a business and a legal argument.

works.title: Histoire d'O
works.note: as publisher rather than as author; issued openly with a preface

works.title: Oeuvres completes de Sade
works.note: issued over some twenty-five years; the span needs verification

works.title: Anthologie historique des lectures erotiques
works.note: multi-volume, issued over subsequent years

entries.name: Marguerite Duras
entries.description: The pack's model for erotic writing that never describes the act and loses no intensity.
entries.meta: French, born in French Indochina, 1914–1996. The surname is a personal pen name taken from her father's home village and laid over her legal one, and it is entirely hers.
entries.knownFor: A late short novel of memory and distance that became her most widely read book, and the screenplay that made her name in cinema.
entries.signature: Desire written almost entirely in ellipsis and repetition. The sexual event is circled, deferred and restated in slightly altered words, and is usually narrated from a temporal distance that makes it already lost. The second move is an unstable narrative person, sliding between first and third for the same figure inside a paragraph, which turns autobiography into an object the narrator can look at. The third is extreme paratactic short sentences with heavy white space, so that rhythm rather than vocabulary carries the charge.

works.title: Le Ravissement de Lol V. Stein
L'Amant de la Chine du Nord

entries.name: Catherine Millet
entries.description: The art-critical register applied to a sexual history, with an organising schema other than time.
entries.meta: French, born 1 April 1948; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Founder and editor of an art magazine, and the writer who moved explicit first-person sexual autobiography into mainstream French literary publishing.
entries.knownFor: A memoir published in April 2001 whose initial-only title is a redaction everybody can complete, and the absence of a pseudonym is its point.
entries.signature: The art-critical register applied to her own sexual history — taxonomy, inventory, spatial analysis and the vocabulary of exhibition, with the confessional's emotional escalation deliberately withheld. She organises by category rather than by chronology, and that is what keeps a memoir of this kind from becoming a sequence of anecdotes; the transferable lesson is an organising schema other than time. Note the date trap: reference works give 2002, which is the English translation year, and the original-language rule settles it at 2001.

works.title: La Vie sexuelle de Catherine M
works.note: card the French year, not the 2002 translation

entries.name: Virginie Despentes
entries.description: Register violence — sex written in the vocabulary of the street with no modulation into literary softness.
entries.meta: French, born 13 June 1969; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Whether the surname is a pen name was not settled in this pack's research and the name is carded plainly rather than classified.
entries.knownFor: A first novel of sexual violence and refusal, a book-length feminist argument, and a trilogy that made her a mainstream literary figure.
entries.signature: Register violence. She writes sex in the vocabulary of the street and the pornography industry and then, without changing gear, has the same voice deliver sustained analytic argument; the refusal to modulate is the technique, with no euphemism ladder, no literary softening at the moment of the act, and no ironic distance to protect the reader. The second move is free indirect discourse rotated rapidly through many characters, so that the same sexual event is described in incompatible vocabularies by the people inside it.

works.title: Vernon Subutex
works.note: three volumes issued to 2017

entries.name: Pierre Guyotat
entries.description: The outer limit of syntax as the carrier of the erotic, and the counter-example to every clarity rule in the pack.
entries.meta: French, 9 January 1940 – 7 February 2020. The writer at whom the French state's post-1968 censorship apparatus was last seriously aimed.
entries.knownFor: A 1970 text of formal extremity, and a later invented and deformed French that made his sexual material unreadable as titillation.
entries.signature: The single unbroken sentence as erotic form. The text runs without paragraph break, with a private punctuation system and no fixed narrative subject, so that bodies and acts are grammatically continuous with landscape and war. He later invented a deformed French with phonetic spellings and invented inflections, which makes the sexual material legible only as language under pressure. This is the outer limit of syntax as the carrier of the erotic and the standing counter-example to every clarity rule elsewhere in this pack's craft collection.

works.title: Tombeau pour cinq cent mille soldats

entries.name: Alina Reyes
entries.description: Desire produced entirely by voice and by proximity in a workplace, with almost no action at all.
entries.meta: French, born 1956; a pen name over her legal name. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against her own journal, which carries dated posts through April 2026 — a status this pack earlier carried as unconfirmed, now resolved.
entries.knownFor: A very short first novel published by a literary house in 1988, and the clearest French case between the post-war landmarks and the memoir wave of a literary erotic debut by a woman.
entries.signature: Desire produced entirely by voice and by proximity. The novel is built as a sustained monologue by a butcher, overheard across a counter by an assistant on a summer job, with almost no action anywhere in it — the erotic pressure is generated by being unable to leave and unable to stop hearing. The technique transfers directly to any confined workplace, and it is the cheapest way in the pack to make a scene erotic without an encounter in it. No prize is recorded for the book.

entries.name: Angela Carter
entries.description: The bridge between erotic writing and criticism of erotic writing, done in the same voice.
entries.meta: English, 7 May 1940 – 16 February 1992, born in London. She published the short-fiction collection and the critical study in the same year, which is why the pair reads as one argument.
entries.knownFor: A collection of rewritten folk tales, and the essay reading Sade as a moral pornographer that gives this pack much of its critical vocabulary.
entries.signature: The baroque sentence used as an instrument of analysis. The prose is dense with subordinate clause, catalogue and period diction, and every ornament does argumentative work — the excess is how she shows that desire is culturally manufactured rather than natural. The second move is generic transposition: she takes a folk-tale plot whose sexual content is latent and rewrites it with the content explicit and the moral inverted, so the reader watches the same machine run with the cover off. The third is a narratorial address that implicates the reader in the looking.

works.title: The Sadeian Woman and the Ideology of Pornography
The Infernal Desire Machines of Doctor Hoffman

entries.name: Erica Jong
entries.description: Comic first person as a defence against shame, and a poet writing sex on cadence rather than description.
entries.meta: American, born 1942; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated report of June 2025, with nothing later found. The surname is a married name rather than a pen name, and her best-known narrator is routinely collapsed into her, which is a persona confusion and not a pseudonym.
entries.knownFor: The 1973 novel that put a woman's first-person sexual appetite into American mass-market literary fiction, and the coinage that came with it.
entries.signature: Comic first person as a defence against shame. The narrator jokes at exactly the point where the material would otherwise turn confessional, which lets the book be explicit without pleading. The second move is that she is a poet writing prose: the sex is built on cadence and repeated figure rather than on description, and the famous coinage works because it is a compressed poetic image doing the work of a paragraph. The third is analytic digression braided into the scene, so the erotic is always being interpreted while it is happening.

works.title: How to Save Your Own Life

entries.name: Nicholson Baker
entries.description: Constraint-first erotic construction — three books, three formal restrictions, three different results.
entries.meta: American, born 7 January 1957 in New York City; living status carried as unconfirmed, since the pre-release re-check of September 2026 found no death record and no dated item since an April 2024 interview. A miniaturist who made three formally distinct attempts at explicit writing across two decades.
entries.knownFor: A novel consisting of a single telephone conversation, which was his first bestseller, and two subsequent experiments that took the constraint in opposite directions.
entries.signature: Constraint-first erotic construction. Each book takes one formal restriction and derives everything from it: a single unbroken two-voice dialogue with no narration at all, so every physical fact must be spoken; a time-stop conceit that converts the erotic into pure looking and forces the moral problem into the open; and an abandonment of realism for a comic invented geography that relocates the writing from arousal to invention. The transferable lesson is that in explicit writing the formal constraint rather than the vocabulary is what produces variety. The second move is his hyper-detailed attention to ordinary objects, applied to bodies.

entries.name: Jeanette Winterson
entries.description: The ungendered narrator, sustained for a whole book without evasion.
entries.meta: British, born 27 August 1959; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. The novel that carries her into this pack is a queer erotic text written in a high-literary lyric register rather than a genre one.
entries.knownFor: A 1992 novel whose narrator is never assigned a sex, and a body of work that keeps erotic writing inside literary prose.
entries.signature: The ungendered narrator. The first person is never assigned a sex and the book sustains it for its whole length without evasion, which forces the erotic writing to work without the reader's default anatomical scaffolding and makes every physical description carry more load. The second move is the anatomical lexicon used as love poetry: she writes the body in the vocabulary of the medical textbook — cells, clavicle, marrow — and lets the technical register produce tenderness by contrast. The third is short lyric sections with heavy white space borrowed from the prose poem, so the sexual passages are formally set apart from narrative.

works.title: Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit

entries.name: Ian McEwan
entries.description: The best single study in the pack of sex that fails, written at almost real time.
entries.meta: British, born 21 June 1948; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. An early reputation for flat-affect transgressive short fiction, and a late novel that is the tradition's most useful case of a failed encounter.
entries.knownFor: The 2007 novel in which a marriage and two lives turn on a few minutes of misread physical signalling.
entries.signature: The sexual scene as a plot mechanism with irreversible consequence. He puts the encounter at the structural centre and makes a life turn on it, writing clinically and slowing almost to real time, with the interest lying in the discrepancy between two interiorities occupying one event. The second move is free indirect discourse alternated across both participants inside a single continuous scene, so the reader holds information neither character has. The third, from the early work, is a flat affect applied to transgressive material and a deliberate refusal of authorial commentary.

entries.name: John Updike
entries.description: The metaphor-dense sex paragraph, carded honestly as a high-risk technique.
entries.meta: American, 18 March 1932 – 27 January 2009. The novel that carried explicit heterosexual adultery into the American literary mainstream appeared in 1968, and he later received a lifetime award from a prize that exists to mock the literary sex scene.
entries.knownFor: A body of work in which sex is written at a metaphorical density no other writer in this line attempts, and which is both his best pages and the entire case against him.
entries.signature: The metaphor-dense, lexically ornate sex paragraph — the body written through simile drawn from landscape, weather, machinery and religion. This pack cards it as a high-risk technique rather than as a model, because the same procedure produces the peaks and the parodies, and a writer adopting it is taking on both. The second move is sex located inside a fully specified social economy of money, church, suburb and profession, so that an encounter is legible as class information before it is legible as desire.

entries.name: Philip Roth
entries.description: The monologue under pressure, which licenses obscenity as symptom rather than as description.
entries.meta: American, 19 March 1933 – 22 May 2018. His recurring narrators are characters rather than pen names, which makes him a useful negative example for this pack's pseudonym taxonomy.
entries.knownFor: The 1969 monologue novel, a late novel of compulsive appetite, and a long argument that such appetite is a legitimate subject for the highest literary register.
entries.signature: The monologue under pressure. The novel is a single unbroken address to an unspeaking listener, which licenses obscenity as symptom rather than as description and gives the prose its runaway comic acceleration — long periodic sentences, escalating lists, self-interruption. The second move is shame as the engine of the erotic paragraph: the act and the narrator's disgust at it are written in the same breath, so the reader cannot separate arousal from mortification. The third, in the late work, is sex written from the vantage of physical decline, which changes the tense of desire from anticipation to loss.

entries.name: Mary Gaitskill
entries.description: Desire that the desirer does not endorse, with the authorial verdict withheld.
entries.meta: American, born 11 November 1954; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Her best-known story was adapted as a 2002 film, and in 2023 she published a magazine sequel to the same material under changed consent norms — an author re-running her own scene thirty-five years later.
entries.knownFor: A first collection of stories about transactional and ambiguous encounters, and a career spent refusing to tell the reader how to feel about them.
entries.signature: The withheld authorial verdict on consent. She writes transactional, masochistic and ambiguous encounters and declines to supply the sentence that would settle them, displacing the moral work onto precise physical and social detail. The second move is a flat, slightly clinical mid-length sentence used for humiliating material, with a single lyric image arriving once per story and detonating the accumulated flatness. The third is that she narrates the aftermath as carefully as the act, so scenes run act and then interpretation, and the interpretation is usually wrong.

entries.name: Anne Rice
entries.description: Three pen names doing three different jobs, and a parallel explicit line later merged into the main brand.
entries.meta: American, born Howard Allen Frances O'Brien on 4 October 1941 in New Orleans and died 11 December 2021 at Rancho Mirage. Three author-owned names, none of them a publisher's: the working name over the legal one, a deliberately opaque one for the erotic trilogy, and a semi-transparent one keeping her first name for the contemporary erotic novels.
entries.knownFor: A major commercial career in supernatural fiction, and a demonstration that such a novelist could run an explicit line under managed pen names and later consolidate it.
entries.signature: The sustained fairy-tale frame as a permission structure. By setting the erotic trilogy in an explicitly unreal and timeless kingdom she removes every naturalistic constraint — consequence, biography, period — and can therefore write a long systematised sequence with no plot obligation except escalation itself. The second move is serial escalation architecture across three volumes rather than within one. The third, in the contemporary books, is realism with an institutionalised erotic setting, which is the opposite structural approach to the same material.

works.title: The Claiming of Sleeping Beauty
works.note: under a deliberately opaque pen name

works.title: Exit to Eden
works.note: under a second pen name that keeps her first name

entries.name: Nikki Gemmell
entries.description: Second person, present tense, numbered fragments — and anonymity used as a marketing structure rather than a concealment.
entries.meta: Australian, born 17 November 1966; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. The 2003 novel appeared with no name on it at all rather than a false one, and she was identified publicly as its author before publication, which makes it anonymity rather than pseudonymity and a fourth mode this pack's taxonomy does not cover.
entries.knownFor: The best-selling book by an Australian author in 2003, later named among the best Australian novels of the following quarter-century.
entries.signature: Second person, present tense, numbered fragments. The novel addresses its protagonist as you throughout and is built from short numbered sections keyed to a period conduct-book structure, so the second person does the work anonymity is usually asked to do — it puts the reader inside a sexual life while keeping the speaker unlocatable. The transferable technique is borrowed non-fiction scaffolding, a marriage manual or a conduct book, used as the ordering device for an erotic narrative.

works.title: The Bride Stripped Bare
works.note: published anonymously, with the author named before publication

entries.name: Susie Bright
entries.description: The editor as author — the anthology pipeline that gave short erotic fiction a repeatable annual venue.
entries.meta: American, born 25 March 1958 in Arlington, Virginia; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against her own dated post of September 2026, three days before the check. Co-founder and editor of a lesbian sex magazine from 1984, editor of an anthology series from 1988, and editor of an annual best-of series from 1993 to 2008.
entries.knownFor: Building the American anthology infrastructure for short erotic fiction, and writing the period's most useful craft manual for the form.
entries.signature: Editorial, and it is the carded craft. She applied the prestige best-of franchise form to material the prize system would not touch, which imported packaging and a visible standard onto a genre that had neither. Her selection signature is voice-first: pieces chosen for a distinctive first-person register rather than for act or orientation, and sequenced so consecutive pieces contrast in tone. As a writer her signature is the instructional register with a comic narrator, and her craft manual is a primary source for this pack rather than a secondary one.

works.title: Herotica
works.note: the anthology she edited, and the series it began

works.title: Best American Erotica
works.note: edited annually through 2008

works.title: How to Write a Dirty Story

entries.name: Alexander Trocchi
entries.description: One writer producing commissioned house erotica and formally radical literature at the same time, with different apparatus for each.
entries.meta: Scottish, 30 July 1925 – 15 April 1984. He wrote to commission under two names the Paris house controlled rather than owned by him, and later reclaimed one of those books under his own.
entries.knownFor: The hinge between the two halves of this line — an Anglophone modernist who paid for his serious work by writing French-published erotica to a publisher's order.
entries.signature: The picaresque first-person erotic novel written at speed, with a plain propulsive chapter-a-scene construction and a female narrator sustained across a whole book. In the signed work the method inverts entirely: a self-observing drifting present-tense narration in which sex, drugs and boredom occupy one flat register. The pairing is the lesson, and it is the clearest case in the pack that commissioned genre erotica and formally radical literature can come from the same hand in the same years, using different apparatus for each.

works.title: Helen and Desire
works.note: written to commission under a house-controlled name

works.title: Young Adam
works.note: issued under the same house name and later republished under his own

works.title: Thongs
works.note: under a second house-controlled name

works.title: Cain's Book
works.note: under his own name

entries.name: A. M. Homes
entries.description: The deadpan domestic register carrying unspeakable content, with no escalation in the prose to warn the reader.
entries.meta: American, born 18 December 1961; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a university course listing for the autumn 2026 term. The initialised byline is an abbreviation rather than a pen name, a distinction this pack needs in order not to card every initialised woman writer as pseudonymous. One novel in her bibliography falls entirely within this pack's categorical exclusion; it is not named, not described and not carded, and its absence is policy rather than oversight.
entries.knownFor: Transgressive American domestic fiction in which sexual material is used to detonate suburban surfaces.
entries.signature: The deadpan domestic register carrying unspeakable content. She writes catastrophic sexual material in the sentence rhythms of a realist domestic novel with no escalation in the prose to warn the reader, so the shock is produced by register mismatch rather than by description. The second move is the object as erotic proxy, where desire is displaced onto a manufactured thing and the displacement is played entirely straight. The third is an unreliable first person maintained without any authorial correction anywhere in the text.

works.title: This Book Will Save Your Life

entries.name: Anne Lister
entries.description: Encryption used as tonal modulation, and the proof that this line predates the presses.
entries.meta: English, 3 April 1791 – 22 September 1840, dead at Kutaisi in Georgia at forty-nine. She published nothing: her medium was a private manuscript, and she enters this pack through edited editions whose years are the editions' rather than hers.
entries.knownFor: A diary of some five million words in twenty-six volumes, of which roughly one sixth is in a cipher she devised herself from the Greek alphabet, the zodiac, punctuation and mathematical symbols.
entries.signature: The cipher as a formal device. The coded passages are not a separate secret text kept elsewhere; they are interleaved sentence by sentence with the plain diary, so the register shifts mid-paragraph and the erotic material sits in the same line at a different frequency. What a writer takes from it is encryption used as tonal modulation rather than as concealment. She used no modern term for herself and this pack puts none in her mouth. She holds no literary award and could not: the honour routinely misreported as one is an archival inscription attaching to the manuscript rather than a prize.

works.title: I Know My Own Heart
works.note: the first edited edition; a 1992 date is also given and neither is settled

works.title: No Priest But Love
works.note: a 1993 date is also given

entries.name: Djuna Barnes
entries.description: The aphoristic baroque, and a censorship case with no trial in it at all.
entries.meta: American, 12 June 1892 – 18 June 1982. A 1928 novel of hers was censored by the United States Postal Service, which had illustrations removed and textual passages replaced with asterisks — administrative suppression rather than judicial, with no verdict and no hearing, just a carrier refusing carriage.
entries.knownFor: A 1936 novel that is the tradition's most difficult and most imitated queer prose, and a privately printed almanac issued under a mock-archaic byline.
entries.signature: The aphoristic baroque. She writes desire in long, heavily subordinated, deliberately archaic sentences whose grammar keeps deferring the object, so that longing is enacted by syntax rather than described. The second move is character delivered almost entirely through monologue by a third party: the person desired is constructed out of someone else's talking and is barely present in her own right. The third is accidental — the visible asterisk in the censored novel, which makes absence typographically legible and is worth carding as a technique nobody chose.

works.title: Ladies Almanack
works.note: privately printed under a mock-archaic byline that is also the book's voice

works.title: Ryder
works.note: censored by the Postal Service, with passages replaced by asterisks

entries.name: Jean Genet
entries.description: Sustained high register applied to degraded material, without irony.
entries.meta: French, 19 December 1910 – 15 April 1986, both in Paris. Facing possible life imprisonment after ten convictions, he was spared in 1949 when Cocteau, Sartre and Picasso among others successfully petitioned the President of France to set the sentence aside.
entries.knownFor: The most notorious queer erotic prose of the 1940s, published under the writer's own name by a convict, while Anglophone writers of far tamer material used cover names.
entries.signature: The reversal of moral valence as a prose engine. He writes theft, betrayal and prison in the vocabulary of liturgy and heraldry, so the erotic passages arrive already elevated; technically it is sustained high register applied to degraded material without irony, which is why the sentences carry content that would be merely reportorial in a plainer style. The dating is the standing problem: his major prose exists in clandestine first printings and later trade editions, sources disagree about which year to give, and this pack cards the verified trade years while carrying the dispute rather than asserting a clandestine year nobody has verified.

works.title: Miracle de la rose
works.note: a clandestine printing of 1946 is widely cited and is not verified here

works.title: Querelle de Brest
works.note: a clandestine printing of 1947 is widely cited and is not verified here

works.title: Les Bonnes
works.note: a premiere year rather than a publication year

entries.name: Marijane Meaker
entries.description: The punitive ending as a condition of publication, with the seam left visible.
entries.meta: American, 27 May 1927 – 21 November 2022, born at Auburn and dead at Springs, New York, at ninety-five. Six working names across six markets — crime, lesbian paperback, paperback non-fiction, young adult, books for younger readers, and her own name for a late memoir — all of them personal and portable, which makes her the clearest illustration in the pack that a writer can own many names at once.
entries.knownFor: The 1952 paperback credited with launching the American lesbian paperback line, written under one of those names for a mass-market house.
entries.signature: The punitive ending as a condition of publication. The closing turn of her founding paperback was shaped by what the distributor would carry through the mails, and the craft interest is the visible seam between the book the writer wrote and the ending the postal regime required — censorship operating as a structural force rather than a lexical one, and legible on the page. She is also the counter-example to the assumption that pulp names were owned by the houses that printed them: hers were market-keyed and hers.

works.title: Spring Fire
works.note: published under her crime-fiction name for a mass-market house

works.title: We Walk Alone
works.note: paperback-original non-fiction under a third name

works.title: Highsmith: A Romance of the 1950s
works.note: under her own name

entries.name: Ann Bannon
entries.description: Prose doing its work by pressure against a censored lexicon rather than by description.
entries.meta: American, born 15 September 1932; living status carried as unconfirmed. This card previously asserted `living, checked in September 2026`; the pre-release re-check of September 2026 found no death record and no dated item since a December 2021 interview, so the assertion is withdrawn rather than repeated. She wrote the paperbacks as a young suburban housewife and took a doctorate in linguistics afterwards, so the academic career follows the fiction rather than informing it.
entries.knownFor: A sequence of Gold Medal paperbacks that became the best-known body of American lesbian pulp, published under a name she chose herself.
entries.signature: First-person retrospective narration inside a mass-market length and price, with the erotic charge carried entirely by withheld naming. The characters' situation is stated in the vocabulary available to a 1950s drugstore paperback, so the prose works by pressure against a censored lexicon rather than by description — which is the same mechanism the euphemistic register uses two centuries earlier, arrived at independently and under a commercial rather than a legal constraint. Her honours are career awards rather than book prizes, and the award bearing her name is a popular vote she did not win.

entries.name: Valerie Taylor
entries.description: The bridge from the mass-market paperback to the movement press, and the reason the line survived its own market.
entries.meta: American, 7 September 1913 – 22 October 1997, born Velma Nacella Young. Three market-keyed working names, with no source establishing who chose them, so the classification is probable rather than verified.
entries.knownFor: A run of lesbian paperbacks from the late 1950s, and a second career founding the institutions the writing needed.
entries.signature: The crossing from mass market to movement press, which no other writer in this block makes so completely — Gold Medal and Midwood at one end, Naiad and Womanpress at the other. That range is why she matters more than her sales: she co-founded a homophile organisation in 1965, wrote for the movement's own magazine, and co-founded a lesbian writers' conference in 1974, so the distribution infrastructure that carried the next generation is partly hers. The craft lesson is institutional rather than stylistic, and this pack cards it as craft because in this line the two are not separable.

works.title: Prism
works.note: issued by a movement press rather than a paperback house

entries.name: James Baldwin
entries.description: Desire rendered as a problem of the sentence's forward motion.
entries.meta: American and long resident in France, 2 August 1924 – 1 December 1987, dead at Saint-Paul-de-Vence of stomach cancer. His second novel was declined by his own publisher over its content and taken by another house in the autumn of 1956, which is the separate threshold operating on a literary novelist rather than on a pulp imprint.
entries.knownFor: A short novel of 1956 that is the tradition's most durable account of a desire its narrator cannot hold, and a career that refused to separate the sexual subject from the political one.
entries.signature: The erotic carried by shame's syntax. His sexual passages are written in long self-interrupting sentences whose subordinate clauses are the narrator arguing with himself; the physical detail is sparse and the pressure comes from the delay. The transferable technique is desire rendered as a problem of the sentence's forward motion rather than of its content. He won no major American book prize for the queer novels and the 1956 one is uncrowned, which is worth stating because cards elsewhere gesture at an award that does not exist.

works.title: Giovanni's Room
works.note: declined by his own publisher and issued by another

works.title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
Tell Me How Long the Train's Been Gone

entries.name: Samuel Steward
entries.description: The pack's proof case for the persona pseudonym — a pen name that is also the narrator.
entries.meta: American, 23 July 1909 – 31 December 1993, born in Ohio and dead at Berkeley. A tattoo artist who mentored several of the trade's best-known figures, and from 1949 an unofficial collaborator of Alfred Kinsey, supplying sexual records and research contacts — which makes him the rare figure who is a primary source and an author at once.
entries.knownFor: A body of erotic short fiction published under a name that is also the name of its narrator, and a separate career under a separate name entirely.
entries.signature: The persona that claims authorship from inside the fiction. His erotic byline functions as both pen name and narrating character, which is the defining test for that category and the reason this card is the taxonomy's proof case: the claim of authorship is part of the work rather than a wrapper around it. He also ran a second personal name for essays and a third for other prose, so his practice separates the persona from ordinary pen naming within one career and lets the two be compared directly.

works.title: $tud
works.note: under the persona byline that is also the narrator

works.title: Angels on the Bough
works.note: under his own name

entries.name: John Preston
entries.description: The writer who declined a cover name for explicit fiction and built an editorial career on the same name.
entries.meta: American, 11 December 1945 – 28 April 1994, dead at Portland, Maine, at forty-eight of complications from AIDS. Editor of a national gay magazine in 1975, and the block's principal anthologist.
entries.knownFor: An explicit novel published under his own name, and an anthology series from 1992 that moved explicit gay writing into general trade distribution under a named editor.
entries.signature: Refusing the cover name, and then using the same name to edit. He is the clearest case in this block of a writer who declined pseudonymity for explicit fiction and made the byline itself an argument, and his anthologies are how the line reproduced itself — an editorial rather than a stylistic contribution, and the more consequential of the two. Note that this pack cards no year for his best-known novel: the serial and first book editions could not be separated from any source consulted, and the pack's own rule requires that separation, so the gap is stated rather than filled.

works.title: I Once Had a Master and Other Tales of Erotic Love
Hometowns: Gay Men Write About Where They Belong
Flesh and the Word
