works.note: an anthology series that ran on into the 1990s

entries.name: Larry Townsend
entries.description: The infrastructure builder at the origin of the periodical spine of American leather fiction.
entries.meta: American, born Michael Lawrence Townsend, 27 October 1930 – 29 July 2008, dead at Los Angeles of pneumonia complications. He wrote under a personal name built from his own middle and last names, carried across both an American adult-paperback house and a Paris-descended imprint.
entries.knownFor: A 1972 manual that is the founding written statement of American leather practice, and a set of organisational roles that produced the magazine the whole fiction line ran on.
entries.signature: The manual written as working practice with reasons attached rather than as rules, which is what makes it usable as craft rather than as etiquette. His larger contribution is structural: he presided over a legal-protection organisation from 1969 and led the group whose 1972 newsletter became the periodical that carried the American leather-fiction line, so he sits at that line's origin as an infrastructure builder and not only as an author. His awards are leather-community honours, one of them posthumous; he holds no literary award, and none was possible for the 1970s work.

entries.name: Monique Wittig
entries.description: A first novel that took a major French prize thirty-six years before the Anglophone system had a category for the work.
entries.meta: French and later resident in the United States, 13 July 1935 – 3 January 2003. Her positions on gender categories are contested inside the communities concerned and are carded here as hers rather than as settled.
entries.knownFor: A 1973 prose sequence that is the most formally radical lesbian erotic text of its century, and a first novel that won the Prix Medicis in 1964.
entries.signature: Grammar attacked directly. The prose sequence dismantles the first person itself, splitting the pronoun typographically so that the speaking subject is visibly divided on the page, and the erotic material is inseparable from that operation — this is the block's clearest case of a formal device carrying an argument the content alone could not make. The award record is the block's strongest single piece of evidence for its separate-track claim: a major French literary prize went to a lesbian first novel in 1964, while the Anglophone distribution system was still suppressing the equivalent work and would not have a category for it for another thirty-eight years. Her erotic book itself won nothing.

works.title: Le Corps lesbien
works.note: catalogues differ on whether to call it a novel or a prose poem

works.title: L'Opoponax
works.note: winner of the Prix Medicis that year

works.title: Brouillon pour un dictionnaire des amantes

entries.name: Audre Lorde
entries.description: The theoretical statement the block would have a hole without, arguing the erotic as a source of power distinct from the pornographic.
entries.meta: Caribbean-American, 18 February 1934 – 17 November 1992, born in New York to Grenadian parents and dead at St Croix. She described herself as Black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet, and the serial form is the point rather than a flourish: her own argument is that the terms are not separable.
entries.knownFor: A 1981 essay that is the most cited theoretical statement in queer erotic writing, and a memoir she called a biomythography, which is a genre problem this pack flags rather than silently resolves.
entries.signature: The erotic argued as a source of power rather than as a subject for depiction. The essay's move is to separate the erotic from the pornographic on the ground of self-knowledge rather than of explicitness, which gives writers a criterion that does not depend on how much is shown — and it is the criterion most often reached for, and most often misquoted, in craft writing about this genre. A pack that carded only practitioners and no theorist of the erotic would have a hole where its argument should be.

works.title: Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power
Zami: A New Spelling of My Name
works.note: her own term for it is biomythography

entries.name: Patrick Califia
entries.description: Negotiation written as characterisation rather than as procedure, and aftercare written as part of the scene.
entries.meta: American, born 8 March 1954 in Corpus Christi; living status carried as unconfirmed. This card previously asserted `living, checked in September 2026`; the pre-release re-check found no death record and no dated item since 2013, so the assertion is withdrawn rather than repeated. A bisexual trans man who uses he and him, and who began transition in 1999; the pre-1999 books were published under a different form of the name, which is a fact about those editions rather than a competing identity, and this pack neither retro-fits nor erases it. The name change is not a pen name, which is a useful negative for the taxonomy.
entries.knownFor: A 1988 collection of explicit short fiction, and the anthology produced by the collective he co-founded, which was the first lesbian organisation of its kind in the United States and ran from 1978 to 1983.
entries.signature: Negotiation as characterisation rather than as procedure. Each clause of a negotiated scene reveals who is asking, which is the only reliable way to stop the passage reading as paperwork, and it is the technique the entire modern apparatus of on-page consent has been reaching for since. The second move is that he writes the aftermath as part of the scene rather than after it, and the inclusion changes the genre of the whole passage — the strongest single argument in the canon that where a writer stops determines what the scene means.

works.title: Sapphistry: The Book of Lesbian Sexuality
Coming to Power
works.note: the collective's anthology, issued by a movement press

works.title: Public Sex: The Culture of Radical Sex

entries.name: Samuel R. Delany
entries.description: Anonymity written as an infrastructure with places, hours and rules — and a body of explicit fiction that is entirely unhonoured.
entries.meta: American, born 1 April 1942 in Harlem; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. He describes his long partnership as nonexclusive and has identified as gay since adolescence, and those are his terms. One title in his record falls under this pack's categorical exclusion, is not named and carries no further detail.
entries.knownFor: A major science fiction career and, under the same byline, explicit pornographic novels — a writer with four Nebulas and two Hugos who put the pornography out under the name that carried the science fiction.
entries.signature: Anonymity written as infrastructure. He gives the anonymous encounter places, hours, prices and rules, and that specificity is what stops it reading as a fantasy of nobody in particular; it is the opposite of the usual treatment, in which anonymity is written as an absence of detail rather than a different kind of detail. The award record is itself evidence: every honour he holds is a science fiction, fantasy or general-letters award, and the explicit fiction has been given nothing at all.

works.title: Equinox
works.note: the title is unstable across editions and also appears as The Tides of Lust

works.title: Times Square Red, Times Square Blue
Through the Valley of the Nest of Spiders

entries.name: Leslie Feinberg
entries.description: The body written through the institutions that read it, so the reader gets a sequence of readings rather than a definition.
entries.meta: American, 1 September 1949 – 15 November 2014, dead at sixty-five of complications from tick-borne infections carried since the 1970s. Feinberg favoured she and her before general audiences and also used he and him and the gender-neutral zie and hir depending on context; hir widow states the preference was for she and zie, her and hir, and that respectful intent mattered more than correctness. This pack reproduces that formulation rather than selecting one set.
entries.knownFor: A 1993 novel issued by a movement press, and two later works of non-fiction on transgender history and politics.
entries.signature: The body written through the institutions that read it. Bars, factories, hospitals and police each read the protagonist differently, so the reader receives a sequence of readings rather than a definition, and the disagreement between them is the material. The presses matter as much as the prose: the movement-press route is the same infrastructure that carried the previous generation's late careers, and it is why this line's books exist at all.

works.title: Stone Butch Blues
works.note: issued by a movement press rather than a trade house

works.title: Trans Liberation: Beyond Pink or Blue
works.note: a 1998 date is widely given and the two are not reconciled

entries.name: Sarah Waters
entries.description: A scholar of the tradition writing inside it, and the proof that by 2000 the prize system had stopped quarantining the work.
entries.meta: Welsh, born 21 July 1966; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Her doctorate is on lesbian and gay historical fiction from 1870 onward, so the pastiche is informed rather than incidental.
entries.knownFor: A 1998 first novel of Victorian pastiche, and a run of literary prizes and shortlists across the following decade.
entries.signature: Historical pastiche built from research rather than from period atmosphere. The Victorian sentence is reconstructed accurately enough to carry explicit content without anachronism, which is the technically hard part: the erotic passages have to work inside a diction that had no vocabulary for them, and the solution is the same withheld-naming pressure the pulp writers used under a different constraint. Her award record is the finding: the most sexually explicit novel on this block's list won a fiction prize rather than an erotica one, and she holds no erotica-category award at all — by 2000 the Anglophone prize system was rewarding explicit lesbian historical fiction inside its general categories rather than quarantining it.

works.title: Tipping the Velvet
works.note: winner of the Betty Trask Award in 1999 and a Lambda Literary Award for lesbian fiction in 2000

entries.name: Jul Maroh
entries.description: The cost of concealment put into the colour rather than the dialogue, and a work whose famous prize went to somebody else entirely.
entries.meta: French, born 1985; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Maroh is openly transgender and nonbinary and uses they and them; the 2010 book was first published under a different form of the name, which is a fact about that edition. The name change is not a pen name, which makes this the second worked example in this block of what is not a pseudonym.
entries.knownFor: A 2010 graphic novel that became internationally known through a 2013 film adaptation, and won a public prize at a comics festival in 2011.
entries.signature: The cost of separation put into the colour. The diary frame keeps the concealed and the disclosed on separate pages, and the comics form puts the price of that separation into the palette rather than into the dialogue, which is a move prose has to simulate and cannot do directly. The award record carries a trap the pack states plainly: the Palme d'Or of 2013 went to the film, its director and its lead actresses, and not to the book or to its author.

works.title: Le bleu est une couleur chaude
works.note: card the French year; the English edition and the film are both 2013 and neither is admissible

entries.name: Nancy Friday
entries.description: The solicited account — material a first person could not offer, licensed by being somebody else's.
entries.meta: American, 27 August 1933 – 5 November 2017. Her first book appeared in 1973 into an argument about whether women had sexual fantasies at all, and its evidence was the answer.
entries.knownFor: A 1973 collection of reported fantasy that was the first mass-market book to treat women's sexual imagination as a subject with data rather than a question with an answer.
entries.signature: The solicited account. The book is built entirely from fantasy reported by other people to an intermediary who has promised anonymity, and the promise is what the material depends on — a structural discovery available to novelists as readily as to interviewers, because an account solicited from someone else licenses material a first person could not offer. The second move is arrangement: the pieces are grouped by theme rather than by contributor, so the book argues by accumulation without ever stating the argument.

entries.name: Andrea Dworkin
entries.description: The civil-rights argument at its strongest, carded because a pack that omitted it would be arguing rather than reporting.
entries.meta: American, 26 September 1946 – 9 April 2005. Her position is carded here at full strength and is not adjudicated; the opposing position is carded separately in this collection, and both are held by serious people.
entries.knownFor: Two book-length arguments of 1981 and 1987, and a model ordinance drafted with Catharine MacKinnon that was enacted in 1984 and struck down by a federal appellate court in 1985.
entries.signature: The argument that pornography is not speech about subordination but an act of it — produced through coercion of real women and consumed as training in contempt — and the deliberate choice to frame the remedy as a civil rights claim giving harmed individuals a private cause of action rather than as criminal obscenity law. That framing is the part most often missed, and it is what makes the position a legal innovation rather than a restatement of censorship. Her prose signature is the flat declarative repeated to the point of incantation, which is the same device the modernists used for the opposite purpose.

entries.name: Ellen Willis
entries.description: The prediction that the machinery would be turned first on the material it was meant to protect.
entries.meta: American, 14 December 1941 – 9 November 2006. Her 1981 essay coined the term for the position it argued, and her side of the argument is carded here at the same strength as the other.
entries.knownFor: A 1981 essay that named pro-sex feminism, and a career of criticism that treated popular culture and sexual politics as one subject.
entries.signature: The argument that any state machinery built to suppress pornography would be turned first on feminist, lesbian and sexually dissident material — a prediction rather than a principle, and one whose subsequent record is itself contested. Her prose signature is the essayist's turn: she concedes the opposing case in its strongest form early and then shows what follows from accepting it, which is why her side of the argument reads as reasoning rather than as position-taking. Note that the founding of the anti-censorship task force of 1984 is attributed to her in some accounts and to Ann Snitow in others, and this pack records the disagreement.

works.title: Lust Horizons
works.note: the essay that coined the term for its own position

works.title: Out of the Vinyl Deeps
works.note: posthumous

entries.name: Gayle Rubin
entries.description: The argument that sexuality needs a theory of its own rather than a derivative one.
entries.meta: American, born 1949; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against her department's own published course list for the winter 2026 term, which names her as the instructor — a status this pack earlier carried as unconfirmed, now resolved. An anthropologist whose two best-known essays are separated by nine years and by a change of subject.
entries.knownFor: A 1975 essay on the social organisation of sex and gender, and a 1984 essay arguing that sexuality requires its own analysis rather than a feminist one.
entries.signature: The separation of two questions that had been treated as one. The 1984 essay argues that sexuality needs a theory distinct from feminism and that the anti-pornography faction did not speak for feminism as such — a move that reframed the argument rather than taking a side in it, and the reason the essay is still assigned. Her method is anthropological rather than polemical: she describes a hierarchy of sexual practices as a working social fact and then asks what the hierarchy is for, which is a more durable procedure than argument by principle.

works.title: Thinking Sex: Notes for a Radical Theory of the Politics of Sexuality

entries.name: Dorothy Allison
entries.description: Class written into the erotic, and the refusal to make either respectable.
entries.meta: American, 11 April 1949 – 2024, dead in November of that year. She co-founded a New York sexual-politics organisation in 1981, and her death postdates this pack's first research pass, which had carried her status as unresolved.
entries.knownFor: A 1988 collection and a 1992 novel that put Southern working-class life and sexual violence into literary fiction without softening either.
entries.signature: Class written into the erotic. She refuses to let desire float free of economic circumstance, so the sexual material carries information about money, work and shame simultaneously and cannot be extracted from them. The second move is the flat first-person declarative applied to material the reader expects to be delivered with more cushioning, which produces the effect of testimony rather than of confession. She is also the block's demonstration that the sex-wars argument was fought by writers as well as about them.

works.title: Skin: Talking About Sex, Class and Literature

entries.name: Carole S. Vance
entries.description: The conference and the anthology that gave the other side its founding document.
entries.meta: American, life dates unresolved; this pack's research could not confirm a living status either way, so the card asserts neither. An anthropologist and the academic organiser of the 1982 conference from whose planning anti-pornography feminists were excluded and outside which they picketed.
entries.knownFor: Editing the 1984 collection that came out of that conference, which is the anti-censorship side's founding document in the way the ordinance is the other side's.
entries.signature: The edited collection as an argument. She assembled a volume in which the contributors do not agree with each other and let the disagreement stand, which is a different rhetorical act from writing a monograph and a more durable one — the book cannot be answered by refuting a thesis because it does not have one. The pairing of pleasure and danger in its framing is the substantive move: it refuses to let either half of the argument claim the whole subject, and every serious treatment since has had to work inside that framing or explain why not.

works.title: Pleasure and Danger: Exploring Female Sexuality
works.note: three circulating years exist for this title and the pack has not settled them

entries.name: Shere Hite
entries.description: The questionnaire as a literary form, and a data set assembled to answer a question the field was not asking.
entries.meta: American and later German, 2 November 1942 – 9 September 2020. She renounced her American citizenship in 1995 after sustained hostility to her work.
entries.knownFor: A 1976 report built from thousands of returned questionnaires, which reported women's own accounts of their sexuality in their own words and at length.
entries.signature: The questionnaire as a literary form. The reports are constructed largely from extended verbatim responses rather than from summary statistics, so the book reads as a chorus rather than as a study, and the method is what made it both influential and attackable. For a writer the interest is the register: hundreds of people describing sexual experience in unliterary language, which is the largest available corpus of how the subject is actually spoken about outside fiction, and it does not sound like fiction.

works.title: The Hite Report on Male Sexuality
The Hite Report on the Family

entries.name: Erica Fischer
entries.description: The recovered account, and the documentary method applied to a queer erotic history that nearly vanished.
entries.meta: Austrian, born 1 January 1943 at St Albans in England, to parents who had emigrated in 1938 and returned to Vienna after the war, so the nationality and the birthplace are not the same country; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a national-broadcaster interview of August 2025 — a status this pack earlier carried as unconfirmed, now resolved. A journalist, writer and translator working in German, which places her outside the Anglophone frame this category otherwise sits in.
entries.knownFor: A 1994 documentary reconstruction of a wartime love affair between two women in Berlin, assembled from interviews, letters and archival record.
entries.signature: The recovered account. The book is built from a surviving participant's testimony cross-checked against documents, and its erotic material arrives as evidence rather than as narration — which is the opposite of every other technique in this category and produces a different kind of pressure, because the reader knows the events are attested. It is also this pack's reminder that the second wave was not only Anglophone, and that a category assembled from one language will mistake its own boundaries for the subject's.

entries.name: Alan Hollinghurst
entries.description: The refusal of tonal escalation — sex and social observation given identical attention.
entries.meta: British, born 26 May 1954 at Stroud in Gloucestershire; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. His 2004 Booker win is the point at which a novel with explicit gay sex took Britain's principal literary prize outright, and it should be read against a novel destroyed by order in the same country in 1928.
entries.knownFor: A 1988 first novel of two interleaved chronologies, and a 2004 novel that won the Booker Prize.
entries.signature: The long free-indirect paragraph that treats sex and social observation with identical attention. He does not change register when a scene becomes explicit: the same comic, appraising, class-attentive prose continues, so the sexual material is neither climactic nor set apart and the erotic effect comes from its being noticed as precisely as the furniture. He holds no erotica prize of any kind; his explicit content has only ever been honoured inside general literary categories, which is the same pattern as his contemporaries and is evidence that the Anglophone prize system absorbed rather than segregated this material after about 2000.

works.title: The Line of Beauty
works.note: winner of the Booker Prize that year

works.title: The Stranger's Child
works.note: longlisted rather than shortlisted, which is not a win

entries.name: Edmund White
entries.description: The autofictional first person that reports desire without pleading for it.
entries.meta: American, born Edmund Valentine White III, 13 January 1940 – 3 June 2025, dead at his home in Manhattan at eighty-five. He published a book in the year he died, which is exactly the profile that produces a false claim that a writer is living; this pack's second research pass found him dead against four independent sources, and the card exists partly as the record of that catch.
entries.knownFor: A 1982 autofictional novel, a 1977 sex manual written with a collaborator, and a professorship in creative writing held from 1999.
entries.signature: The autofictional first person that reports desire without pleading for it. His narrators supply social and aesthetic context at the same density as physical detail, so an erotic scene arrives inside an essay-like paragraph, and the technique is a refusal of the confessional apology — no framing sentence tells the reader how to feel about what has been described. His major awards attach to a biography and to a career; the most explicit books are unhonoured, which is the same pattern that holds across this whole line.

works.title: The Joy of Gay Sex
works.note: written with a collaborator

works.title: Nocturnes for the King of Naples
Genet: A Biography
works.note: winner of the National Book Critics Circle Award for biography that year

works.title: The Loves of My Life: A Sex Memoir

entries.name: Guy Baldwin
entries.description: The column-length ethical essay, reasoning one disputed question of practice through from stated premises.
entries.meta: American, born 1946; life dates unresolved, because this pack's research could not positively confirm a living status and the absence of a death record is weaker than a confirmation. A psychotherapist writing for his own community, and the only holder of one national leather title ever to win the other.
entries.knownFor: A 1993 collection of essays on practice, a contest guide from the same year, and a 2002 co-authored account of erotic servitude.
entries.signature: The column-length ethical essay. Each short piece takes one disputed question of practice and reasons it through from stated premises, in the community's own vocabulary and without appeal to any outside authority, which is the register that distinguishes this line's non-fiction from both the sexology tradition and the sex-wars polemic. The later book is a rarer form and the one worth stealing: a co-authored first-person account in which the practitioner's testimony and the therapist's commentary run alongside each other. His contest titles are titles rather than literary awards and must be carded as such.

works.title: Ties That Bind
works.note: a second name appears on the title and whether as co-author or editor is unsettled

entries.name: Carol Queen
entries.description: The editor whose thesis is carried entirely by the table of contents.
entries.meta: American, born 1957; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Whether the carded name is a pen name could not be established and no type is asserted. Staff sexologist and cultural officer at the retail institution founded by the publisher who issued this line's first anthologies, which makes her the direct link between that infrastructure and the anthology industry of the 2000s.
entries.knownFor: A 1998 novel structured around movement across gender and role lines, and a run of anthologies edited to make a taxonomic claim.
entries.signature: The erotic novel written as an argument about categories — the narrator's movement across gender and role lines is the plot rather than the ornament. The second signature is anthology as polemic: her collections are edited to argue that the existing categories do not fit the material, and they make that argument by arrangement rather than by assertion. She is the best example in the pack of an editor whose thesis is carried entirely by the table of contents, which is a form of authorship the field depends on and rarely credits.

works.title: The Leather Daddy and the Femme
PoMoSexuals
works.note: co-edited

works.title: Best Bisexual Erotica
works.note: a series edited across the following years

entries.name: Marco Vassi
entries.description: The erotic narrative as consciousness-report, and the formal opposite of the procedural mode.
entries.meta: American, died 14 January 1989; his birth year is commonly given as 1937 and was not verified. His carded name is a shortening of his own legal name rather than a pen name, which is worth saying because the full form invites the opposite assumption.
entries.knownFor: A concept he named for sex outside the bounds of heterosexual marriage, developed into a theory that treats eroticism as a set of qualities of consciousness rather than a set of acts.
entries.signature: The erotic narrative as consciousness-report. The prose tracks the shifting state of attention rather than the sequence of acts, which is why the books read as interior monologue with events in them rather than as scene-writing. It is the formal opposite of the procedural manual mode carded elsewhere in this category, and the two make the sharpest contrast pair in the pack for what the same material looks like written from inside and from outside. He is carded here as an adjacency rather than as part of the feminist line: he arrives at a parallel vocabulary from phenomenology and Zen rather than from feminism.

entries.name: Joseph W. Bean
entries.description: The instructional book written for practitioners rather than about them, and the editorial hand behind much of the line.
entries.meta: American, life dates unresolved; this pack's research treated him as a candidate rather than a verified subject and no status is asserted. His name appears on the title page of one of the category's founding essay collections without it being settled whether as co-author or as editor.
entries.knownFor: Practitioner-facing instructional writing and a substantial editorial role in the leather community's press.
entries.signature: The instructional book addressed to practitioners rather than to observers. The register assumes the reader intends to do the thing described, which changes every sentence: no explanation of why anyone would, no framing for a curious outsider, and no defensive apparatus. That address is what distinguishes this line's manuals from the sexology tradition, and it is the reason a novelist reading them gets procedure rather than justification. His unsettled position on a shared title page is carded as unsettled, because the alternative is inventing a credit.

entries.name: Jack Fritscher
entries.description: The magazine that carried the fiction, edited by the man who also wrote it.
entries.meta: American, born 1939; life dates unresolved, since this pack's research did not positively confirm a living status and asserts none. The founding San Francisco editor of the periodical that was the American leather line's spine, and a novelist and photographer in the same years.
entries.knownFor: Editing the magazine through its formative period, and a body of fiction and documentary writing about the same community from inside it.
entries.signature: Writing and editing the same material in the same years, which is the working condition of this whole line and is invisible when its authors are carded separately from its periodicals. His fiction carries the magazine's habits — the short unit, the scene that has to work without a preceding chapter, the address to a reader who already knows the vocabulary — and reading it as periodical writing rather than as book writing explains the shape. This card exists partly to put the magazine into the roster, since the periodical rather than the novel is what this line actually ran on.

works.title: Drummer
works.note: the magazine he edited from its San Francisco period

entries.name: Catharine A. MacKinnon
entries.description: The definitional argument — winning by controlling what the thing is before anyone argues about it.
entries.meta: American, born 7 October 1946; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. In 1983 Minneapolis officials engaged her and Andrea Dworkin to draft an ordinance defining pornography as a civil rights violation actionable in civil court; it was passed in December of that year and vetoed, passed again in July 1984 and vetoed again, and the Indianapolis version signed in May 1984 was struck down by a federal appellate court in 1985.
entries.knownFor: The legal architecture of the anti-pornography position, and the sexual-harassment doctrine that American law adopted — which is the fact that makes the pornography argument legible, since she had already succeeded once at converting a private harm into a civil rights claim.
entries.signature: The definitional argument. She wins by controlling what the thing under discussion is before anybody argues about what should be done with it, and the prose device is the reversal of an idiom mid-sentence, so a phrase the reader has already accepted turns out to mean the opposite. Her position is carded here at full strength and is not adjudicated. Note the award trap in her own record: the 2014 honour carries a jurist's name and is not given by that jurist, which is the same class of trap as the leather line's memorial awards arising in a legal apparatus instead.

works.title: Toward a Feminist Theory of the State

entries.name: Joani Blank
entries.description: The person who built the press and the shop, without which this line's literature would not exist.
entries.meta: American, 4 July 1937 – 6 August 2016. She founded a press in 1975 and a retail institution in 1977; the press published the anthology series that professionalised American short erotic fiction, and the shop became the institution inside which the next generation held posts. One 1978 title in her bibliography falls under this pack's categorical exclusion and is not named, described or researched.
entries.knownFor: Building the infrastructure the rest of this category published through, and a run of first-person anthologies on subjects the trade would not print.
entries.signature: The first-person anthology as a publishing programme. Her method is to define a demographic or an experience the trade will not print, solicit unsolicited first-person accounts, and publish them with minimal editorial mediation — the 2000 volume on older women's sexuality is the clearest case of the method being used to open a subject rather than to serve a market. She is carded as a publisher and editor, and that is the point: this line's literature exists because somebody built a press and a shop for it.

works.title: The Playbook for Women About Sex
I Am My Lover
works.note: revised and reissued in 1997

entries.name: Tristan Taormino
entries.description: The series editor selecting against her own previous year, so a line develops by deliberate self-contradiction.
entries.meta: American, born 9 May 1971; living status carried as unconfirmed. This card previously asserted `living, checked in September 2026`; the pre-release re-check found no death record and no dated item since her 2023 book and its tour, so the assertion is withdrawn rather than repeated. She edited an annual anthology series across fourteen consecutive volumes from 1996 to 2009, which is the longest continuous editorial tenure in this territory.
entries.knownFor: The series-editor role treated as a craft position, and a 2013 collection in which the pro-sex position states its twenty-first-century case in its own terms.
entries.signature: The annual-anthology editorial method. A series editor selecting against her own previous year's selections makes the line develop by deliberate self-contradiction rather than by consolidation, which is the opposite of a house style and is why fourteen volumes do not converge. Her authorial signature is the instructional register done as prose: the how-to written with narrative examples, so the technical instruction is embedded in a scene and the reader learns the practice and the vocabulary at once. Her one juried award is for a manual rather than for fiction.

works.title: Best Lesbian Erotica
works.note: edited annually through 2009; the editorial work is the contribution

works.title: The Ultimate Guide to Anal Sex for Women
works.note: winner of the Firecracker Alternative Book Award in 1998

works.title: Take Me There: Trans and Genderqueer Erotica
The Feminist Porn Book
works.note: co-edited

entries.name: E L James
entries.description: The proof case that a fan-community text could be converted into the best-selling erotic sequence in English.
entries.meta: British, born 1963; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026. Her authorial identity began as a fan-fiction platform handle rather than as a pen name, which is a fifth mode this pack's four-type taxonomy does not cover: a handle that becomes a legal byline.
entries.knownFor: A sequence that reached print through three distinct stages — fan fiction under a handle, then an ebook and print-on-demand edition from a small press in May 2011, then a trade reissue in April 2012 — of which only the first commercial publication is the carded year.
entries.signature: Sustained close first-person present-tense interiority carrying a negotiation plot. The prose runs almost entirely inside one consciousness in the present tense, so the contract, the terms and the hesitation are all delivered as thought rather than as scene, and the negotiation becomes the book's forward motion. The award record is a trap in itself: the 2012 category award was a public vote rather than a juried prize, and this pack's own rule refuses to card a popular vote as a prize.

works.title: Fifty Shades of Grey
works.note: first commercial publication as ebook and print-on-demand; the trade reissue is 2012

entries.name: Anna Todd
entries.description: Instalment-scale escalation written for a comment thread, and the fullest documented case of filing off the serial numbers.
entries.meta: American, born 1989; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated interview of August 2026 — a status this pack earlier carried as unconfirmed, now resolved. Her platform identity was a posting handle rather than a pen name, which is the same taxonomy problem the block's largest seller presents.
entries.knownFor: The platform-to-print pipeline at its largest scale — a serial posted in short instalments from January 2013, accumulating an enormous readership before print publication in 2014.
entries.signature: Instalment-scale escalation written for a comment thread. The unit is sized to a single sitting and ends on an unresolved turn because the next instalment is already expected, and the readership's real-time response shapes the following unit — which is the Victorian part-issue's formal signature arrived at through an entirely different mechanism. The conversion to print is the second card: the male lead was renamed for the book edition, and the documented process of detaching a serial from the property it was written against is the clearest case available of what that revision actually involves.

works.title: After
works.note: posted in instalments from January 2013; the print edition followed in 2014

entries.name: Christina Lauren
entries.description: Antagonism as foreplay, and one pen name owned jointly by two writers.
entries.meta: American; two writers, Christina Hobbs and Lauren Billings, publishing under one name built from their first names, with life dates unresolved for both. This pack's research found no death notice and no dated item inside its confirmation window, so neither is carded as living. The joint pen name is a wrinkle the four-type taxonomy does not have a slot for: personal and portable, and owned by two people at once.
entries.knownFor: Converting a fan fiction into a trade erotic-romance franchise from 2013, and then into a general commercial-fiction career.
entries.signature: Antagonism as foreplay, run as a workplace-adversary two-hander. Two points of view alternate, each hearing the other's lines differently, so the hostility the reader is watching is being misread by both participants — which supplies the tension a courtship plot would otherwise have to import. It is the most efficient structure in the contemporary commercial form and it is why the workplace setting recurs: the institution supplies the enforced proximity and the antagonism supplies the rest.

works.title: Beautiful Bastard
works.note: originated as a fan fiction posted under a handle

entries.name: Jaid Black
entries.description: The strongest case in the pack of a writer owning both her name and the publisher it appeared under.
entries.meta: American, based in northeast Ohio; life dates unresolved, and living confirmed by dated posts on her own site in 2026. She founded the first commercially significant digital-native erotic-romance publisher in English and ran it for sixteen years, and she coined and branded the term it sold under.
entries.knownFor: Founding that house — whose founding year is given variously as 1999, 2000 and 2001 by different sources, one trade account resolving it as selling from 2000 and incorporating in 2001 — and writing for it under a name she owned.
entries.signature: The explicit scene fitted to a romance skeleton. Her house term names a formal contract rather than a mood: an emotionally committed ending is structurally required, and the explicit material is arranged to arrive on the way to it rather than instead of it. That is the boundary this whole pack is built on, stated as a commercial specification by the person selling it, and it is the clearest evidence available that the distinction between the two forms is a contract with readers rather than a judgement about content. Award claims attached to her record are author-side and are not carded here.

works.title: The Empress' New Clothes
works.note: the year is carried as a candidate and needs verification

works.title: Trek Mi Q'an
works.note: a series issued across subsequent years

entries.name: Zane
entries.description: The confessional short-story cycle in a spoken register, and a mononym chosen for anonymity and kept after it ended.
entries.meta: American, from Washington, D.C. — the district and not the state; born 1966 or 1967, with the reference works themselves flagging the year as uncertain; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated report of an author talk and signing in May 2025. The carded name is a mononym with no surname, chosen for anonymity in the early internet period and retained long after the anonymity had gone.
entries.knownFor: Building Black American erotica into a mass-market trade category, from chat-room short stories to an imprint inside a major house, which she founded and ran.
entries.signature: The confessional short-story cycle in a spoken register. Her origin form is the standalone first-person confession circulated to an online readership, and the cycle keeps that unit intact when it becomes a book — so the collection reads as a set of voices rather than as a narrated whole, and the register stays spoken rather than literary. She holds no juried award; her standing is measured in bestseller placement and in having founded an imprint inside a Big Five house, which is a different and arguably larger achievement than a prize.

works.title: The Sex Chronicles: Shattering the Myth
works.note: published over publisher resistance; the year needs verification

entries.name: Sylvia Day
entries.description: Trauma-keyed desire, with the sexual scene used as a diagnostic rather than as a reward.
entries.meta: American, born 1973; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against dated items on her own site. She has published under two further personal names, so the practice is a portable multi-name estate rather than a single byline.
entries.knownFor: The 2012 sequence most often used to date the trade erotic-romance boom that followed the previous year's breakout, with over twenty million copies in print across the series.
entries.signature: Trauma-keyed desire, with the sexual scene used as a diagnostic. Two damaged first-person histories are put into a relationship where every explicit passage reveals something about what happened earlier rather than advancing an appetite, so the scenes carry exposition that dialogue would make unbearable. It is the commercial form's most-copied solution to the repetition problem, and it works because each encounter is answering a different question. Award claims associated with the romance trade bodies should not be carded against her without a specific category and year.

entries.name: Tiffany Reisz
entries.description: Consequence as the engine, and explicit material carried by a mass-market romance house rather than an erotica imprint.
entries.meta: American, from Owensboro in Kentucky, born 1978 by report rather than by a sourced date; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated local-press feature of August 2025 — a status this pack earlier carried as unconfirmed, now resolved. **This card previously read that she publishes under her legal name, and that was wrong.** The erotica appears under her maiden name and, from 2023, her mainstream fiction appears under a separate pen name, so she runs two bylines rather than declining the convention — and searching only the erotica name is exactly why this pack could not confirm her the first time.
entries.knownFor: A literary-register series issued by a mass-market romance imprint, which put explicit material into general trade distribution without an erotica label on it.
entries.signature: Consequence as the engine. Her own formulation is that it is not erotica until somebody gets hurt, and the books are built so that every sexual choice incurs a cost that persists into later volumes — which is one of the three non-finite engines this pack identifies as an alternative to escalation, worked out in a commercial series rather than in a literary one. Publishing under a legal name and inside a romance house are the same decision twice: she declines both of the field's usual forms of cover.

entries.name: Chuck Tingle
entries.description: The clearest character persona in the pack, and one that survived crossing into trade publishing intact.
entries.meta: Legal identity undisclosed and deliberately so, with life dates unresolved and none assigned, because they are unknowable while the persona holds; and the byline is confirmed active by a dated 2025 interview. The pseudonym is a fictional character who claims to be the author, which is the defining test, and the fiction of authorship is inseparable from the work.
entries.knownFor: Absurdist short-form erotica sold direct on digital platforms, and later straight-faced horror novels published under the same persona by a trade house.
entries.signature: The title as the entire premise, with sincerity as the joke's delivery system. The unit of invention is a title-length high concept, so the reader knows the whole idea before opening the file and the text's job is to execute it without winking. That earnestness is what separates the work from parody and is why the persona survived the move into trade horror publishing unchanged. The one real award credit in this block is a trap in itself: a 2016 Hugo nomination, not a win, and the nomination's own circumstances are part of the story.

works.title: Space Raptor Butt Invasion
works.note: nominated for a Hugo Award for best short story that year, and not a winner

works.title: Slammed in the Butt by My Hugo Nomination

entries.name: Stjepan Sejic
entries.description: Retrospective narration over present-tense art, and the free webcomic that became a trade series.
entries.meta: Croatian, born 1981; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against his own first-person statements in trade coverage of March and May 2026. The December 2025 item this card previously cited was a reissue announcement, and a publishing announcement is the one kind of trade item that keeps appearing after a creator has died, so it was the wrong evidence for a right verdict. He publishes print work under his legal name; the serial first appeared under an art-platform handle, which is the same handle-to-byline pattern the block's prose writers show.
entries.knownFor: A long-form romance comic about a negotiated relationship that went from free webcomic to collected trade volumes, and is the most-cited example of explicit comics work reaching a general readership.
entries.signature: Retrospective narration over present-tense art. A future-voice caption track runs above scenes drawn in the present, so the reader is told how the relationship turns out while watching it begin — which removes suspense about the outcome and relocates all the tension into how the participants get there. It also makes the awkwardness comic rather than painful, because the narrator has survived it. No award exists: the comics award apparatus has no erotica category, so the absence is structural rather than a judgement.

works.title: Sunstone
works.note: first appeared as a free webcomic; collected print volumes followed from 2014

works.title: Harleen

entries.name: Charlotte Roche
entries.description: The body written as material rather than as image, four years before the Anglophone commercial breakout.
entries.meta: British-born, German-resident and German-writing, born 18 March 1978 at High Wycombe; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated item of March 2025 and nothing later, which makes it one of the two thinnest confirmations in this pack. She was already a public television personality when the novel appeared, so it was published into an existing public identity rather than creating one.
entries.knownFor: A German-language succes de scandale of February 2008 that put explicit first-person bodily writing onto international bestseller lists, and reached English in 2009 in translation.
entries.signature: The body written as material rather than as image. The method is a relentless and unembarrassed first-person catalogue of bodily fact — secretions, wounds, procedures — with the erotic and the medical kept in one register and no signal telling the reader which is which. It is the strongest modern instance of the estrangement technique this pack cards, and it demonstrates the cost as well as the effect: sustained self-inspection converts an erotic register into a clinical one, and the book is arguing about whether that conversion is a loss. No erotica award exists in her language or in English for the book to have won.

works.note: card the German year; the English translation is 2009 and is inadmissible

entries.name: Portia da Costa
entries.description: The through-line of the imprint that defined British women's erotica, across its whole life.
entries.meta: British, living in West Yorkshire, life dates unresolved — the birth year of 1952 this card previously carried could be sourced to nothing at the re-check and has been withdrawn. Living status carried as unconfirmed: the pre-release re-check of September 2026 found no death record and no dated activity since February 2022. A personal pen name and at least two others, portable across a mass-market imprint, a romance house, a digital-first line and self-published novellas, writing from about 1990 and published from 1994; her own two pages disagree over the starting year, which is why this card no longer states one.
entries.knownFor: Carrying the best-known British erotica imprint from its 1993 founding through its 2012 relaunch, for which she wrote the lead title.
entries.signature: The domestic English erotic novel — desire staged in ordinary settings and mediated by class and manners. Her books put explicit material into recognisably mundane English surroundings and let the constraint come from what people will and will not say to each other, which is a different engine from the institutional and transactional ones the American commercial line runs on. She is also the pack's best evidence for what an imprint actually is: a house style transmitted by one writer across two decades and three ownership changes.

entries.name: Rachel Kramer Bussel
entries.description: The single-constraint themed anthology, and the editor most contemporary short erotic fiction reaches print through.
entries.meta: American, born 1975; living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026 against a dated 2025 interview. She works as editor, journalist and author of explicit fiction under one legal name, which is professionally significant in a field where separating those functions by pseudonym is the norm.
entries.knownFor: Editing dozens of themed erotica collections, principally through one press, and thereby being the route by which a large share of contemporary short erotic fiction reaches print at all.
entries.signature: The single-constraint themed anthology. Her method is to set one narrow formal or situational constraint and commission against it, so the volume's interest is the range of solutions rather than the theme itself — which is the anthology equivalent of the constraint-first construction this pack cards on the literary side, arrived at editorially. It is also the mechanism by which new writers enter the form, since a narrow brief is answerable by somebody with one good idea and no publication record.

entries.name: Ars Amatoria
entries.text: A didactic poem in elegiac couplets that adopts the form of a technical manual and uses it for social comedy, so the instructional voice is a fiction rather than the poet's own. Its third book addresses women and systematically undoes the advice of the first two, which is a manual turning on itself and has no equivalent in the period. Two dating conventions circulate — around 1 BCE and around 2 CE for the first books — and neither has displaced the other, so a reference should give the range. Its author connected his own relegation to it, which makes it the first recorded case in the Western line of an erotic text costing a career.

entries.author: Ovid
entries.awards: No award, and none was possible. The relegation of 8 CE is a punishment and is sometimes reported in secondary writing as though it conferred a distinction; it did not, and the poem carries no honour of any kind.

entries.name: Carmina
entries.text: A transmitted collection in which a poem of extreme metrical polish sits beside one of deliberate coarseness, at the same register level and by design. That juxtaposition is the technique: the obscenity is the lyric's structural partner rather than a lapse from it, and controlling the distance between the two registers is the answer to the diction problem the whole tradition inherits. Whether the poet arranged the collection himself or it was assembled after his death is a live editorial question and is not settled here. The beloved is pseudonymous inside the work, which is a persona applied to a subject rather than an author.
entries.description: A transmitted collection in which a poem of extreme metrical polish sits beside one of deliberate coarseness, at the same register level and by design…
entries.author: Catullus
entries.awards: No award; none existed. The corpus's survival through a single medieval manuscript is a bibliographic fact routinely dressed up as a distinction, and it is neither.

entries.name: Epigrammata
entries.text: Twelve books of short poems in which the obscene punchline is a structural device rather than a flourish: the whole architecture of a piece exists to land one word in its final position. The compression is the lesson, and it is the opposite technique to the sustained erotic description that later traditions default to. The books were issued across roughly two decades and their individual dates are conventional rather than documentary. The collection is also the ancient tradition's clearest evidence that obscenity and social observation were a single literary mode rather than two.

entries.author: Martial
entries.awards: No award; none existed in the period. Imperial patronage is not a prize and should not be carded as one.

entries.name: Ode to Aphrodite
entries.text: The only poem of its author's to survive complete, out of an estimated ten thousand lines of which roughly six hundred and fifty remain. Its erotic method is the symptom catalogue: desire rendered as a sequence of discrete bodily failures reported in order, so the reader infers the emotion from the inventory rather than being told it. That is a description of the autonomic nervous system rather than of an act, which is the harder and more durable move and the ancestor of every physiological register the modern form uses. The date is a convention rather than evidence, and the number of books in the ancient critical edition is disputed.

entries.author: Sappho
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Modern inclusion in canonical anthologies is editorial selection rather than an honour.

entries.name: Satyricon
entries.text: The earliest surviving European prose fiction in which sexual incident is narrated in a low comic register by a first-person narrator who is himself the joke. Its narrator reports his own humiliations without recognising them as such, and the reader's pleasure lives in that gap — which makes the book a sustained treatment of sexual failure as a subject, the hardest thing for the later form to do. It survives in fragments, and the conventional claim that these come from three books of a much longer original could not be confirmed for this pack. Its episodic structure, in which encounters could be reordered without loss, is the shape the whole tradition inherits.

entries.author: Petronius
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its standing rests on survival and on scholarship, neither of which is an honour conferred on the work.

entries.name: The Golden Ass
entries.text: A picaresque of transformation in which the protagonist's change of species strips him of standing and thereby lets him see everyone else's, which is the joke the device was invented for. Sexual material arrives inside comedy and inside a religious frame at once, and the ending imports a conversion that the preceding episodes do not require — an early and very visible instance of a terminus attached from outside. The dating was not independently verified for this pack. It is also the tradition's model for the licensed interval, in which festival or transformation suspends the ordinary rules for a bounded time.

entries.author: Apuleius
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its author's acquittal on a charge of magic is a legal outcome and is not a literary distinction.

entries.name: Kama Sutra
entries.text: The foundational Sanskrit treatise on kama, of which the sexual-technique material is one part of a much larger work on social conduct — courtship, marriage, household and the professional classes. Its method is exhaustive classification in a condensed aphoristic form that requires a commentary to be usable, and what a writer takes from it is the demonstration that enumeration is itself a rhetorical mode with an erotic effect. Its framework treats sexual conduct as a legitimate field of systematic knowledge rather than as transgression, which is the single most important structural contrast with the Western line. The date rests on internal evidence about which dynasties it names, and a much wider scholarly range remains in circulation.

entries.author: Vatsyayana
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Nineteenth-century European translation prizes attach to translators and their editions, never to the Sanskrit text.

entries.name: Al-Rawd al-Atir
entries.text: A manual compiled at the request of a named ruler, which is a firmer dating anchor than the bare century usually printed, and written inside a religious framework that treated pleasure as licit within marriage. It justifies itself religiously and structurally before it instructs, which is the earliest clean instance in the tradition of the apparatus of permission that erotic writing has used to reach print in every period since. Its European transmission is a case study in translation as distortion: it reached English through a French version rather than the Arabic, and one chapter was omitted from both without disclosure. Translations made directly from the Arabic did not appear until the second half of the twentieth century.

entries.author: al-Nafzawi
entries.awards: No award; none existed. A nineteenth-century English version's association with a famous translator is a publishing fact and confers nothing on the text.

entries.name: Nuzhat al-Albab
entries.text: An encyclopaedic compilation in the Arabic erotological tradition, organised by category and type rather than by narrative, and unusually direct about same-sex material at a period when the European record has almost none. Its method is anthology as authorship: the compiler's contribution is selection, arrangement and commentary rather than composition, which is a form of making the modern anthology tradition inherits without acknowledging its ancestry. The dating is conventional. It is carded here partly to prevent the tradition being read as a single work, since the best known Arabic title is one of several.

entries.author: al-Tifashi
entries.awards: No award; none existed for the original. A 1989 Lambda Literary Award attaches to a twentieth-century English translation and its translator, and carding it against the thirteenth-century text is the exact misattribution this line prevents.

entries.name: Kōshoku Ichidai Otoko
entries.text: The founding work of floating-world prose, written for and about an urban merchant class and sold in a functioning commercial book trade seventy years before the first English erotic novel. Its structure is an accounting ledger: encounters are enumerated with running totals, so a life is measured in incidents, and the arithmetic supplies the terminus the sexual material cannot supply itself. Each entry is a different social situation rather than a different act, which is the distinction most later catalogues miss. It developed with no obscenity-law antagonist of the European kind, which is why any account treating legal antagonism as a necessary condition of the form is wrong on the evidence.

entries.author: Ihara Saikaku
entries.awards: No award; none existed in the period. Its status as the founding work of a genre is a scholarly judgement and not an honour.

entries.name: Kōshoku Ichidai Onna
entries.text: A catalogue bounded by a confession frame, in which an elderly narrator recounts a descent through the licensed quarter's grades one at a time. The structure is an occupational ladder rather than a moral one, which makes it the earliest workplace novel in the tradition, and the frame supplies a moral weather the episodes do not have on their own. Because the account is told as confession, every episode arrives pre-judged, and the gap between the telling voice and the recounted self is the book's engine. It is the clearest pre-modern demonstration that a frame installed at the start rather than the end is what allows a catalogue to close.

entries.author: Ihara Saikaku
entries.awards: No award; none existed in the period.

entries.name: Nanshoku Ōkagami
entries.text: A collection in two halves, one drawn from the samurai class and one from the townsmen, which crosses rank in opposite directions and lets the two be read against each other. That comparison is the clearest historical evidence in the pack that a status gradient's erotic meaning is local to its society rather than universal. Its existence in a commercial market with no legal antagonist is the second finding: a large body of male-male erotic prose was published openly and profitably at a date when the European equivalent was clandestine or nonexistent. The collection is carded for the structure rather than for the content it is usually cited for.

entries.author: Ihara Saikaku
entries.awards: No award; none existed in the period.

entries.name: Jin Ping Mei
entries.text: A domestic novel of a merchant household in which the sexual material is inseparable from the accounting — property, marriage settlements, servants, debts — and the satire lives in the distance between what is common knowledge and what is formally unmentioned. Its architecture does the plotting: a household full of listeners at doors means every arrangement is eventually found out, and the finding out is structural rather than incidental. The authorship is unknown and the attributions on the record are traditional rather than evidenced. It is the tradition's fullest demonstration that an open secret is the domestic form of a power gradient.

entries.author: Anonymous
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its place in later canonical lists of Chinese fiction is a modern scholarly designation and not a prize.

entries.name: Rou Putuan
entries.text: An erotic novel with a retribution architecture attached structurally rather than decoratively: the episodes are made to serve a doctrinal scheme, so the ending is supplied by doctrine rather than earned by narrative. That is this pack's imported-ending mechanism appearing in a non-Western tradition with a non-romance import, and the comparison is the whole reason the book is carded. Its protagonist is nominally in command of every arrangement and materially at the mercy of all of them, which is the comic version of the dependent superior and the oldest. Written in 1657 and published in 1693, with the attribution recorded as disputed rather than settled.

entries.author: Li Yu
entries.awards: No award; none existed. The attribution itself is disputed, so any honour attached to the author would in any case be attached to a contested name.

entries.name: Ragionamenti
entries.text: Dialogues in which the sexual material is delivered as shop talk between women who work, with the economics visible and the instruction passed downward, so the content has a speaker, a purpose and an addressee and therefore a shape. The form is a prose dialogue and this pack cards it as a novel under protest, because the twelve-value medium list has no term for the dialogue and the pack declines to mint one. The first part appeared in 1534 and the second in 1536. Its author is the first European writer to make erotic publication a commercial and political instrument, and the dialogues are where that programme is most legible.

entries.author: Pietro Aretino
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Placement on the Index in 1559 is a condemnation and is occasionally reported as though notoriety were a distinction; it is not.

entries.name: The Decameron
entries.text: A hundred tales inside a frame that supplies an occasion, a duration and a dispersal, none of which any individual tale has to earn — which makes it the tradition's model for the frame as an ending machine, and the most transferable device in this pack. Its exchanges are of favours, secrets and standing rather than of money, and the tales are precise about the rate. It also already contains the elision, the moral gloss and the servant who out-manoeuvres a master, several centuries before any of the statutes this pack describes, which is the limit of the claim that obscenity law created these conventions.

entries.author: Giovanni Boccaccio
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its canonical standing is a matter of reception rather than of any honour conferred.

entries.name: L'École des filles
entries.text: The founding French instruction dialogue, in which an experienced cousin instructs an inexperienced one and the knowledge gap is the engine — it supplies a reason for exposition, a built-in reader surrogate and a natural escalation ladder in one device. Every later work in the libertine line is a variation on that machine. It was published anonymously and the attribution names two men without settling between them, which is the ordinary condition of this canon rather than an exception. Carded as a novel because the pack's medium list has no term for the prose dialogue.

entries.author: Michel Millot, with Jean L'Ange
entries.awards: No award; none existed. The 1655 prosecution of its publisher is a criminal proceeding and is not a distinction.

entries.name: Satyra Sotadica
entries.text: The seventeenth century's most influential Latin erotic dialogue, and the conduit by which the Aretine form reached the eighteenth. Writing obscenity in humanist Latin restricts the audience, signals status and supplies a rhetorical armature at once, so the erudition is not a disguise over the content but the thing that makes it sayable — the strongest single case in the pack that register is a permission technology. Its attribution frame is doubled and fabricated: the work claims to be by a real historical poet and translated by a real humanist professor, and both are inventions. That is a persona applied to living or historical third parties without consent, which is a different act from inventing one.

entries.author: Nicolas Chorier
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: Vénus dans le cloître
entries.text: The convent dialogue that carried the Aretine form into a specifically institutional setting, where enclosure supplies confinement, hierarchy, a vow to violate and a devotional vocabulary available for reuse — four things the form otherwise has to manufacture. It is the origin of the institution-as-pressure-vessel move that modern erotica still runs in workplaces, ships and monasteries. Its English translation of 1724 produced the prosecution generally described as the first obscenity conviction in England, a ruling that selling such material was a misdemeanour, and a sentence of a fine and an hour in the pillory. The author is unknown and two candidates are on the record without either being settled.

entries.author: Abbé du Prat (attributed)
entries.awards: No award; none existed. The 1727 King's Bench proceeding against its English publisher is a conviction, and the same trap runs in the opposite direction to a prize.

entries.name: Les Égarements du coeur et de l'esprit
entries.text: The psychological libertine novel in its founding form, in which seduction is rendered as a social and conversational process rather than as physical incident. Its characteristic move is the ellipsis at the moment of consummation: the dialogue runs up to the act and breaks off, so the erotic charge lives entirely in the negotiation and the tension improves under withholding. For a pack whose central problem is that explicit sequence has no native terminus, this is the counter-case. Issued across 1736 to 1738 and left incomplete, so a single year misrepresents it.

entries.author: Crébillon fils
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: Histoire de Dom Bougre, Portier des Chartreux
entries.text: The century's most durable anticlerical libertine novel, organised as a first-person working life inside an institution so that the episodes acquire a professional progression rather than remaining a sequence. That is the same structural answer the Japanese catalogue reaches by arithmetic, arrived at instead by a career ladder. It is also the clearest case in the canon of erotic writing whose sexual content is the vehicle for a political argument, which inverts this pack's own boundary rule and is worth carding as the boundary's hardest case. Published anonymously; the attribution is standard and remains an attribution.

entries.author: Jean-Charles Gervaise de Latouche (attributed)
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: La Nuit et le moment
entries.text: A single conversation conducted in one room across one night, in which the entire erotic event is the talk that surrounds it. The constraint is the achievement: with no change of scene and no narration, everything must be established, negotiated and revised in speech, which makes it the eighteenth century's clearest demonstration that dialogue alone can carry an erotic structure. Carded as a novel because the pack's medium list has no term for the prose dialogue, and the strain is declared rather than hidden. It should be read against the same author's earlier book, where the ellipsis does the work that here is done by continuous talk.

entries.author: Crébillon fils
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure
entries.text: An entire long book of erotic prose written without the Anglo-Saxon vocabulary, substituting an extended and internally consistent figurative register. The choice has measurable costs: the euphemism buys legality and elevation and pays in monotony, since the same metaphor family deployed dozens of times produces exactly the repetition failure the form is prone to. It is a solved problem that created the next problem, and that is how it should be read. Issued in two volumes in November 1748 and February 1749; its author and publisher were arrested the following November and the book was withdrawn after he renounced it in court.

entries.author: John Cleland
entries.awards: No award; none existed. A 1966 United States Supreme Court decision concerning the book is a court ruling and not a prize, and it is routinely described as a landmark, which in careless metadata becomes an honour.

entries.name: Thérèse Philosophe
entries.text: The purest instance in the canon of erotica as a delivery system for a proposition: the materialist argument is not a frame around the sexual content, the sexual content is the demonstration of it. That makes it a better teaching case than its more famous successor, because the technique arrives without the content problem attached. It is the direct ancestor of the philosophical libertine method that dominates the end of the century. Published anonymously, with the attribution unsettled and a much longer transmitted title also in circulation; the pack cards the attribution rather than asserting the man.

entries.author: Boyer d'Argens (attributed)
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: Les Bijoux indiscrets
entries.text: A conceit that compels sexual truth-telling from parties who would not otherwise speak, converting an unstructured subject into a sequence of depositions — a genuine formal solution to the ending problem, because a testimony sequence ends when the testimonies run out. That is an imported terminus of a distinct kind, alongside the doctrinal and the marital ones carded elsewhere in this pack. The satire is about what testimony is worth when nobody can be held to it. Published anonymously, early and for money, before the work its author is otherwise known for.

entries.author: Denis Diderot
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its author's later reputation attaches to the encyclopaedia and confers nothing retrospectively on this book.

entries.name: Manon Lescaut
entries.text: A transaction the participants refuse to name while the reader counts. The price is unspoken between the lovers and explicit everywhere else in the book, and the gap between those two registers is where the tragedy is generated rather than in any event. Its go-between insists throughout on being outside an arrangement he is inside, which is the broker's characteristic move and the reason the figure recurs. Carded here for the economics rather than for the romance, because the accounting is what the erotic material is actually made of.

entries.author: Abbé Prévost
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its suppression in France shortly after publication is a censorship action and is not a distinction.

entries.name: Point de lendemain
entries.text: A single night, a single encounter, and an ending that refuses to be a consequence — the most compressed demonstration in the canon that an erotic narrative can be complete without accumulating anything. Its economy is the lesson: the whole apparatus of the libertine novel is executed in a few thousand words, which shows how much of that apparatus was length rather than structure. It exists in two authorial versions and the differences between them are a teaching case in their own right. It is the canon's strongest argument that the short form is not a reduced novel but a different machine.

entries.author: Vivant Denon
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: Justine
entries.text: A demonstration wager rather than a story: two sisters, opposite principles, and a proposition to be proved by outcome. Reading it as a bet explains why the ending has to be arbitrary, and why the punishment falls where it does. Its punishments are argued as well as staged, and the interleaving is the structural lesson — a discipline scene without a stated rationale is choreography, and the rationale is what the reader is made to hold. Published anonymously, like almost all of its author's libertine work; the respectable work he signed, and the signature proved legally costly.

entries.author: Marquis de Sade
entries.awards: No award; none existed. A modern French prize bearing its author's name was founded in 2001 by other people and is not his, and it confers nothing on the eighteenth-century books.

entries.name: La Philosophie dans le boudoir
entries.text: The libertine philosophical mode at its most explicit about its own procedure: a proposition is stated, enacted, and then discussed by the participants, and the discussion is the point rather than an interruption. It shows what the instruction dialogue is structurally for by pushing it past its use, until the pedagogic frame is carrying a thesis it was never built to carry. It is written in speech prefixes and was never intended for performance, so this pack cards it as a novel rather than as a stage work — assigning it to the stage would assert a performance history that does not exist. Published anonymously in 1795.

entries.author: Marquis de Sade
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: Histoire de Juliette
entries.text: The companion demonstration to its author's earlier novel, in which the sister who prospers is the one who abandons the principle the other keeps — so the design is an argument against consequence as a narrative law rather than a story with an outcome. Its tableaux exist to be witnessed by a character with no option to leave, and the compelled watcher is how the philosophy gets stated inside the scene rather than beside it. The run is given as 1797 to 1799 and also as 1797 to 1801, and neither dating was settled for this pack. It reached a courtroom in Japan in 1969 in a language its author never wrote in, with the case turning on the translation rather than on the work.

entries.author: Marquis de Sade
entries.awards: No award; none existed. Its twentieth-century prosecutions in several jurisdictions are convictions rather than distinctions, and the same trap runs in both directions.

entries.name: Les Crimes de l'amour
entries.text: The one book of its author's libertine years published under his own name, and the signature had legal consequences — which makes the contrast with his anonymous work the eighteenth-century original of this pack's entire pen-name argument. Formally it is the outlier in his output: short pieces with conventional moral framing, written to be publishable, and therefore the clearest available measure of what the anonymous books were doing differently. The stories are worth reading against the novels as a controlled comparison rather than on their own. A prefatory essay on the novel accompanies them and is a serious piece of criticism.

entries.author: Marquis de Sade
entries.awards: No award; none existed.

entries.name: L'Anti-Justine
entries.text: A book written explicitly against another book — an attempt to prove that the explicit register can carry pleasure without cruelty — which makes it the only clear pre-1900 instance of erotic writing conducted as an argument with another erotic writer. That practice is entirely live now in the response, the corrective and the reclamation, and it has no other example in this canon. Its author set much of his own work in type himself, so author and compositor are one person and the book is a made object in a stronger sense than its neighbours. The year is contested between 1793 and 1798 and it appeared pseudonymously.
